3.1 Flexible component 
Recommendation: 
3.1.1 The Committee is of the view that the National Ayush Mission's (NAM) initiatives like 
Health and Wellness Centres (HWCs/Arogya Mandirs) and co-location of Ayush facilities with 
Primary Health Centres (PHCs) and Community Health Centres (CHCs) represent a unique 
opportunity to strengthen clinical evidence and promote research and development (R&D) in 
Ayush systems. Standardised electronic medical records in HWCs and co-located Ayush facilities 
can systematically capture patient data on diagnoses, treatments, and outcomes, enabling large-
scale epidemiological studies and comparative effectiveness research. HWCs and co-located 
facilities can build trust with communities, facilitating long-term monitoring of patients and 
providing valuable insights into the chronic disease management potential of Ayush therapies. 
(Para 2.4 of the Report) 
Recommendation: 
3.1.2 The Committee believes that standardized data collection can pave the way for identifying 
biomarkers associated with specific Ayush interventions, opening doors for further research into 
mechanisms of action and personalized medicine. 
(Para 2.5 of the Report) 
3.1.3 The Committee recommends the following measures to develop clinical Research 
Infrastructure: 
 Strengthening manpower and training: Upgrading infrastructure and providing 
training opportunities for Ayush practitioners at HWCs can enhance their research 
skills and capacity to participate in clinical trials. 
 Establishing research networks: Collaboration among Ayush facilities and institutions 
can facilitate multicentric clinical trials and improve research quality. 
 Standardization of protocols and interventions: Developing standardized protocols for 
Ayush interventions can ensure data consistency and enable robust clinical research. 
 Community Engagement: Engaging communities in research design and 
implementation through Ayush facilities can address their specific needs and ensure 
culturally relevant research outcomes. 

12 
 
 Evidence Recording: Data gathered and generated in centres should be recorded and 
publicized. The clinically supported research and peer-reviewed articles should be 
placed in Ayush and allopathic medical colleges for better outreach, understanding, 
and coordination. 
(Para 2.6 of the Report) 
Action Taken: 
3.1.4 Research and Development in Ayush is mandate of Research Councils, autonomous 
organizations of Ministry of Ayush. Further, however, during different Regional Review 
Meetings under National Ayush Mission, autonomous organizations under Ministry of Ayush 
like Research Councils& their peripheral institutes and National Institutes have been asked to 
provide their active support for the effective implementation ongoing activities/programmes of 
the National Ayush Mission (NAM) in the States/UTs especially for capacity building and 
training of State Programme Management Unit (SPMU)/ Community Health Officer (CHO), 
Telemedicine- hub and spoke model, Ayush Public Health Programmes etc. 
3.1.5 Further, State/UT Governments are furnishing beneficiaries data on monthly basis who 
have availed the services in the different Ayush facilities. Furthermore, 10,000 Geriatric Health 
Camps have been planned to organize from 15th June, 2024 to 15th September, 2024 through 
AyushmanArogyaMandir (Ayush) in States/UTs. In this regard, the Ministry of Ayush has 
developed standardized protocols for the said camp and shared with States/UTs for organizing 
Geriatric Health Camps uniformly. State/UT Governments have been requested to furnish the 
beneficiaries’ data to Ministry of Ayush. 
3.1.6 Standardization of protocols and interventions: Ayush vertical in DGHS has taken the 
initiative to publish the series of Standard Treatment Guidelines (STGs) in different Ayush 
systems of medicine for the benefit of practitioners in the field. In this regard the STGs on 
Musculoskeletal disorders were released on 10thApril, 2024. National level modular training for 
master trainers from the States/UTs was also conducted for orientation in these STGs. 
Further Recommendation: 
3.1.7 The Committee would like the Ministry to address the aspect like strengthening 
manpower and training, establishing research networks and enhancing community 
engagement as well and furnish a complete action taken note. 
3.2 Quality Control of Ayush Drugs 
Recommendation: 
3.2.1 The Committee understands that the quality of the medicines is essential as concerns have 
been raised over the high metal contents in the Ayush drugs, which damage people's health. In 
this regard, the Committee acknowledges the measures taken by the Ministry in 

13 
 
pharmacovigilance of the Ayush drugs. To accentuate these measures, the Committee 
recommends that the Ministry further strengthen regulatory frameworks by developing user-
friendly systems for healthcare professionals and consumers to report adverse events related to 
Ayush medicines. The Ministry should also conduct regular post-marketing surveillance of Ayush 
medicines to monitor real-world safety and efficacy. This provides ongoing data for continuous 
improvement of quality. The data generated may also help identify potential safety concerns and 
take prompt action. 
(Para 3.3 of the Report) 
3.2.2 The Ministry may explore collaborating with the World Health Organization (WHO) and 
the International Organisation for Standardisation (ISO) to harmonise Ayush quality standards 
with international norms. This may facilitate global trade and recognition of Ayush products. The 
Ministry should also sign Mutual Recognition Agreements (MRAs) with other countries for 
regulatory compliance. The Committee is of the view that these steps may reduce duplicate 
testing and certification procedures, resulting in ease of the export and import of Ayush products. 
(Para 3.4 of the Report) 
Action Taken: 
3.2.3 Drug Policy Section :  Ministry of Ayush requested to National Pharmacovigilance 
Coordination Centre to provide details regarding below mentioned points (vide letter no. T-
11012/03/2019DCC (AYUSH) dated 23rd April 2024).  
 
i. To publish a review article/booklet on all reported ADR and Herb-Drug interaction.  
ii. Report the therapeutic claims made by botanical products licensed under FSSAI in 
print/electronic media.  
iii. Report on product Licensed under FSSAI that covered under definition of 3a, 3h section 
of chapter IV-A of Drug and Cosmetics Act-1945. 
iv. To ensure reporting of all violation as mentioned under advisory no J11019/01/2017-DCC 
(AYUSH) dated 18-04-2024 issued by Ministry of Ayush. 
 
3.2.4 Drug Policy Section: Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS), the National Standards body of 
India has submitted a proposal to International Organization for Standardization (ISO) for 
creation of a dedicated technical Committee for Ayurveda and Yoga. As per ISO directives, the 
proposal has completed two stages of review  
• Four-week internal review  
• Four-week review with relevant groups (TMB, SPCG, IEC, SAGs and CCs).  
The proposal has been revised in response to feedback received during the both the stages of 
review and is now resubmitted to the ISO Central Secretariat. It is expected that, the proposal will 
soon undergo balloting among ISO member countries for a duration of 12 weeks. 

14 
 
3.2.5 IC Section: Ministry of Ayush has already collaborating with WHO on various 
projects/activities for the promotion of Ayush or Indian Traditional system of medicine globally 
i.e. establishment of WHO GTMC, in Jamnagar (India); Project Collaboration Agreements 
signed with WHO for developing Benchmarks Documents for Ayush, WHO terminology 
documents for Ayush etc.; Donor Agreement towards the implementation of developing a Second 
Module in the Traditional Medicine (TM) Chapter of the International Classification of Diseases 
-11 Revision (ICD-11); developing WHO M-Yoga App. etc. BIS has collaborated with ISO for 
developing global standards for Ayush and BIS has submitted a proposal to establish an ISO 
Technical Committee (TC) dedicated to Ayurveda and Yoga to ISO which is under consideration. 
Ministry of Ayush signed country level MoUs with 23 countries for cooperation in the field of 
traditional medicine. 
Further Recommendation: 
3.2.6 The Committee is of the view that a more proactive approach should be adopted, 
rather than asking some details from NPCC, for strict quality control of Ayush drugs. The 
Committee, accordingly, reiterates its recommendation and urges upon the Government to 
furnish a detailed status note clearly mentioning about the affirmative action taken in the 
direction to further strengthen the regulatory framework where cases of adverse effects 
related to Ayush medicine can be reported.  Also, apprise the Committee of the action taken 
in the direction of conducting regular post marketing surveillance of Ayush medicines to 
monitor safety and efficacy of these drugs. 
3.3 Implementation Status of National Ayush Mission 
Recommendation: 
3.3.1 The Committee understands that the National Ayush Mission has certainly provided the 
required fillip to the traditional medicine sector of the country. The Committee notes that the 
scheme has provisioned for the establishment of Ayush hospitals, dispensaries, and Health and 
Wellness Centres across the length and breadth of the country, however, the Committeeis 
concerned to observe that more than 69% of the integrated Ayush hospitals approved under 
NAM are still either under construction or the construction has not started yet. Similarly, only 
about 65% of the sanctioned A-HWCs have been established. The Committee recommends that 
since the Ayush sector is rising gradually and there are still important milestones and targets 
yet to be achieved under NAM, the Ministry should consider extending the period of the scheme 
beyond FY24 for at least 5 more years. 
(Para 3.6 of the Report) 
 
Action Taken: 
3.3.2 Suggestion Noted.  National Ayush Mission (NAM) has been launched in 2014. NAM 
has been continued from time to time and present continuation is till 31.03.2026. The Ministry of 
Ayush has approved 167 integrated Ayush hospitals from 2014-15 to 2023-24 and the status of 

15 
 
which is - Functional-39, Construction Completed-7, Under Construction-99 and Construction 
not Started-22. Further, the Ministry of Ayush has approved 12500 Ayushman Arogya Mandir 
(Ayush) from 2019-20 to 2023-24and as reported by the State/UT Governments, 12121 units are 
functional as on date. Ministry of Ayush has sought extension from Department of Expenditure, 
Ministry of Finance for operationalization of all the remaining AAM (Ayush) functional till 
2024-25 and same has been approved by them. 
3.3.3 Regional Review Meetings (RRM) were held under chairmanship of Hon’ble Union 
Minister of Ayush to review the progress of the NAM. Various periodic review meetings were 
also conducted under the chairmanship of Secretary (Ayush) and Joint Secretary, Government of 
India. One-to-one meetings were also held to review the progress of the NAM in the Ministry of 
Ayush. Central team is also hand holding the States/UTs for smooth implementation of the NAM 
Scheme. 
Further Recommendation: 
3.3.4  One of NAM's primary components is providing Ayush Services. A decade after the 
launch of the scheme, the Committee is concerned about the slow progress in creating 
integrated AYUSH hospitals nationwide. Only 39 of the 167 approved hospitals are 
operational, which is just 23.35% of the sanctioned facilities. Hence, the Committee urges a 
more proactive and result-driven approach to accelerate the establishment of integrated 
AYUSH hospitals, given the rising demand for holistic healthcare. 
3.3.5 Further, the Committee still feels that the extension of time period of NAM for 
another  5 years would be required to achieve the set targets in a realistic and recommends 
accordingly. 
 
3.4 Challenges faced in the implementation of the National Ayush Mission 
Recommendation: 
3.4.1 The Committee observed that finalising the State Annual Action Plan (SAAP) and its 
approval process takes longer. Based on the pace of utilisation and availability of funds with the 
Ministry, funds are released in installments very late in the financial year. One of the reasons 
noticed was the large number of budget line items in the Action Plans. The Committee observes 
that reducing the budget line items in the Action Plans can improve the processing time and 
enhance administrative efficiency. Strengthening the outcome-based budgeting nudge the states 
to transform their health profile and promote cooperative federalism. The Ministry can also 
consider releasing a percentage of funds without waiting for the SAAP within the first month of 
the financial year. 
(Para 3.11 of the Report) 
Action Taken: 
3.4.2 Ministry of Ayush usually allocates resource pool to States/UTs in the month of February 
every year based on the parameters of the Scheme including the physical and financial 

16 
 
performance of the States/UTs and request them submit the proposals through SAAPs as per their 
requirements. State/UT Governmentsare required to furnish the commitment of respective State 
share with due approval of Governing Body while submitting the SAAPs to Ministry of Ayush. 
Funds are only released after fulfilling the compliance of DoE guidelines by the States/UTs. 
 
3.4.3 As per DoE guidelines received during 2024-25, funds will be released in two 
installments. In the Ministry also there are two stage approval processes as common to other 
scheme guidelines. 
 
3.4.4 So far as outcome-based budgeting is concerned, the NAM guidelines have the provision 
to calculate the resource pool based on the physical and financial performance of the States/UTs. 
Further, while approving proposals, eachaspect of the implementation status is also examined. 
Moreover, the outcome parameters of the States/UTs are also evaluated by NITI Aayog for each 
Centrally Sponsored Scheme including NAM through Output Outcome Monitoring Framework 
(OOMF) Mechanism. 
 
3.4.5 Under NAM guidelines, there is a provisionto incentivize good performing States/UTs i.e. 
performance-based budgeting has been made. For this purpose, 20% of total allocation of 
Flexipool budget may be earmarked and this fund will be allocated to good performing 
States/UTs in the same proportion in which main budget of NAM is allocated. 
Further Recommendation: 
3.4.6 The Committee recommends the Ministry to furnish the measures taken to reduce 
budget line items in the State Annual Action Plan (SAAP) to improve the processing time 
and enhance the administrative efficiency instead of narrating the extant processes 
involved.  

17 
 
CHAPTER IV 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH FINAL 
REPLIES OF THE GOVERNMENT HAVE NOT BEEN RECEIVED 
 
4.1 Flexible component 
Recommendation: 
4.1.1 The Committee notes that in its vision, NAM intends to create an enabling environment 
for research and development in Ayush through various initiatives, programs, and aspects of its 
implementation. The Committee is, therefore, of the opinion that "Promotion of Research and 
Development" should be prominently included as one of the components of NAM. Similarly, the 
flexible component, which allows 25% flexible usage of funds, should include research and 
development as a supported activity. 
(Para 2.3 of the Report) 
Action Taken: 
4.1.2 Suggestions noted. During review of NAM guidelines, the same will be incorporated.  
However, it is also informed that research and development in Ayush is mandate of Research 
Councils, Autonomous organizations of Ministry of Ayush. Further, under Ayurgyan Central 
Sector Scheme, many organizations involved in Research & Development are supported. 
Moreover, State/UT Governments may avail financial assistance for activities under flexipool 
component as per local requirement. 
4.2 Traditional Medicine Systems in India, China, South Korea and Africa 
Recommendation: 
4.2.1 The Committee notes that, like China, the Ministry of Ayush's efforts to establish 12,500 
Health and Wellness Centres (since renamed as Arogya Mandirs) go a long way in establishing 
Ayush as a medicinal system with the potential to fulfill the objectives of the universal health 
program. Like China, the Government of India should also devise ways to integrate the Ayush 
system with poverty alleviation initiatives to boost community engagement. Similarly, the 
Ministry of Ayush should collaborate with the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare to 
implement measures ensuring that the health workforce comprehends the importance of 
integrating systems. This collaboration aims to establish a pluralistic health system that caters to 
the population's diverse needs. Facilitating a dialogue among health providers from various 
systems becomes imperative for optimising patient outcomes. Substantial reforms in Indian 
medical education are essential to instill in medical students and practitioners an attitude 
supportive of the integration of modern medicine and traditional medicine. As a recommendation, 
the Committee suggests incorporating awareness of Ayush systems into school curricula, a 
significant step towards minimising knowledge barriers between Ayush and modern medicine. 

18 
 
(Para 2.22 of the Report) 
Action Taken: 
4.2.2 Under NAM guidelines, Ayurvidya programme has been made to focus special emphasis 
on school children for promotion of healthy lifestyle & integrative diet education encompassing 
dietary principles from Ayush System in vulnerable regions where health indicators are poor, to 
create awareness about medicinal plants and home remedies in lucid, attractive manner that 
captures the mind of the School children so that they inculcate positive healthy behaviour as 
described in Ayush Systems of Medicine and to educate children about the role of yoga for 
fitness and wellbeing.  
 
4.2.3 Further, Ministry of Ayush constituted an Advisory Group and Committee to develop 
educational material for students of school education and higher education, dated 22/09/2022. 
The first meeting of the Advisory Group was conducted on 13/10/2022 and it was decided to 
form four sub-groups depending on age and standard of students. In this regard, a meeting was 
conducted by NITI Ayog at its premises on 20.11.2023, where Prof. B.S. Prasad, President, 
Board of Ayurveda, National Commission for Indian System of Medicine (NCISM), participated 
in which the frameworks of topics for school education were discussed.  
 
4.2.4 To incorporate Ayush component in the school education curricula, it needs to be 
mentioned/stated in the National Curriculum Framework for School Education (NCFSF), but it is 
observed that the present NCFSF does not have such specific mention of Ayush component in its 
deliberations". However, in this regard it was emphasized that, Ministry of School Education 
should take into consideration, the recommendations/request of Ministry of Ayush, which were 
earlier also stated in its letter (D.O. letter) addressed to the Secretary, Department of School 
Education and Literacy, Ministry of Education, New Delhi in the 29th September, 2021 and letter 
on reminders were also sent on 25.05.2022, 03.08.2023 and13.12.2023 from Secretary, Ministry 
of Ayush.

PREFACE 
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Health and Family Welfare, having been authorized by the Committee to present the Report 
on its behalf, hereby present this 163rd Report of the Committee on the Demands for Grants 
(Demand No. 46) for the year 2025-26 of the Department of Health and Family Welfare, 
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. 
 
2.  The Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committees are entrusted with the 
constitutional role of ensuring accountability of executive to the Parliament.  In this regard, 
Rule 270 (a) of Rules & Procedure and Conduct & Business in the Council of States (Rajya 
Sabha) empowered the Department-related Standing Committees to consider the Demands for 
Grants of the related Departments/Ministries with the objective of ensuring financial 
accountability of the executive and report thereon. In exercise of its constitutional mandate, 
the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Health & Family Welfare 
scrutinised the Demands for Grants for the year 2025-26 (Demand No. 46) of the Department 
of Health and Family Welfare, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. The Committee at its 
sitting held for examination of Demands for Grants (2025-26) of the Department of Health 
and Family Welfare on 14th February, 2025 heard the Secretary and other Officers of the 
Department. 
 
3.  The Committee, in its meeting held on 11th March, 2025, considered the Draft Report 
and adopted the same.  
 
4.  The Committee while making its observations/recommendations has mainly relied 
upon the following documents:– 
i. Detailed Demands for Grants of the Department of Health and Family Welfare for 
the year 2025-26; 
ii. Annual Report of the Department for the year 2024-25; 
iii. Detailed Explanatory Note on Demands for Grants of the Department of Health 
and Family Welfare for the year 2025-26; 
iv. Written replies furnished by the Department to the Questionnaires sent to them by 
the Secretariat;

other concerned officers; 
vi. Economic Survey 2024-25;

viii. Global Multidimensional Poverty Index 2024; 
ix. Budget Speech of the Finance Minister; and 
x. WHO's World Health Statistics 2022 Report etc.

Committee have been printed in bold letters in the body of the Report.

CHAPTER I 
INTRODUCTION 
 
1.1.1  Health is central to well-being, influenced by cultural, socio-economic, and 
biomedical factors. India's rich public health tradition dates back to the Indus Valley 
civilization's concept of “Arogya” (holistic well-being). The Constitution of the World Health 
Organization (WHO) defined health “as a state of complete physical, mental and social well-
being, not merely the absence of disease and infirmity”. Though the notion of complete 
absence of disease is unimaginable, nevertheless in 2015, a total of 195 nations committed to 
the UN’s Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) including universal health coverage, 
financial risk protection, access to quality essential health-care services and access to safe, 
effective, quality and affordable essential medicines and vaccines for all (target 3.8 of Goal 
3).  
1.1.2  With the progression of new millennium, the concept of health has evolved 
from being an entity which was to be achieved with the advancement of healthcare 
technology, along with the Universal Coverage of Health, to be an achievement which is 
possible only when the human beings are in attune with their physical and mental 
environment. This new concept of “One Health” is an approach calling for the collaborative 
efforts of multiple disciplines integrating human, animal, and environmental health. 
1.1.3  India is undergoing a rapid health transition, encompassing demographic, 
epidemiological, nutritional, and socio-cultural changes, marking a new era in global health. 
The access to affordable and quality healthcare services is crucial for optimizing the 
productivity of human resources in National economic growth and development. The National 
Health Policy-2017 recognized the pivotal importance of UN’s SDGs and envisaged the 
attainment of the highest possible level of health and well-being for all, at all ages, as its goal. 
The Government of India has made concerted and sustained efforts to march in the direction 
of achieving universal health coverage and delivering quality health care services to all at 
affordable cost that resonate with the targets set in SDGs. With economic growth and shifting 
health needs, India is advancing policies for comprehensive healthcare.

1.5 FLAGSHIP SCHEMES 
1.5.1  Besides, some of the Flagship Schemes of the Ministry of Health and Family 
Welfare are enumerated as under: 
A. Pradhan Mantri Swasthya Suraksha Yojana (PMSSY): 
 The Pradhan Mantri Swasthya Suraksha Yojana (PMSSY) aims at correcting 
regional imbalances in the availability of affordable tertiary healthcare Services and to 
augment facilities for quality medical education in the country. The Scheme has two 
components, namely - (i) Setting up of All India Institute of Medical Sciences 
(AIIMS); and (ii) Upgradation of existing Government Medical Colleges/institutions 
(GMCIs). So far setting up of 22 new AIIMS and 75 up-gradation projects of existing 
GMCIs have been approved under the Scheme in various phases. The Up-gradation 
programme broadly envisages improving tertiary health infrastructure through 
construction of Super Speciality Blocks / Trauma Care Centres etc. and/or 
procurement of medical equipment at/for existing Government Medical Colleges / 
Institution.  
B. Central Government Health Scheme: 
 This Scheme provides comprehensive medical facilities to Central Government 
Employees, pensioners and members of their families in addition to other specified 

5 
 
categories like Members of Parliament (MPs), ex-MPs, ex-Governors, ex-Vice-
Presidents, Retired Judges of Supreme Court and High Court, Freedom Fighters and 
members of their family,etc. The facilities under this scheme include outpatient care 
through a network of allopathic, ayurvedic, homoepathic, unani/siddha 
dispensaries/units. 
C. Ayushman Bharat - Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PMJAY): 
Being the world's largest health assurance scheme, AB- PMJAY aims to 
provide health cover of Rs. 5 Lakhs per family per year for secondary and tertiary care 
hospitalization to poor and vulnerable population of the country. Initially, with 12 
crore families under the scheme, the beneficiary base has been further expanded by 
including 37 lakh ASHAs/Anganwadi Workers (AWWs)/Anganwadi Helpers 
(AWHs) and approximate 4.5 crore senior citizens across the country. 
D. Pradhan Mantri Ayushman Bharat Health Infrastructure Mission (PM- 
ABHIM):  
 
 This is a Centrally Sponsored Scheme with  some Central Sector component  
spread over 5 years from 2021-22 to 2025-26 for implementation of the Atmanirbhar 
Bharat Package for Health Sector announced by the Hon’ble Prime Minister as part of 
the series of Government measures for providing stimulus to the economy. The 
measures under the PM ABHIM focus on developing capacities of health systems and 
institutions across the continuum of care at all levels; primary, secondary and tertiary, 
to prepare health systems in responding effectively to the current and future 
pandemics/disasters 
 
E. Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM): 
 Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM) provides for creating a National 
Digital health ecosystem that supports universal health coverage in an efficient, 
accessible, inclusive, affordable, timely and safe manner through provision of a wide 
range of data, information and infrastructure services, duly leveraging open, 
interoperable, standards based digital systems and ensuring the security, 
confidentiality and privacy of health-related personal information. 
1.5.2  The Committee takes notes of the flagship schemes of the Department, 
successful implementation thereof ultimately rates the success of the Department as a 
whole. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should enhance the 
executing capacity of the implementing agency so that the absorbing capacity of the 
scheme is increased to the optimal level. This would ensure the optimum utilisation of 
the allocated funds under the schemes which would enable the Department to seek the 
budgetary allocation as per the projected demand in the ensuing financial years.

2.2.8  The Committee notes that the primary determinant for revenue and 
capital outlay in healthcare budgeting is the annual, recurring demands from program 
divisions within the Department of Health & Family Welfare, coupled with the progress 
of ongoing projects. While the social service nature of the Department inherently limits 
capital expenditure, a recent push for infrastructure upgrades is evident, with "GIA-
Capital Creation" (grants-in-aid for capital creation) playing a significant role in 
boosting effective capital spending, despite being categorized under revenue. Analyzing 
the five-year trend reveals to the Committee that revenue expenditure consistently 
dominates, averaging over 90% of the total budget. However, the effective capital 
expenditure, including GIA-Capital, shows a fluctuating pattern in the period from FY 
2021-22 to FY 2025-26, decreasing consistently since the FY 2023-24, from 27.22 % in 
2022-23 to 15.60% in 2025-26 of the total allocation. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends establishing a formalized, multi-year strategic capital expenditure plan, 
distinct from annual recurring demands, that clearly outlines infrastructure 
development priorities and targets, including specific allocations for GIA-Capital, to 
ensure sustained and predictable growth in healthcare capital assets, thereby creating a 
more balanced approach between revenue and capital spending.

2.3.3  National Health Policy (NHP), 2017 prescribed increasing Government 
Health Expenditure (GHE) as a share of GDP to 2.5% by 2025. Following the objective 
of NHP, 2017, GHE, as a share of GDP, has increased from 1.35% in 2017-18 to 1.84% 
in 2021-22, indicating progress in health sector investment. The Committee notes that 
the upward trend in GHE is positive; however, further acceleration is required to meet 
the 2.5% GDP target by 2025. The current pace of increase may not be sufficient to 
achieve this goal within the remaining timeframe. A strategic focus on public health 
infrastructure, preventive care, and efficient resource utilization will be crucial in 
ensuring long-term improvements in healthcare accessibility and quality. 
 
2.3.4  A close scrutiny of the Health Budget reflects the lack of priority assigned 
to health. The Committee observes that the declining trend in health budget allocation in 
terms of BE as % of GDP (at Current Price) between 2020-21 and 2024-25 (refer to 
Table 2.3 above) do not align with the target set in National Health Policy. The 
Committee is of the opinion that adequate health financing forms the pillar of a well-
functioning health system which is crucial for reduction of Out-of-Pocket Expenditure 
(OOPE) in health. The pandemic further reaffirmed the need of a sustainable health 
financing ecosystem especially in tackling a sudden public health crisis. The Committee 
recommends the Government to prioritize Health Sector in Budget Allocation by 
increasing the annual budget allocation for healthcare to maintain the momentum and 
ensure sufficient resources for infrastructure, medical research, and service delivery. 
 
2.3.5  The Committee, in its 126 th Report on DFG (2022-23), had also 
recommended the Government for increasing its health expenditure to 5% of GDP by 
2025. However, with such stagnant allocation to health and the slow pace of increase in 
allocation, the goal of achieving the NHP target of health expenditure to 2.5% seems a 
distant dream.  
 
2.3.6  The Committee is of the view that strengthening of public health 
infrastructure,  enhancing preventive and primary care services, leveraging Public-
Private Partnerships (PPP), exploring additional revenue sources, innovation in health, 
robust monitoring and evaluation mechanism to track the utilization of health funds and 
assess the impact are crucial for establishing an affordable and accessible healthcare 

delivery system, especially for a developing economy like India. The need of the hour is to recognize health as a key sector for economic as well as social development. 2.3.14  The Committee, in its 134th Report, had highlighted the existing wide 
inter-State and intra-State disparity in healthcare infrastructure across the country. The 
Committee observes that States with poor financial resources and inefficient fiscal 
capacity face umpteen challenges in establishing a robust health infrastructure. The

must persuade the remaining State/UT Governments to achieve the prescribed 
budgetary health expenditure to 8% of State General Government Expenditure.  
 
2.3.15  The Committee observes that the data on General Health Expenditure

significantly hampers the assessment of the progress made by various government 
schemes and policies. The Committee, therefore, recommends the Government to 
update data pertaining to GHE, THE, OOPE, etc. without delay, sooner the better.  
 
2.3.16  In today's digital age, where Information Technology and Artificial 
Intelligence play a key role, it is crucial to leverage these tools for the efficient collection 
and real-time processing of data. Therefore, the Committee recommends that the 
Government take immediate steps to integrate digital tools into the data collection 
process. Additionally, the Government should ensure that data for a given financial year 
is made available by the last quarter of the following financial year. This approach will 
rationalize data analysis, enabling more effective evaluation and improvement of 
government schemes and policies, ensuring they are aligned with the intended objectives 
and targeted effectively.

3.1.4  The Committee acknowledges the Government's efforts to digitize 
healthcare resources through the Healthcare Management Information System (HMIS), 
establish new Wellness Centres in tier-II cities, and promote Ayush Centres. However, 
the examination of budget allocation and utilization under Revenue Head reflects a 
significant gap between the RE allocation of Rs. 2245.82 crore for CGHS and the actual 
expenditure of Rs. 1842.51 crore, representing only 82% utilization as of February 7, 
2025. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department conducts a thorough 
and immediate review of the CGHS expenditure process, specifically focusing on 
identifying and addressing the bottlenecks causing the underutilization of allocated 
funds. By streamlining administrative procedures, improving procurement processes, 
and ensuring timely disbursement of funds, the Department can ensure that the 
allocated resources are effectively used to enhance healthcare services for beneficiaries, 
thereby maintaining the intended continuity between budget allocation and service 
delivery. 
3.1.5  In its 155th Report, the Committee observed that, as of August 2023, 26% 
of the 340 allopathic wellness centres (spread across 80 cities) were concentrated in the 
Delhi NCR region. Additionally, only six states (excluding Delhi NCR) have more than 
ten CGHS centres, while Arunachal Pradesh and the Union Territories of Ladakh, 
Andaman & Nicobar Islands, and Lakshadweep have none. The Committee noted that 
CGHS services are unevenly distributed, limiting accessibility in many regions. The 
Committee, therefore, wishes to highlight that numerous cities and towns with a 
significant population of Central Government employees, pensioners, and their 
dependents lack CGHS wellness centres. As a result, beneficiaries—particularly 
retirees—have to travel long distances for medical treatment, causing financial strain 
and other hardships. To address this, the Committee urges the Ministry to proactively 
advocate for new CGHS centres in underserved areas, particularly in suburban regions 
with a substantial number of serving and retired beneficiaries. The Committee 
recommends that the Ministry engage with the Ministry of Finance for speedy approval 
of new CGHS Wellness Centres. Moreover, the Committee suggests that the 
Government should consider revising existing norms or introducing new ones to

regions. 
3.1.6  The Committee notes the Government’s initiative to integrate the Indian 
system of medicine with the CGHS wellness centre network. However, in its 155th 
Report, the Committee notes that the number of Ayush centres increased from 85 in 
March 2014 to 107 in August 2023, a modest 25% growth over nine years. As of 
February 2025, this number has just risen slightly to 111. The Committee observes with 
concern that such limited slow pace of expansion does not align with the Government’s 
vision to promote indigenous healthcare to under-served regions especially in remote 
areas. The Committee, therefore, recommends the speedy operationalisation of the 
remaining 23 Ayush units out of the targeted 53 and urges the Government to establish 
additional Ayush centres nationwide while actively promoting traditional Indian 
medicine among CGHS beneficiaries. 
3.1.7  The Committee takes into account the proposal to establish a State-of-the-
Art Multi-facility Centre in Mumbai. The Committee reiterates its recommendation, as 
made in its 155th Report, for setting up at least ten CGHS hospitals with advanced 
facilities and research capabilities, particularly for critical illnesses such as cancer, 
cardiovascular diseases, and renal failure. The Committee further desires that at least 
one such advanced multi-facility centre be established in major cities across the country. 
3.1.8  In response to a specific query on strengthening of monitoring mechanism for 
quality assurance of drugs supplied through CGHS, the Ministry informed that in the bulk 
procurement of medicines in CGHS {procured by the Medical Store Organisation (MSO) of 
DGHS, MoHFW}, each batch of medicine is tested twice (by two independent CDSCO-
approved labs) before the consignment is accepted at the time of procurement. In the case of 
supply of medicines through Jan Aushadhi Pariyojana (JAP), each medicine is tested by an 
independent NABL-accredited lab before acceptance of supply by Pharmaceuticals and 
Medical Devices Bureau of India (PMBI).  
3.1.9  The Committee wishes to highlight with concerns over the quality of 
medicines dispensed at dispensary/pharmacy counters. At several time, apprehensions 
and complaints have been raised regarding the effectiveness of medicines procured 
through MSO and JAP, underscoring the critical importance of quality in healthcare 
services. Ensuring compliance with the World Health Organization’s (WHO) Good 
Manufacturing Practice (GMP) standards is essential, and any quality-related 
complaints must be addressed seriously and quickly to generate faith towards quality of 
medicines delivered at dispensary counters.  
3.1.10  The Committee takes into account the acknowledgement of the 
Department about the quality assurance of drugs, and the need for stronger quality 
assurance measures viz. implementing a systematic drug testing program at the Wellness 
Centre level. The Directorate is also considering empanelling the Quality Council of 
India for enhanced monitoring. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the 
Government establish a rigorous quality control mechanism without delay, ensuring 
systematic drug testing at the Wellness Centre level. Additionally, the Department 

23 
 
should conduct surprise audits by randomly testing medicine batches through an 
independent NABL-accredited or internationally reputed laboratory. 
3.1.11  The Ministry inter-alia informed that the following measures have been taken 
to simplify referrals and drug dispensing under CGHS: 
i) The referral process has been simplified wherein the validity of referral has been 
extended to 03 months with six consultations, and no further endorsement is needed 
for routine listed investigations/minor surgeries.  
ii) Direct Specialist Consultation has now been allowed for pensioner beneficiaries 
aged 70 and above without the need of a CGHS referral. 
iii) Restricted medicines have been clearly defined and new instructions have been 
issued for restricted medicines that pave the way for a systematic inclusion of new 
medicines for use by CGHS beneficiaries.  
iv) In case of medical emergency, no referral is required for undergoing treatment from 
CGHS empanelled Hospitals and even from non-empanelled hospitals. CGHS 
empanelled hospitals have been instructed to provide treatment on a cashless basis.  
v) In case a CGHS beneficiary is not in a position to physically visit the CGHS 
Wellness Centre, a request for referral to an empanelled hospital/endorsement may 
be submitted through an authorized representative. 
vi) In case of emergency, permission from the competent Authority for any non-listed 
investigations shall not be required. 
3.1.12  The Committee continues to recommend the Department to simplify 
referral procedures further as there is need to significantly reduce the burden on 
patients and their families by eliminating the requirement for repeated visits to 
dispensaries during illness. The Committee notes the provision made allowing CGHS 
pensioner beneficiaries aged 70 and above to directly consult specialists without 
requiring a CGHS referral, however, the Committee reiterates its recommendation 
made in the 155th Report to further review the guidelines and extend the benefit to all 
CGHS pensioners/beneficiaries aged 60 and above for continuing medical care to CGHS 
beneficiaries. Allowing direct specialist consultations at empanelled private hospitals 
without a CGHS referral would ensure consistency and continuity of care with the 
existing system, where pensioners/beneficiaries aged 60 and above already receive 
cashless treatment from these hospitals.

3.6.9  The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Health and Family 
Welfare, in collaboration with state governments, establish a standardized and 
expedited process for land acquisition and obtaining statutory clearances for AIIMS 
projects. This should include formulating clear guidelines and timelines for state 
governments regarding the provision of providing encumbrance-free land; creating a 
fast-track mechanism for obtaining environmental and other necessary clearances; and 
establishing a dedicated coordination cell to address site-related hindrances. Delays in 
land acquisition and statutory clearances are significant bottlenecks in the timely 
completion of AIIMS projects. As evident by the situations in Darbhanga, Madurai, and 
Rewari, these delays lead to cost escalations and hinder the delivery of essential 
healthcare services. 
 
3.6.10  In a reply, the following challenges have been informed by the Department 
which were faced in project implementation that resulted in delay: -  
i. Provision of encumbrance free land by the State Government;  
ii. Time taken in obtaining Statutory Clearances including Environmental Clearance;  
iii. Site related hindrance both man-made and natural including removal of HT Lines, 
IOC Pipe line passing through the land in Madurai, Natural formations like nallah 
in rock outcrops;  
iv. Timely provision of regular supply of potable water, electricity, road 
connectivity, road over-bridge due to a railway line, construction of subway to 
join two land patches across the road; 
v. Land acquisition related issues, encroachment /land disputes; 
vi. Limited availability of labour and harsh weather conditions in remote locations 
like Awantipora;  
vii. Creation of Posts for New AIIMS;  
viii. Recruitment, Shortage of Faculty, Technicians, issues in retaining faculty and 
staff in remote locations like Deogarh, Bilaspur, Raipur;  
ix. Procurement of Medical Equipment by HITES, issues relating to finalisations of 
specifications, single tenders in propriety items, delay in import of high end 
equipment; 
x. Delay in signing of MoU as in case of AIIMS Deogarh by the Jharkhand 
Government; and 
xi. Mentoring of New AIIMS on Clinical and Academic Front. 
 
3.6.11  The following measures/strategies have been taken to combat these challenges 
and for effective utilisation of funds earmarked to various institutes under PMSSY: - 
i. A Project Review Committees under the chairpersonship of Joint Secretary 
(PMSSY) has been set for each ongoing project of setting up of AIIMS. Further, 
progress of projects is reviewed regularly in the Ministry at various levels with 
the Executing Agencies and Procurement Support Agency to ensure timely 
completion of the project and supply of medical equipment. 

41 
 
ii. The Project Monitoring Group (PMG), headed by Secretary (Coordination) in the 
Cabinet Secretariat, supports all mid and large sized Public, Private and ‘Public – 
Private Partnership’ (PPP) Projects with fast-tracking of approvals, sectoral 
policy issues and removal of bottlenecks for expediting project commissioning. 
PMG helps in resolving issues in projects through regular coordination with the 
concerned State Governments and also with other Ministries of the Union 
Government. 
iii. Through Pro-Active Governance and Timely Implementation (PRAGATI) portal, 
the Prime Minister reviews the issues with all the stakeholders including Central 
Ministries/Departments and State Governments for expeditious resolution of 
various issues like land acquisition, utility shifting and other issues for timely 
completion of projects. The PRAGATI portal ensures quick and effective 
decision making for swift resolution. 
iv. In addition to the aforesaid structural institutional arrangements, the issues 
affecting progress of the projects are also taken up with the State Government 
through letters from Secretary (HFW) to the Chief Secretary of the concerned 
State Government. Need-based directions are also given to Institutes/Executive 
Agencies/PSA for expeditious resolution of the issues.  
v. Further, site visits by senior officers of the Ministry and Minister of Health and 
Family Welfare are also being undertaken to monitor the progress.  
vi. Low value medical equipment i.e costing below Rs 5 lakh as per DPR in r/o 11 
AIIMS have been de-scoped from the ambit of HITES and AIIMS to procure the 
same.

by the Prime Minister for expeditious resolution of various issues like land acquisition,

3.6.17  The Committee notes the provisons made by the Department for 
augmenting faculty and non-faculty strength in the newly set-up AIIMS viz. Standing 
Selection Committees, Centralised Nursing Officer Recruitment Common Eligiblity Test 
(NORCET), CRE, rolling advertisement for recruitment, INI-CET, INI-SS and the 
Committee hopes that measures so undertaken would yield outcome in a time-frame 
manner. The Committee urges upon the Ministry to implement comprehensive 
strategies for the recruitment and retention of faculty and staff in new AIIMS, 
particularly in remote locations. The Department should offer attractive compensation 
packages and incentives to attract and retain qualified personnel; developing robust 
mentoring programs; addressing the challenges of creating adequate living conditions 
and infrastructure in remote areas. The Committee is of the considered view that 
shortages of faculty and staff, especially in remote AIIMS, certainly impede the delivery 
of quality healthcare and medical education, therefore, addressing these human 
resource challenges is crucial for imbibing professional pursuits in new AIIMS for the 
successful functioning of these institutions.

monitoring and coordination mechanisms for PMSSY projects, including both AIIMS 
and GMC upgrades. This should involve enhancing the effectiveness of Project Review 
Committees and utilizing the PRAGATI portal for timely issue resolution; conducting 
regular site visits by senior ministry officials to monitor progress and address 
challenges; improving coordination with state governments and executing agencies to 
ensure seamless implementation. The Committee considers that effective monitoring and 
coordination are essential for ensuring the timely completion of PMSSY projects and the 
efficient utilization of funds. Strengthening these mechanisms will help mitigate delays 
and improve overall project outcomes.

initiation and retention on treatment to prevent spread of AIDS and STDs in the country. The 
key strategies/actions adopted by the Government to prevent outspread of AIDS and STDs in 
the country have been informed as under: - 
 
i. Covering of more than 1.25 crore high-risk and bridge population through 1590 
targeted interventions and 164 link worker schemes,  
ii. Management of more than one crore of persons suffering from STI/RTI through 
1127 designated STI/RTI centres,  
iii. Doing more than 6 crore HIV tests annually through 4657 confirmatory HIV 
counselling and testing centres,  
iv. Providing free, high quality, life long anti-retroviral treatment to around 1.25 
lakh HIV-infected persons every month through 794 anti-retroviral treatment 
centers, and  
v. Undertaken around 13.78 lakh viral load tests among HIV-infected persons in 
2023-24 with 97% having suppressed viral load.  
vi. Integrated STI, HIV, TB & Hepatitis (ISHTH) Campaign among inmates of 
prison and other closed settings covering 4.14 lakh inmates identifying around 
2100 HIV-positive inmates, 
vii. Integrated Health Campaigns in 73 districts (till November 2024) covering 
around 1.02 lakh persons and identifying 1650 HIV positive persons,  
viii. Index testing campaign eliciting around 17.81 lakh partners and biological 
children of HIV-positive persons and identifying 22074 HIV-positive among 
them, 
ix. Intensified IEC campaign reaching out to around 2.20 crore individuals in 1.24 
lakh villgaes, 8794 slums, 14594 colleges and 51,446 schools.  
 
3.7.5  These efforts have led to a 44% reduction in new HIV infections (2010-2023), 
79% decline in AIDS-related deaths, and improved case detection and treatment access (88% 
People living with HIV are on treatment).  
 
3.7.6  The Committee has been apprised of the following activities that can be 
undertaken to achieve the objectives of the programme: 
 
i. State-specific intensive awareness generation campaigns to improve the 
knowledge about HIV/AIDS focusing on demand generation for update of 
services, 
ii. Undertaking of integrated health campaigns among high-risk groups and bridge 
population in select districts for early identification of HIV-positive population, 
iii. Institutionalize index testing campaigns for partners and biological children of 
HIV positive persons, 
iv. Lost-to-follow up tracking campaigns for HIV-infected persons to ensure their 
continuity on treatment, and  
v. Increasing the uptake of IT-enabled SOCH MIS system of NACP to improve 
tracking of beneficiaries and services offered to them. 

47 
 
vi. Completion of round 2 of programmatic mapping and population size 
estimation to guide evidence-based programme designing for high-risk group 
populations. 
 
3.7.7  The NACP program highlights the importance of integrated health 
campaigns among high-risk and bridge populations for early HIV identification. The 
Committee recommends the Department to increase the frequency and scope of 
integrated health campaigns in select high-risk districts, focusing on early HIV detection 
and STI/RTI management; the strengthening of link worker schemes by providing 
enhanced training and resources, ensuring they can effectively reach and engage with 
high-risk populations; increase in the usage of the SOCH MIS system to better track the 
beneficiaries and services offered to them; and to complete and utilize the data from the 
round 2 of programmatic mapping and population size estimation to refine targeted 
interventions. 
 
3.7.8  The Committee highlights that NACP emphasizes index testing campaigns 
for partners and biological children of HIV-positive persons and Lost-to-follow-up 
tracking campaigns are crucial to ensure continuity of treatment. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends the Department for institutionalizing and expanding index 
testing campaigns, providing incentives and support to HIV-positive individuals to 
encourage partner notification. A robust, technology-driven lost-to-follow-up tracking 
system, utilizing mobile technology and community health workers to reconnect 
individuals with treatment services should be implemented to achieve the objective of 
the Programme.   
 
3.7.9   The Committee takes into consideration the Intensify and Tailor IEC 
Campaigns and Community Engagement to Reduce Stigma and Discrimination and 
Increase Service Uptake. NACP recognizes the importance of 360-degree multimedia 
campaigns and community outreach with reducing stigma and discrimination as a key 
objective. The Committee, therefore, recommends developing culturally sensitive IEC 
campaigns that address local stigma and misconceptions about HIV/AIDS; expanding 
community engagement through partnerships with local NGOs, community leaders, and 
faith-based organizations; and providing targeted training and sensitization programs 
for key stakeholders, including Self-Help Groups, Anganwadi workers, ASHAs, etc. to 
promote understanding and reduce stigma.

Family Welfare Schemes which are crucial for attaining the goals and objectives laid out in 
National Health Policy 2017, and international commitments in the form of Sustainable 
Development Goals.  
 
i. Swastha Nagrik Abhiyan (SNA): Aims to improve health-seeking behavior 
through awareness and service uptake. Health surveys and research, along with 
Population Research Centers, monitor progress and enable course correction. 
Social marketing and free contraceptives support population stabilization and 
maternal/child health.  
ii. PNDT Act Awareness: Focuses on enforcing the Pre-Conception and Pre-
Natal Diagnostic Techniques Act, 1994, to prevent sex selection and female 
foeticide.  
iii. Population Research Centers (PRCs): The Ministry of Health and Family 
Welfare, Government of India has established Population Research Centers 
(PRCs) in various Universities and research Institutions in the Country. 
Objective of the PRCs are critical research-based input to the Health and 
Family Welfare programmes and policies of the Government of India and 
states. 18 centers (funded by MoHFW) conduct research on family planning, 
demographics, and population control, supporting government health policies 
and surveys like NFHS and LASI.  
iv. Health Surveys (NFHS): The National Family Health Survey (NFHS), 
conducted with IIPS, provides data on population, health, and family welfare, 
enabling policy evaluation and benchmarking.  
v. Contraceptive Distribution: Provides free contraceptives (condoms, pills, 
IUCDs, etc.) to achieve population stabilization and reduce maternal/child 
mortality.  
vi. WHO-NPS Support: WHO-supported National Polio Surveillance Project 
provides technical and operational support for vaccine-preventable disease 
surveillance, immunization, and other health initiatives.

3.9.4 The Committee observes that, for the FY 2024-25, BE was Rs. 694.72

monitoring of key performance indicators, enabling timely identification of program 
gaps and areas requiring intervention. The Department should utilize this data to 

52 
 
conduct regular, evidence-based reviews of program effectiveness and resource 
allocation, ensuring that funding is aligned with program priorities and achieving 
desired outcomes. Further, the department should create a system that tracks the 
percentage of program goals achieved, versus the percentage of budget spent ensuring 
effective and optimal/rational utilization of funds. 
 
3.9.5  The Committee notes that the success of the Family Welfare Scheme 
depends on the synergistic interaction between its various components (SNA, 
Contraceptive Distribution, PNDT Act Awareness, etc.). Further, the general public 
awareness of the programs is vital to the programs’ success. The Committee 
recommends the Department to develop a comprehensive communication strategy that 
integrates messaging across all components of the Family Welfare Scheme. The 
Department should leverage a variety of communication channels, including digital 
media and community outreach programs to reach diverse populations focusing on 
raising public awareness about the availability of services, promoting healthy behaviors, 
and addressing social and cultural barriers to accessing care. The Committee believes 
that the co-ordination and collaboration among various programs should be further 
enhanced to increase their effectiveness due to co-location of activities, and caution the 
Department that the programs do not progress in silos.

3.10.5  The Committee recommends a sustained and expanded focus on capacity 
building across all programs, with a particular emphasis on AMR containment and 
zoonotic disease management. Leveraging the existing network of laboratories, training 
sites, and regional coordinators, the program should prioritize consistent, high-quality 
training delivery to strengthen expertise and ensure standardized practices. For AMR 
containment, the Committee recommends the expansion of laboratory networks must be 
accompanied by rigorous, standardized training in bacteriology and HAI surveillance, 
ensuring quality-assured testing and evidence-based treatment. Similarly, for zoonotic 
disease management, the successful approach of multi-stakeholder consultations and 
hands-on training should be scaled up, with a strong focus on developing and 
implementing standardized training modules for medical officers and frontline workers. 
Additionally, the expansion of Regional Venom Centers and the establishment of Poison 
Information Centers for snakebite management should be supported through 
comprehensive training programs. The Committee recommends for wider dissemination 
of IEC material for snakebite prevention and control, and protocols on initial 
management of snakebite especially in remote/rural areas. The Committee also 
recommends for launching snakebite Helpline Project and training for medical officers 
on snakebite in all States/UTs. The Committee is of the opinion that a continuous 
investment in human resource development will be the key to ensure long-term success 
and sustainability of these critical public health initiatives. 
3.10.6  The Committee recommends strengthening surveillance systems and data 
integration to enhance proactive disease management. Building on the AMR 
surveillance network and NOHP-PCZ integration into IHIP, programs should 
implement robust surveillance protocols and data management systems. For AMR, data 
collection and reporting to Global Antimicrobial Resistance and Use Surveillance 
System (GLASS) should be complemented by facility-based antibiograms to support 
evidence-based antibiotic treatment. For zoonotic diseases, implementing the 
Augmented Zoonotic Disease Surveillance (AZDS) proposal is critical for strengthening 
pathogen surveillance in hotspot areas. Additionally, the Rabies Helpline expansion and 
snakebite case notifications should be integrated into a unified national surveillance 
platform for timely data analysis and informed decision-making. The Committee is of 
the view that establishing a Programme Management Unit (PMU) at NCDC will ensure 
coordinated surveillance, data quality, and rapid information dissemination.

3.10.8  The Committee notes that for construction of NCDC branches across the 
country, the land has not yet been identified in the State of Chhattisgarh. Further, the 
construction has been started in eight States only. The Committee recommends that the 
NCDC prioritize and expedite the establishment of fully functional branch 
infrastructure across all states, particularly focusing on Chhattisgarh where land 
identification is still pending and accelerating construction in the remaining states where 
it has not yet commenced. This is crucial for maintaining the continuity and 
effectiveness of the NCDC's national disease surveillance and response capabilities, 
ensuring timely implementation of the Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme 
(IDSP) and the Integrated Health Information Platform (IHIP), and strengthening the 
national public health framework. 
 
3.10.9  INTEGRATED DISEASE SURVEILLANCE PROGRAMME (IDSP) - The 
Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (IDSP), under the National Health Mission 
(NHM), aims to establish and maintain a decentralized, laboratory-based, IT-enabled disease 
surveillance system for epidemic-prone communicable diseases. Currently, IDSP monitors 
33+ syndromes/diseases, with special surveillance for ILI/SARI, COVID-19, and Mpox. 
IDSP operates through a multi-tiered surveillance network, comprising Central Surveillance 
Unit (CSU) at NCDC Delhi; State Surveillance Units (SSU) at all State/UT headquarters; and 
District Surveillance Units (DSU) at all districts. Rapid Response Teams (RRTs) at district, 
state, and central levels investigate outbreak-prone diseases and recommend necessary 
precautions to prevent disease spread. Designated laboratories, including District Public 
Health Laboratories (DPHLs) and State Referral Laboratories (SRLs), support disease 
surveillance and investigation. 
 
3.10.10 IDSP has fully transitioned to a near real-time, GIS-enabled Integrated Health 
Information Platform (IHIP). As of December 2024, all 36 States/UTs report data through 
IHIP. Key Functions under IDSP are: - 
 

59 
 
i. Outbreak Investigations: Rapid response to disease outbreaks across districts, 
states, and the country. 
ii. Media Scanning & Verification: Monitors print and electronic media for event-
based surveillance, utilizing AI tools for early warning detection and timely 
outbreak response. 
iii. Health Preparedness: Enables early detection and quick response by state health 
authorities. 
 
3.10.11 Outcomes under IDSP have been informed as follows: - 
 
i. IHIP Implementation- On an average 76%, 79% and 80% Reporting Units have 
reported in S (Syndromic) form, P (Presumptive) form and L (Laboratory 
Confirmed) form respectively under IDSP-IHIP Portal (1st Jan 2024 to 31st 
December 2024). 
 
ii. Outbreak Investigations- A total of 2947 outbreaks have been reported during the 
period 1st Jan 2024 to 15th December 2024 (Week 50).  
 
iii. Public Health Emergency Operation Centre (PHEOC)- at NCDC was activated on 
23rd April, 2024 in response to Multi-State H5N1 outbreak (Level 2), on 9th May’ 
2024 in response to Avian Influenza in Kerala & Jharkhand (Level 1), on 21st 
august’ 2024 in response to Mpox, on 28th August’ 2024 in response to Avian 
Influenza outbreak in Ajmer Rajasthan, and on 4th September’2024 in response to 
Avian Influenza outbreak in Odisha. 
 
iv. Media Scanning and Verification Cell- IDSP performs media scanning & 
verification of print and electronic media to strengthen the event-based 
surveillance. IDSP also uses Artificial Intelligence tools in Media Scanning and 
Verification to detect early warning signals and generating alerts for timely 
management of the potential outbreaks. A total of 2,338 media alerts were 
generated (1st January 2024 to 31st December 2024). 
 
v. Laboratory strengthening- Strengthening of public health labs is an important 
component of IDSP that focuses on developing lab capacity in India. As on 
December’ 2024, 439 district public Health labs in 36 States/ UTs have been 
approved for strengthening out of which 382 (87%) labs are performing as per 
tests recommended by IDSP. State Referral labs (SRLs) network is currently 
present in 27 States/UTs involving 163 sanctioned SRLs. 
 
3.10.12 To ensure the sustained effectiveness and responsiveness of the Integrated 
Disease Surveillance Programme (IDSP), the Committee recommends a targeted 
initiative to enhance data collection and analysis to arrive at a decision in specific time-
frame in the Integrated Health Information Platform (IHIP). The Committee believes 
that it can be achieved through: (i) intensified training and capacity building for 
healthcare workers at all levels on IHIP data entry & analytics and utilization; (ii) 

60 
 
streamlined data entry processes and user interface improvements to minimize 
reporting burdens; (iii) regular monitoring and feedback mechanisms to identify and 
rectify reporting challenges; and (iv) leveraging the recently launched community 
reporting tool to supplement and validate data from health facilities, thereby fostering a 
more comprehensive and robust surveillance system. 
 
3.10.13 NATIONAL PROGRAM FOR SURVEILLANCE OF VIRAL HEPATITIS 
(NPSVH): The National Program for Surveillance of Viral Hepatitis (NPSVH) helps in 
determining the seroprevalence of Hepatitis B and Hepatitis C and this helps in estimating the 
burden of infection. This data is used for planning, policy, prevention and control of Viral 
Hepatitis through National Viral Hepatitis Control Program (NVHCP) to achieve SDG target 
3.3. 
 
3.10.14 The Committee recommends building on existing collaborations with 
NACP and NFHS, it should implement a standardized framework for data collection 
and scientific analysis of data, integrating seroprevalence data across multiple disease 
areas to ensure continuity and clarity between surveillance of data and programmatic 
action. This expansion will optimize laboratory infrastructure, generate a 
comprehensive dataset essential for informed policymaking, targeted interventions, and 
effective disease control. 
 
3.11 NATIONAL PHARMACOVIGILANCE PROGRAMME 
 
3.11.1  National Pharmacovigilance Program of India (PvPI) is a Central Sector (CS) 
Scheme being implemented in the country with the objective to collect, collate and analyse 
the Adverse Events reported with the use of medical products marketed in India to safeguard 
the health of Indian population by ensuring that the benefits of use of medicine outweigh the 
risks associated with its use. The key objectives of PvPI are to create a nationwide system for 
patient safety reporting in respect to adverse drug reactions (ADRs) of medical products, to 
identify and analyze the new ADR (Signal) from the reported cases and to analyze the 
benefit-risk ratio of medicinal products.  
 
3.11.2  The PvPI collaborates with national and international stakeholders, ensuring 
patients’ safety by monitoring ADRs. A nationwide network has been set up with Healthcare 
Professionals (HCPs) by enrolling Adverse Drug Reaction Monitoring Centres (AMCs) in 
PvPI and the current outreach is more than 842 AMCs across the country. The National 
Coordination Centre for PvPI has enrolled 1,025 Adverse Drug Reaction Monitoring Centres 
(AMCs) across the country so far. There are 9,22,005 lacs of Individual Case Safety Reports 
(ICSRs) as on 7.2.2025 in VigiBase on behalf of India. PvPI is the 8th largest reporter of 
ICSRs to the WHO Programme of International Drug Monitoring. The Materiovigilance 
Programme of India (MvPI) and Hemovigilance Programme of India (HvPI) are also under 
the ambit of PvPI. IPC is also functioning as a NCC for MvPI and National Institute of 
Biologicals (NIB) is a NCC for HvPI.

3.13.4  On being asked about the reasons for significant reduction in allocation under 
the scheme at the RE stage compared to the BE stage in FY 2024-25, the Department 
explained that a major portion of the scheme’s budget is allocated for infrastructure projects, 
such as establishing NELS Skill Centers and tertiary and secondary-level CBRN medical 
management centers. The reduction in funds at the RE stage for 2024-25 is attributed to the 
following factors: 
 
a) Delays in site identification and changes in location: The identification of 
suitable land/space for tertiary and secondary-level CBRN medical management 
centers faced delays, compounded by frequent site changes. This hindered site 
finalization and the selection of an execution agency, reducing capital outlay. 
 
b) Delayed fund utilization by grantee medical colleges: Funds meant for NELS 
Skill Centers remained pooled at the Central Nodal Agency (CNA) due to slow 
utilization by grantee medical colleges. This restricted further disbursement to newly 
identified institutes for setting up NELS Skill Centers. 
 
c) Unutilized funds earmarked for Health Sector Disaster Preparedness & 
Response: A significant portion of the budget was reserved for immediate logistics in 
response to disasters and public health emergencies. However, as of 2024-25, no such 
requests were received from any State/UT, leading to savings in these funds. 
 
3.13.5  The Department noted that site-related issues are being actively addressed in 
coordination with States/UTs, alongside the finalization of the Project Consultant. As a result, 
the allocated funds are expected to be utilized as planned in BE 2025-26. 
 
3.13.6  The Committee noted the under-utilisation of funds under Health Sector 
Disaster Preparedness and Response and Human Resource Development for Emergency 
Medical Services during the past two years. In the FY 2023-24, Rs. 128.14 crore was 
allocated at BE stage which was reduced to Rs. 70 crore at RE stage. Moreover, the 
actual expenditure was just Rs. 30.50 crore (43.57% of the already reduced revised 

66 
 
estimate). Similarly, in the next FY 2024-25, the amount of Rs. 94 crore allocated at BE 
stage was reduced to Rs. 15 crore at RE stage, and again, the actual expenditure has 
been reported to the tune of Rs. 7.57 crore as on 07.02.2025. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends the Government to implement a rigorous, time-bound monitoring and 
evaluation framework for the "Health Sector Disaster Preparedness and Response and 
Human Resource Development for Emergency Medical Services" scheme, specifically 
focusing on the timely execution of infrastructure projects and Capacity Building 
Initiatives that inter-alia include setting up of National Emergency Life Support (NELS) 
skill centers in medical colleges/institutions under Central/State Government and setting 
up of Chemical, Biological, Radiological and Nuclear (CBRN) medical management 
centers besides imparting skills training of doctors, nurses and paramedics on NELS 
and CBRN, and fund utilization by grantee institutions. 
 
3.13.7  For efficient and optimal utilization of funds under the scheme, the 
Committee believes that the Government should consider the following: (i) pre-
identified and vetted site alternatives to mitigate delays due to site changes; (ii) 
mandatory quarterly fund utilization reports from grantee medical colleges for NELS 
Skill Centers, with clear timelines for disbursement and penalties for non-compliance; 
and (iii) a proactive, needs-based assessment system for disaster and public health 
emergency response logistics, rather than solely relying on state/UT requests, to ensure 
allocated funds are strategically utilized. This systematic approach will address the 
recurrent issues of delayed project execution and underutilization of funds.

and actual expenditures, indicating poor fund utilization. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends the Government to establish a robust mechanism incorporating

including administrative bottlenecks and lack of state-level capacity and overcome the

3.15 NATIONAL TELE MENTAL HEALTH PROGRAMME 
 
3.15.1  The National Tele Mental Health Programme of India, Tele Mental Health 
Assistance and Networking Across States (Tele MANAS) was announced by the Union 
Finance Minister in the Union Budget 2022 on 1st February, 2022 and launched as the digital 
arm of District Mental Health Programme (DMHP) by the Governor of Karnataka at the event 
of the World Mental Health Day ceremony held at NIMHANS on 10th October, 2022. The 
objectives of the program are: - 
 
i. To exponentially scale up the reach of mental health services to anybody who 
reaches out, across India, any time, by setting up a 24x7 tele-mental health 
facility in each of the States and UTs of the country.  
 
ii. To implement a fully-fledged mental health service network that, in addition to 
counselling, provides integrated medical and psychosocial interventions 

69 
 
including video consultations with mental health specialists, e-prescriptions, 
follow-up services and linkages to in-person services.  
 
iii. To extend services to vulnerable groups of the population and difficult to reach 
populations. 
 
The features and achievements under the program are: - 
 
i. Presently, Tele MANAS is Operational in all 36 States/ UT’s through 51 
functional Tele MANAS cells including 2 additional cells at AFMC Pune and at 
Nagpur in collaboration with Aditya Birla Empower Initiative Group (CSR).  
 
ii. More than 18 lakhs calls have been handled on the helpline number (14416) 
since launch till 7th February, 2025.  
 
iii. Tele MANAS helpline is available for all age group while majority of the 
callers (more than 60%) engaging with the T MANAS helpline falls in the age 
group of 19- 45 years. 
 
iv. In the initial phase the numbers of Male callers (68%) were more in comparison 
to the female callers (32%). This gap has reduced to the ratio of 53 (Male 
Callers): 47 (Female callers) now throwing effectiveness of Tele MANAS to 
provide services in the vulnerable group. 
 
v. On October 10th, 2024, the Tele MANAS mobile application was launched on 
the second anniversary of the National Tele Mental Health Program (NTMHP). 
The app provides an invaluable resource for users seeking guidance, 
counselling, and emotional support. 
 
vi. Video consultations in Tele MANAS are another upgrade to the already 
existing audio calling facility. This facility has been initially launched in the 
states of Karnataka, Jammu & Kashmir and Tamil Nadu and will be later scaled 
up to the whole country. 
 
vii. The program also incorporates call-backs for follow-up, reinforcing the care 
plan for individuals. 
 
viii. Tele MANAS services are being actively promoted through various platforms, 
including print media, radio, and social media. These efforts aim to raise 
awareness about mental health services and ensure that people in need can 
easily access free and confidential psychological support.

3.16 NATIONAL DIGITAL HEALTH MISSION (NDHM)/ AYUSHMAN BHARAT 
DIGITAL MISSION (ABDM): 
3.16.1  Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM), earlier known as the National 
Digital Health Mission (NDHM) has been launched in Sep 2021, with the aim of enabling 

71 
 
interoperability of health data within the health ecosystem and helping create longitudinal 
electronic health records for every citizen that ensures continuum of care for citizens. ABDM 
comprises key registries intended through building trusted, verified registries such as 
Ayushman Bharat Health Account (ABHA), Healthcare Professional Registry (HPR) and 
Health Facility registry (HFR). As on 6th February 2025, a total of 73,98,09,607 (Rs. 73.98 
Cr) ABHA have been created, 3,63,520 (Rs. 3.63 Lac) health facilities have registered on 
HFR, 5,64,851 (Rs. 5.64 Lac) healthcare professionals have registered on HPR and 
49,06,02,540 (Rs. 49.06 Cr) health records have been linked with ABHA. 
 
3.16.2  Leveraging the aforesaid registries, ABDM envisages making healthcare 
accessible and affordable. OPD registration has been made simpler by ABHA enabled QR 
code based registration services. As of February 2025, 18,879 facilities across 35 states/UTs 
have generated 8.34 crore tokens, significantly reducing waiting times in the registration 
process for the patients. A public dashboard [dashboard.abdm.gov.in] is available for NHA, 
the implementing body of ABDM, and the states/UTs to assess the different indicators 
reflecting the progress of the scheme. NHA is providing necessary support including technical 
assistance and training for all stakeholders to integrate their solutions under the ABDM 
ecosystem. 
 
3.16.3  To ensure the effective implementation of ABDM, the Union Health Ministry 
provides financial assistance to States/UTs for human resources, information education & 
communication (IEC), and capacity building including necessary handholding support in on 
boarding the facilities/ health professionals and integrate state health digital health 
programs/solutions under ABDM ecosystem. Union Health Ministry also provides financial 
assistance to all States/UTs under National Health Mission for strengthening of health 
infrastructure for the implementation of IT interventions such as Hospital Management 
Information System (HMIS) and telemedicine services across the country.
