CHAPTER I 
 
INTRODUCTION 
 
The Ministry of Ayush formed in 2014, evolved from the Department of Indian System of 
Medicine and Homoeopathy (ISM&H) formed in 1995. The Department was responsible for the 
development of ancient system of medicine prevalent in Indian subcontinent in times of yore. It 
was renamed as the Department of Ayurveda, Yoga, and Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha and 
Homoeopathy (Ayush) in November 2003 with focused attention towards education and 
research in Ayurveda, Yoga and Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha, and Homoeopathy. Sowa Rigpa, a 
traditional medicine system in many parts of Himalyan regions was also brought under the 
umbrella in year 2011.  
 
1.1 Ayurveda is a comprehensive traditional system of medicine evolved in India thousands of 
year ago in medieval and ancient times. Ayurveda emphasizes on holistic approach through 
health promotion, disease prevention and curative roles. Ayurveda considers health as a 
dynamic integration of environment, body, mind and soul and accordingly advocates 
personalized approach for prescribing diet, lifestyle or treatment regimen based on its 
fundamental concept that everyone has distinct psychosomatic constitution and health status. 
Homoeopathy, has also been in practice in India for around 100 years, provides long term 
palliative treatment in both acute and chronic cases owing to its effectiveness, lack of side 
effects and low cost of treatment. The National Health Policy (NHP-2017) advocates 
mainstreaming the potential of Ayush within a pluralistic system of integrated healthcare. In 
convergence with NHP and National Health Mission, the National Ayush Mission (NAM) 
envisages better access to Ayush Services, operationalization of Ayush Health and Wellness 
Centre, quality improvement of Ayush Education and Research in order to achieve Sustainable 
Development Goals and enhanced public health. 
 
1.1.1 The Ministry of Ayush works with the vision to position Ayush systems as the preferred 
systems of living and practice for attaining a healthy India. Such a vision has gradually emerged 
through the thought processes of experts concerned with health care provisioning in the country. 
The Ministry strives to promote these systems through robust policy frameworks, widespread 
awareness, and comprehensive educational initiatives. The core objectives include driving 
research and innovation, ensuring access to quality Ayush products, and fostering global 
acceptance of these practices. The Ministry is dedicated to developing skilled professionals, 
bolstering the medicinal plant sector, and ultimately, enhancing public health through 
sustainable and accessible Ayush solutions. 
 
 
 

2 
 
Thematic Areas of Ayush  
 
1.2 The Ministry envisages its Mission in terms of seven broad thematic areas of Ayush 
activities. The thematic areas are as follows: 
 
(i) Effective Human Resource Development 
(ii) Provision of Quality Ayush Services 
(iii) Information, Education and Communication 
(iv) Quality Research in Ayush 
(v) Growth of the Medicinal Plants Sector 
(vi) Drug Administration 
(vii) International Exchange Programme/Seminars/Workshops in Ayush sector 
 
 
FUNCTIONAL AREAS OF THE MINISTRY 
1.3 With an aim to position India as a Global Health care leader, the Ministry has identified the 
key areas of focus as Globalization and Market Share; Research; Technology; Policy Regulation 
and Standardizations; Manufacturing and Services; and Healthcare and Education. 
 
1.3.1 The Major Activities of Ministry of Ayush are carried out by several autonomous 
institutions, and various institutes/councils under direct control of the Ministry; Centre Sector 
Schemes and the Centrally Sponsored Schemes where grants are provided through National 
Ayush Mission (NAM) to States/UTs to take up Ayush Activities. 
 
1.3.2 The Ministry of Ayush executes its mandate through its 5 Research Councils, 12 National 
Institutes, the 2 Regulatory Commission (i.e. NCISM & NCH), its subordinate offices PCIM&H 
and the Public Sector Undertaking IMPCL.

the quality  (identity, purity and strength) of the ASU&H drugs. AS per the Drugs & Cosmetics 
Act, 1940 and rules there under, the compliance to this quality standards are mandatory for the 
production of ASU&H drugs being manufactured in India. So far, 2259 quality standards on raw 
materials (single drugs of plant/ animal/ mineral/ metal/ chemical origin) used in ASU&H 
drugs, 405 quality standards of ASU formulations and 2666 formulary specifications of ASU 
drugs   has been published. In addition to above, supporting documents in the form of Macro-
Microscopic & TLC Atlas on 351 single drugs incorporated in Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of 
India (API) has also published. Rule 160 A to J of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945 
provides the regulatory guidelines for approval of Drug Testing Laboratory for carrying out 
such tests of identity, purity, quality and strength of Ayurvedic, Siddha and Unani drugs. As on 
date, 34 State Drug Testing Laboratories have been supported for strengthening their 
infrastructural and functional capacity.  Further, 106 laboratories are approved or licensed under 
the provisions of Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945 for quality testing of Ayurvedic, Siddha and 
Unani drugs and raw materials. 03 Drug Testing Laboratories of CCRAS approved under Rule

standard-setting processes under a single authoritative body viz. an independent drug 
controller of AYUSH, in alignment with the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, and its 
associated rules. To achieve this, the Ministry should establish a streamlined and inclusive 
mechanism that actively involves stakeholders in the development of pharmacopoeial 
standards, ensuring greater efficiency and uniformity. Additionally, the Committee 
emphasizes that PCIM&H and CCRAS may come together to coordinate and collaborate 
in this initiative to enhance the scientific testing and evaluation of a larger number of 
ASU&H drug samples to ensure safety, efficacy, and quality strengthening the foundation 
of research and standardization in the sector.

UNIFORM &STANDARD LICENSING  
4.3 The Ministry has informed that it is working in coordination with Ayush Grid and state 
licensing Authority, Gujarat to make e-AUSHADHI portal more user-friendly and robust for 
online licensing of Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani and Homoeopathy drugs. 
4.3.1 The Drugs & Cosmetics Act, 1940 and Drugs Rules, 1945 have exclusive regulatory 
provisions for Ayurvedic, Siddha, Unani, and Homoeopathy drugs. Provisions relating to 
Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani Drugs are contained in Chapter IVA and Schedule- I of the Drugs 
and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and in Rules 151 to 169, Schedules E(I), T & TA of the Drugs and 
Cosmetics Rules, 1945. Further, second schedule (4A) of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 
provides standards for Homoeopathic drugs and  Rules 2dd, 30AA, 67 (C-H), 85 (A to I), 106-
A, Schedule K, Schedule M-I of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945 pertain to Homoeopathic 
drugs. It is mandatory for the manufacturers to adhere to the prescribed requirements for 
licensing of manufacturing units & medicines including proof of safety & effectiveness, 
compliance with the Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP) as per Schedule T & Schedule M-I 
of Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945 and quality standards of drugs given in the respective 
pharmacopoeia. 
4.3.2 The matter related to uniform pattern of license was discussed in the meeting of 
Ayurvedic, Siddha and Unani Drugs Consultative Committee (ASUDCC) held on 14/03/2024, 
wherein   Committee recommended that all the State Licensing Authorities (SLAs) should give 
uniform pattern of license numbers and to make necessary provisions under the rules to display 
manufacturing license number of the particular product in all the advertisements- electronic, 
social media or print media. The said recommendation was placed in ASUDTAB meeting held 
on 24/07/2024, wherein board recommended for draft notification for certain amendment in the 
Drug Rules for uniform license throughout the country. 

57 
 
4.3.3 The Committee is of view that the Ministry must have a standard licensing process 
based on uniform parameters across all the States so that drug formulations do not vary 
from State to State. A standardized approach will eliminate variations in drug 
formulations from state to state, thereby enhancing the quality, safety, and efficacy of 
AYUSH medicines. This will prevent discrepancies in ingredient composition, dosage, and 
therapeutic claims, ensuring that AYUSH drugs meet the same regulatory and scientific 
benchmarks nationwide. It will also strengthen consumer confidence by guaranteeing that 
all licensed AYUSH drugs adhere to nationally recognized quality standards, ultimately 
fostering wider acceptance and integration of AYUSH medicines in mainstream 
healthcare. 
4.3.4 The Committee, keeping in view the obscure and diverse pattern of licensing that 
creates hurdles for the manufactures for seeking license for production of Ayush products. 
The Committee therefore recommends that arrangement be made to have simplified 
procedure for seeking uniform and standard license that will ensure ease of doing business 
for Ayush manufacturers thereby seeking the objective of AtmaNirbhar Bharat and Make 
in India mission. Moreover, the manufacturers will be encouraged to setup AYUSH 
industry in the country for production of AYUSH products that will ultimately promote 
AYUSH sector in domestic as well as the global market. 
 
Clinical Trials Registry- India (CTRI) 
4.4 The Clinical Trials Registry- India (CTRI), hosted at the ICMR’s National Institute of 
Medical Statistics is a free and online public record system for registration of clinical trials 
being conducted in India that was launched on 20th July 2007. The CTRI also has data sets 
specific to the AYUSH system of medicine where AYUSH-specific information is being 
captured during the trial registration process.  The Committee has been apprised that the 
information pertaining to R&D protocol, approval and subsequent outcomes is maintained 
separately at respective institutes, research councils and other autonomous bodies etc. Clinical 
Trial of CCRAS is being monitored through an elaborated mechanism “Electronic Data 
Capture(EDC)” which is scrutinized at the headquarters level. CCRH is registering all its 
clinical trials on Clinical trial Registry of India before initiation of its research project. NIA has 
established the PMU (Project management Unit) to develop a robust CTMS and also launched 
IMR(Intra Mural Research) Policy for better R&D outcomes. NIA has also developed DDDU ( 
Drug development and Discovery Unit) for development of New Drugs. 
 
4.4.1 The Committee is of considered view that implementing a robust Clinical Trial 
Management System (CTMS) will significantly improve documentation, efficiency, and 
compliance in AYUSH clinical research. All the research councils, institutes and other 
autonomous bodies engaged in R&D, clinic trials and related activities should be brought 
onto to this single platform. Automation of key trial processes, including patient 
recruitment, randomization, monitoring, adverse event reporting, and regulatory 
submissions, will enhance efficiency. By automating workflows, it will reduce manual 
errors, enhance regulatory transparency, and accelerate trial approvals. Standardizing 
research protocols with ICMR/GCP guidelines will ensure uniformity across AYUSH 

58 
 
disciplines, strengthening the scientific validation of traditional medicine. AI-driven 
analytics will support data-driven decision-making, enabling better tracking of adverse 
events and treatment outcomes. Furthermore, a well-integrated CTMS will allow multi-
center trials, facilitating global acceptance of AYUSH-based interventions and positioning 
India as a leader in integrative medicine research. 
4.4.2 The Committee further desires that information on reported claims regarding Ayush 
treatment for controlling cholesterol levels using tablets or injections, supported by 
research-based evidence, if available, may be provided.

educational administration through NIEPA, New Delhi. Around 5000 teachers were trained 
through NI-MSME, University of Hyderabad, Pune University & different educational 
institutions.100 PG students qualified for PG star program were trained in a workshop on Ayur 
Tech for precision health & integrative medicine at IIT Jodhpur. Further, NCISM has initiated 
the assessment of education sector under NCISM to assess the readiness of the sector. NCISM 
has taken initiative to create a data-base to be used for development of AI tools which should be 
completed in ensuing years. 
 
4.6.1 National registration has been issued to 320000 practitioners from 28 states till date & that 
is an ongoing process to ensure the availability of qualified professionals at Pan India level. So 
far, 57679 ISM practitioners have been enrolled in ABDM program so that digital presence of 
these practitioners are available for everyone accessing for anyone from anywhere in the 
country.  Four new state councils have been established since inception of NCISM.Robust 
regulations have been issued to ensure the rights of health care seekers as well as the health 
professionals. 
 
4.6.2 The Secretary, MoA in his oral evidence submitted before the Committee the following 
information that “Sir, regarding education, you will see that our 570 colleges in 2013-14 have 
now become 883. The number of PG colleges, which was 138, has now become 269. Our UG 
seats have also significantly increased by almost more than double. PG seats have also 
increased by almost more than double. Many innovations have taken place. For example, we 
have created a digital ecosystem through the E-Learning Management System and Education 
Lifestyle Management. Interdisciplinary Courses have been created as electives. Credit-based 
courses, and all members will be pleased to know that integration has also been done within 
AYUSH. For instance, an Ayurveda student can take a Homeopathy elective. A Homeopathy 
student can take a Unani elective if they wish. Such innovations have taken place. 
Sir, the entrepreneurship electives, sociology electives, and soft skills electives are very popular 
among students, and they are signing up for them more than required. This is our 
experience.(15 days) Mandatory one-week internship in Ayush MBBS curriculum has been done 
through NMC. Interdisciplinary education in PG and PhD courses has started within 
Integrative Healthcare. Dual degree programs have also started. Yoga has been integrated into 
the MBBS curriculum. A one-year nursing course has been proposed and started within Ayush 
by the Nursing Council.” 
 
4.6.3 The Committee notes the submission of the Ministry regarding the physical 
performance in field of AYUSH education, however, the Committee feels that the Ayush 
Education System has still require miles to march to play a level playing performance with 
allopathic system of medicine. The Committee recommends that soft skills among Ayush 
practitioners should be incorporated into the syllabus of all components of AYUSH. This 
should aim at instilling highest degree of responsibility discipline and virtue in delivering 
healthcare to the masses. This would in turn lead to increased in the Indian Systems of 
Medicine and would slowly and surely do away with the skepticism towards the 
alternative medicines.  The Committee also recommends Integration of technology in the 
Ayush curriculum for modernization and creating technology enabled work force. 

60 
 
4.6.4 The Committee appreciates the Ministry for the steps taken regarding education in 
integrative healthcare and considers that the mandatory one week internship in Ayush 
MBBS  curriculum be enhanced to atleast 15 days so that a more comprehensive 
knowledge sharing can take place between conventional and alternative system of 
medicine.  Furthermore the Committee is of considered view that one-year nursing course 
that has been proposed and started within Ayush be adopted on a wider scale in line with 
the requirement of  manpower in healthcare sector. 
4.6.5 The Ministry also proposed before the Committee that pay parity be maintained 
between allopathy doctors and Ayush practitioners. The Committee is of considered view 
that the AYUSH system of medicine is still in nascent stage. Despite all the work being 
done in last decade the system is still not a household name as it is for the conventional 
system of medicine. Thus Committee is of view that the matter may be considered by the 
Govt. Of India once the AYUSH system has come at a appreciable footing in comparison 
to allopathy. The Committee, however, recommends putting in a thought-through 
incentivisation schemes at different verticals to encourage the manpower to put in more 
effort to excel in this field, therein ensuring accelerated growth of AYUSH system.  
Further some form of mechanism like incentivisation, mandatory service etc to ensure 
that doctors consider serving in rural areas villages etc as an opportunity to explore fresh 
vistas for Ayush Sector. 
4.6.6 The Committee has been apprised that the All India Institute of Ayurveda, which is 
in Delhi, has a wellness center in LBSNAA, Mussoorie, one in the Supreme Court, one in 
Arogya Van, Ekta Nagar, which is the Statue of Unity, and there are others. Like Ayush 
wings, all AIIMS, and the Department of Ayush are proposed in all upcoming AIIMS. The 
Ministry has decided that all AIIMS should have an academic department of Ayush. The 
Committee appreciates setting up of Ayush Wellness Centres within the complex of 
government institutions and recommends that more such centres may be opened up in 
coming years. The Committee desires that a separate centre of Ayush may also be set up 
in Parliament Complex for treatment of MPs, Ex-MPs and Employees and Ex-Employees 
of Sansad that would not only ensure treatment of Members of Parliament through Ayush 
System but would ensure the popularization/awareness of Ayush to each constituency as 
the Member of Parliament would prove a harbinger to awareness of common masses 
across the country. The Committee strongly recommends that dedicated Department of 
Ayush be setup in all AIIMS across the country in a quick time bound manner. The 
Committee also expects that the departments so instituted be supplied with adequate 
manpower and resources as necessary for the smooth running of the department for 
better service of the public.  
4.6.7 The Committee is of the considered view that the UGs& PGs number of seats be 
increased in Ayush Colleges having adequate infrastructure & manpower so that Ayush 
professionals are available in rural areas where there is severe gap between the 
requirement of Allopathic doctors and strength-in-position. The Committee feels that 
Ayush professional so produced from well-equipped Ayush colleges would be in a position 
to fill up the gap of Allopathic doctors in rural areas and thus connect their position and 
contributing to the human kind even at the remotest region across the country with 
benefits of Ayush Sector of treatment.

compared to many developed countries, introduced of a special Visa category, Ayush Visa

also like to be appraised of the details of healthcare availed and the feedback of travelers 
in respect of 1646 Ayush Visas issued between 1.1.2024 to 4.2.2025.

illegal medical practice in the name of Ayush and Ayush Doctors prescribing scheduled 
allopathic drugs maligning the reputation of Ayush healthcare in the country. The 
Committee believes there are provisions under the National Commission for Indian 
System of Medicine Act, the National Commission for Homeopathy Act and the Drugs and 
Cosmetics Act to check such malpractices.

Committee is of the opinion that the Ministry must explore such activities including Sickel 
Cell Anemia in the Tribal areas and in the northeastern regions and widen the scope of 
collaboration with M/o Tribal Affairs.

Cooperative and Collaborative Approach between Ayush and Allopathy 
 
4.13 The issues relating to integrative approaches and differences of opinion on public 
health, medical education and research, policy formulation and implementation etc. 
between traditional medicine and modern medicine have come up before the Committee 
time and again. The Committee is of the view that these differences affect the 
implementation of health welfare schemes and policies. The Committee therefore feels that 
there should be an institutional mechanism to bring the two systems of medicines on a 
common platform. The Committee desires that through this institutional mechanism, 
regular joint meetings between the M/o Ayush and M/o Health & Family Welfare, NMC 
and NCISM, NCH and Ayush Research Councils may be held to settle the grey areas and 
resolve the issues affecting health policy formulation and implementation strategies. The 
Committee strongly recommends that instead of antagonistic relationship, there should be 
cooperative and collaborative approach and cohesive equilibrium between the Ayush and 
Allopathy so that integrated and coordinated efforts may be made for treatment of 
various diseases.  
 
Promotion of Yoga and Naturopathy 
 
4.14 The role of Yoga and Naturopathy in health promotion and preventive health is 
undeniable. Awareness of Yoga and its significance has reached international dimensions 
as evident in the celebrations of International Day of Yoga and Yoga parvs/camps being 
organized everywhere in the country. The Committee, however, observes that there is an 
unequal distribution of national institutes of Yoga and Naturopathy across the States and 
UTs, particularly in rural and backward areas. The Committee, therefore, recommends 
that national institutes for Yoga and Naturopathy may be opened in states like Bihar, 
Uttar Pradesh, Jharkhand and in NER. The Committee further recommends that Yoga 
camps may be organized not just for jubilation but be organized regularly at Block and 
village levels with the real intention to imbibe attitude and commitment to Yoga and 
Naturopathy by heart. The Committee also desires that Yoga classes may be held 
mandatorily in all primary schools and Yoga instructors in each school may also be 
appointed for this purpose.  
  
Equitable distribution of Ayush Centres 
 
4.15 The Committee has been apprised that there is unequal distribution of Ayush 
healthcare in the country. There are states like Punjab and Maharashtra where there is 
relatively less development of integrated Ayush hospitals and functional Ayush Centres. 
The Committee would like to know how many Ayush Centres and Ayush Grams are 
functional in all states/UTs and recommends that the Ministry of Ayush must ensure 
equitable development of Ayush healthcare and ecosystem across the geographical area of 
the country, including setting up of Ayush Centre at the places where these centres are in 
scarce, keeping in view the region-specific requirements and potential in Ayush industry. 
The Committee has also been apprised of the coming proposals for 50 bedded hospitals in 
every district and 100 bedded hospitals in all tier-2 cities. The Committee expects the

healthcare is less developed.

STATUS OF UTILIZATION CERTIFICATES 
The Committee understands that Utilization Certificate (UC) in government systems is a 
crucial document that verifies how funds allocated for a specific project or scheme have 
been spent. Moreover, UC ensures transparency and accountability by demonstrating that 
the fund allocation has been used for its intended purpose and not misappropriated, and 
that the project achieved its desired outcomes. In this light the Committee has observed 
and recommended time and again regarding the delay in clearing pending UCs. The 
Committee expresses concern over pending UCs to number of 1549 involving Rs. 1608.29 
during 2023-24 and a total number of 1521 pending UCs involving an amount to the tune 
of Rs. 1765.85 in 2024-25. The Committee observes that the largest share in pending UCs 
is that of NAM with 897 UCs worth Rs 1592.09 crores. Timely submission of UCs is very 
crucial in scheme monitoring, subsequent release of funds and successful implementation 
of the scheme. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the Ministry must 
expedite its efforts in liquidating UCs as per standard timeline set for the activity. 
States/Uts may be persuaded and encouraged to use the NAM portal efficiently for the 
submitting UCs, SAAPs etc.  
( Para  4.2.2) 
 
UNIFORM &STANDARD LICENSING  
The Committee is of view that the Ministry must have a standard licensing process based 
on uniform parameters across all the States so that drug formulations do not vary from 
State to State. A standardized approach will eliminate variations in drug formulations 
from state to state, thereby enhancing the quality, safety, and efficacy of AYUSH 
medicines. This will prevent discrepancies in ingredient composition, dosage, and 
therapeutic claims, ensuring that AYUSH drugs meet the same regulatory and scientific 
benchmarks nationwide. It will also strengthen consumer confidence by guaranteeing that 
all licensed AYUSH drugs adhere to nationally recognized quality standards, ultimately 
fostering wider acceptance and integration of AYUSH medicines in mainstream 
healthcare.

( Para 4.3.3)

hurdles for the manufactures for seeking license for production of Ayush products. The 
Committee therefore recommends that arrangement be made to have simplified 
procedure for seeking uniform and standard license that will ensure ease of doing business 
for Ayush manufacturers thereby seeking the objective of AtmaNirbhar Bharat and Make 
in India misson. Moreover, the manufacturers will be encouraged to setup AYUSH 
industry in the country for production of AYUSH products that will ultimately promote 
AYUSH sector in domestic as well as the global market.

Clinical Trials Registry- India (CTRI) 
The Committee is of considered view that implementing a robust Clinical Trial 
Management System (CTMS) will significantly improve documentation, efficiency, and 
compliance in AYUSH clinical research. All the research councils, institutes and other 
autonomous bodies engaged in R&D, clinic trials and related activities should be brought 
onto to this single platform. Automation of key trial processes, including patient 
recruitment, randomization, monitoring, adverse event reporting, and regulatory 
submissions, will enhance efficiency. By automating workflows, it will reduce manual 
errors, enhance regulatory transparency, and accelerate trial approvals. Standardizing 
research protocols with ICMR/GCP guidelines will ensure uniformity across AYUSH 
disciplines, strengthening the scientific validation of traditional medicine. AI-driven 
analytics will support data-driven decision-making, enabling better tracking of adverse 
events and treatment outcomes. Furthermore, a well-integrated CTMS will allow multi-
center trials, facilitating global acceptance of AYUSH-based interventions and positioning 
India as a leader in integrative medicine research. 
( Para 4.4.1) 
The Committee further desires that information on reported claims regarding Ayush 
treatment for controlling cholesterol levels using tablets or injections, supported by 
research-based evidence, if available, may be provided.

for certain achievement of set target and must have provision of mid-term evaluation of 
progress made and if required modify the course of action to achieve the target set. The 
Committee reposes faith in Ministry of Ayush for achieving the goals set in Vision 
Ayush@2047 provided there are adequate budgetary allocation of each of its 
scheme/project, optimum utilization of fund under a resilient monitoring mechanism &co-
ordinating and controlling the factors of deviance. 
( Para 5.1.4) 
 
As deposed by the Secretary, M/o Ayush before the Committee, the Ayush manufacturing 
and services command about US$ 50 billion market size at present and the ambitious plan 
is to reach US$ 200 billion market size in the next 5 years.  While the Committee is 
delighted to note the rapid increase in the size of the Indian Ayush industry, with 
budgetary allocation of 0.012 percent of GDP, the Committee is quite apprehensive of the 
ambitions of the ministry to grow and develop Ayush as per its expectations. The 
Committee is of the view that the Ministry of Ayush needs to come up with more new 
schemes and strategies for growth and development of Ayush activities and claim for a 
much more enhanced budgetary allocation in comparison to the Department of Health & 
Family Welfare. 
( Para 5.1.5) 
 
FUTURE PLANS 
The Committee appreciates the larger vision of Ayush @2047 and the future plans of 
making AYUSH a multi-billion dollar market, yet the Committee is wary about the 
present situation of the healthcare in the country and observes that yearly short term 
goals be given a priority and direction to provide best AYUSH healthcare to the public by 
establishing PHCs/CHCs at district level etc. The Committee is in agreement of the 
Ministry of Ayush that the target of 30 lakh Ayush professionals in country by 2047, 
setting up one Ayush HQ in every district with at least one Ayush College, creation of over 
50 lakh new jobs, increasing contribution of Ayush to up to 7.7% of GDP etc. by the 2047 
is achievable by converting the long duration ambitious targets into short-term plan with 
smaller objective & goals and having co-ordinating and controlling monitoring 
mechanism over the implementation progress of projects/schemes/programmes ensuring 
achievement of set targets/goals/objectives. The Committee, in this regard, recommends 
the Ministry to make concerted efforts to implement the projects/schemes/programme 
through development of botanical drugs, entering into Free Trade Agreements (FTA) with 
favourable countries for enlarging global markets & enhancing exports level to a new 
height, establishing global hub of traditional medicine alongside WHO GTMC, production 
& promotion standard & quality drugs, ensuring widespread availability of 
AyushAushadi Kendra etc.  
( Para 5.2.1) 

96 
 
The Committee understand that the Global Footprint of Yoga needs to be further 
enhanced to tap into the global market and globalization of Yoga and Ayurveda training 
under Yoga Certification Board, Ayurveda Training Accreditation Board(ATAB)  may be 
promoted internationally for highest global participation in receiving and propagating the 
ancient form of knowledge rechristened in Ayush System i.e. Ayurveda, Yoga & 
Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha, Rigpa-Sowa and Homeopathy for alternative mode of 
treatment of diseases and  healthy living. 
( Para 5.2.2)

CHAPTER–I 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS THAT HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY 
THE GOVERNMENT 
 
A. AIIMS BHOPAL 
 
1.1 STATUS OF CONSTRUCTION WORK 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
1.1.1 The Committee observes that the delay in the cons truction work was mainly due to 
non-performance by the selected construction agencies along with improper planning and 
ineffective monitoring. Though the construction status is near completion in the first three 
Packages, under Package IV only 60% of the w ork is complete. It is high time that the 
Institute should strengthen the existing infrastructure and strive to complete the remaining 
work within the stipulated time limits as it has been six years since the Institute has been 
operationalized and the cons truction work is still incomplete. The Committee is inclined to 
observe that the selection of construction agencies was devoid of merit and transparency 
resulting in substantial time and cost overrun. The Committee, therefore, recommends that 
stringent monitoring mechanism should be put in place to ensure timely completion of work 
to avoid time and cost overruns. The Committee recommends that the Ministry should take 
necessary steps to take possession of the area which is under encroachment. The Committee is 
concerned to note that the project consultant HLL has miserably failed in proper monitoring 
of the project and its entire approach reflects unprofessionalism. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends suitable remedial action including fixing accountability a nd appropriate action 
keeping in view the observations of the CAG. 
(Para 2.14 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
 
1.1.2 The observations / recommendation of the Hon‘ble Committee has been noted for 
future guidance. It is submitted that the main reasons for the de lay in construction was due to 
preparation of erroneous Bills of Quantities (BoQ), delays in issue of drawings by original 
design consultants and delays in clearance of deviations, extra items and substituted items by 
original Project Consultant. The progr ess of DPR works is being reviewed regularly at the 
Institute level and in the Ministry, through the online dashboard.  The progress of DPR works 
of all the AIIMS is also reviewed in the CIB meetings. Considerable progress has been 
achieved since the visit made by the Committee. The present progress under various packages 
of civil construction work as in December‘ 2021 is as below:

non-performance. Subsequently, the balance work of Estate Services (Package IV) was

1.1.4 The horticulture work has also been completed.  The system of assigning the

mandated to deploy and use Project Management Software to bring about improved project

Recommendations/Observations  
 
1.1.5 The Committee fails to understand that no cost -benefit analysis was undertaken by the 
Institute before procuring medical equipment in AIIMS,  Bhopal. The Committee wonders 
how AIIMS, Bhopal procured equipment without ascertaining the availability of space, 
manpower and infrastructure required for installation , etc. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends to the Ministry that proper assessment with  respect to cost -benefit analysis 
should be done before the purchase of any equipment. 
(Para 2.19 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
 
1.1.6 The observation / recommendation of the Hon‘ble Committee has been noted for  
future guidance. As the institute is being est ablished, the procurement of medical equipment 
is being done for the first time and is in line with usual equipment available in similar 
departments across other similar INIs. No formal cost -benefit analysis has been done for 
procurement of medical equipme nt. However, whenever department requests for an 
equipment, it does an internal exercise regarding its requirement / essentiality patient care. 
The assessment committee, then thoroughly evaluates the cost justification, the proposed 
benefit for healthcare and a proper justification for expenditure over other competing 
requirements of other departments. It is only after a thorough deliberation & discussion that 
the assessment committee approves the purchase of each and every equipment.  

3 
 
1.1.7 All Procurement is rationalized based on multiple level of assessment such as proper 
justification, Need assessment, utilization, life cycle cost and thoroughly examined at each 
level with the existing committees in place such as SPC, Prioritization, infrastructure 
rationalization committee, negotiation committee etc. Further, the pre offer inspection and site 
readiness certificate has been ensured before the supply in order to mitigate the delay in 
installation and commissioning the equipment.

process and procedure of single bid system was adhered to in purchasing three equipment viz.

1.6 Budgetary Allocation 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
1.6.1 The Committee is anguished to observe there has been underutilization of funds till 
the year 2016 -17 in AIIMS, Rishikesh. The Committee notes that out of a total budget 
estimate of Rs. 426.50 crores during 2018-19, only Rs. 165 crores of funds have been released 
till 15th October, 2018. The Committee also notes that under GIA (CCA) alloca tion has been 
slashed to Rs 250 crores from the projected demand of Rs 1186.96 crores in BE 2018 -19. The 
Committee is of the opinion that AIIMS, Rishikesh has set up over ambitious  targets for itself 
and therefore, needs to reconsider these demands. A cost  benefit analysis also needs to be 
done vis-à-vis availability of other tertiary care services in the adjoining area. The Committee 
recommends that a common criterion along with a rational approach towards utilization of 
financial allocation for each AIIMS  needs to be done. The Committee is not convinced with 
the justification for overall projected demand to the tune of 1363.46 crores which is far above 
the expenditure incurred in other similar tertiary care center with much higher OPD/IPD load. 
Needless to say the Committee is concerned at the audacious projection which alone is almost 
equal to the sum total of all the remaining five regional AIIMS under study. The Committee 
recommends that suitable benchmark for AIIMS standards be formulated by the Central  
Institute Body (CIB) so that fiscal discipline and prudence in the utilization of the resources is 
done under all circumstances. The Committee recommends that AIIMS, Rishikesh should 
review its projections to a more realistic level. 
(Para 3.9 of the report) 
 
1.6.2 The Committee observes that in -principle approval of many important centers like 
Cardiac Science Center, Neuroscience Center, Ad vance Eye Center, Lung Center  with 
estimated expenditure to the tune of Rs. 100 crores each has been given by the Gov erning 
Body but the construction work could not be started due to unavailability of funds. Besides, 
the Committee is concerned to note that when there has already been a construction of a full -
fledged hospital to seek Rs. 97.61 crore for Administrative blo ck, Rs. 100 crore for the 
academic block, Rs. 100 crore for research block and Rs. 383 crore for residential 
accommodation gives an impression that there is no need for optimum/rational utilization of 
scarce resources. The Committee, therefore, recommends to the Ministry to monitor the 
utilization of funds given to AIIMS, Rishikesh with utmost caution and justification. The 
Committee also recommends for a comparative cost -benefit analysis of AIIMS, Rishikesh 
with other regional AIIMS specifically AIIMS, Bhubaneswar in this regard, as the Committee 
finds it to be the better managed in terms of investment outcome scale and rational utilization 
of limited resources. The Committee is of the opinion that regional AIIMS should provide 
tertiary health care in the n eglected region but should not merely duplicate the facilities 
available with AIIMS Delhi. The Committee recommends that setting up of advanced centers 
should be done only when AIIMS Rishikesh achieves at least 50% of the OPD footfall of 
AIIMS Delhi and th e existing infrastructure is put to optimum usage. Availability of

1.9 PROCUREMENT OF EQUIPMENT 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
1.9.1 The Committee, while examining the rationale forwarded by the Institute for the 
procurement of da vinci Robotic Arm is of the opinion that conventional laparoscopic surgery 
takes much lesser time and does not involve usage of expensive consumables. The Committee 
is of the opinion that these resources could have been better utilized in strengthening other 
important ar eas at this nascent stage. The alibi, given regarding training and extended 
warranty as a justification for higher prices, fails to appeal to the Committee, as similar terms 
have been given to other corporate hospitals by the Company across the country. Th e 
Committee is not convinced by these woolly arguments to procure prohibitively expensive 
equipment for a budding Institution like AIIMS. The Committee notes that it has been over 15 
years since the da vinci system (robotic surgery) is being used, but the evidence that it beats 
laparoscopic (minimally invasive surgery) is still lacking. The Committee notes that Robotic 
surgery is several times more expensive than the traditional laparoscopic surgery and engages 
the OT and the surgeon for much longer duratio n. The Committee strongly believes that 
robotic surgery should be used only in centers of excellence like AIIMS Delhi where the 
Institute is in a position to evaluate the efficacy, economics, efficiency and utility of these 
types of surgical intervention a s more research is needed to assess the benefits of robotic 
surgery. The Committee is also concerned that the da vinci system still has monopoly in the 
market and there is every possibility of the company dictating the price and indulging in 
unfair monopol istic practice. The Committee, thus, recommends to the Institute to ensure 
transparency besides appropriate cost/benefit analysis in the procurement of equipment to 
avoid such prohibitively expensive procurement in future. The Committee would like to have 

11 
 
a quarterly report on the usage of the DA Vinci Robotic Arm in both Rishikesh and Jodhpur 
so as to enable it to arrive at a final conclusion in the matter. 
(Para 3.26 of the report)

1.13 BUDGETARY ALLOCATION 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
1.13.1 The Committee is constrained to express its concern that total 
Observation/Recommendation of the Committee has been noted for future guidance. 
Utilization budgetary allocation in respect  of AIIMS, Jodhpur picked up very slowly. The 
Committee wonders that the percentage utilization was nil in the year 2011 -12, 39.48% in 
2012-13, 47.64% in 2013 -14, 61.56% in 2014 -15, 32.53% in 2015 -16, 50.63% in 2016 -17, 
74.16% in 2017 -18 and 70.09% in 2018 -19 (up to 15.10.2018). The Committee berates that 
Jodhpur management failed to monitor over the implementing agencies during the course of 
execution of construction projects resulting into under -utilization of funds in the initial years 
for Grants-in-Aids (capital). The Committee laments that the trend of expenditure witnessed 
an increase only after the year 2016 -17 that speaks of limited absorption capacity of 
implementation agencies. 
 (Para 4.4 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
 
1.13.2 In the initial phase all  the departments became operational gradually depending upon 
the availability of the faculty, equipment, etc. It is also stated that budget estimate under GIA -
General and Salaries were estimated on higher side with the expectations of recruitment of 
faculty and other staff being in place, higher footfall in IPD and OPD and implementation of 
7th CPC. However, a good number of faculty position remained unfilled due to non -
availability of suitable candidates. Due to this, all the departments could not be 
operationalised as envisaged resulting in underutilization of funds under GIA -Salaries and 
GIA-General. However, more faculty and other supporting staff being on board w.e.f. 2016 -
17 and almost 90% departments being operational by 2017 -18 and implementation of 7th 
CPC for Faculty and Non-faculty, budget utilization position has improved substantially since 
2017-18 as brought out in Para 4.3 above in the later years.  
 
1.13.3 The releases have always been made based on the demand of the respective AIIMS 
only after obtaining the utilization certificates. Larger amount of funds were released to the 
AIIMS to enable them to complete the remaining DPR works and to expand the healthcare 
services. As regards underutilization of funds under GIA -Creation of Capital, it is submitted 
that the details of expenditure as provided in the aforesaid table contains only the expenditure 

17 
 
made towards procurement of medical equipment by AIIMS, Jodhpur. The expenditure on 
construction activities was booked by  MoHFW. It was only in the y ear 2015 -16 that all 
payment related to RA Bills of construction activities was transferred to AIIMS, Jodhpur vide 
MoHFW letter No. Z. 28016/267/2 014-SSH dated 31.08.2015. Thus, depicting gradual 
increase in the budget utilization over the years. The Insti tute and Ministry shall take 
necessary action for optimum utilization of funds and shall also ensure effective financial 
monitoring mechanism in future.  Effective financial monitoring and optimum utilization of 
funds are now being ensured as would be seen from the updated status given in Para 4.3. It is 
also evident that total utilization of the funds during the financial years 2019 -20 and 2020-21 
is up to 90.91% and 92.49% respectively. Therefore, the Institute has ensured optimum 
utilization of the funds as per GFR norms. 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
1.13.4 The Committee was given to understand by the Ministry/Institute that the funds 
received were sufficient to meet the construction activities and on-going development projects 
at the Institute. The Com mittee believes that the problematic aspects relate to timely 
execution of the projects. The Committee, therefore, arrives at the conclusion that had the 
implementing agencies executed all segments of the projects in time, with required absorption 
capacity, there would have been optimum utilization of allocated funds and lesser delays. The 
Committee is of the considered view that had the Institute and the Ministry undertaken proper 
planning and periodic monitoring of the project work there would have been o ptimal and 
judicious utilization of resources. The Committee, therefore, recommends to the Ministry to 
institute an enquiry to assess the actual reasons for under -utilization of allocated funds for 
execution of construction projects and accordingly apprise  the Committee of the action taken 
against the implementing agencies as per terms and conditions of the contract. 
 (Para 4.5 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
 
1.13.5 It is submitted that the major reasons for delay in Project is due to delay in 
construction activities happened on account of systematic issues. These delays are attributed 
due to delay in release of GFC drawings and delay in approval of variation, work on hold in 
want of non -finalization of MGPS, Modular OT, CSSD, Kitchen equipment & delay on 
approval due to change in layout or original plans of D&T OT 2nd to 6th Floor. The matter 
has been resolved and  at present the work of modular OT is in progress by M/s MDD & 
accordingly civil work is also in progress as per revised drawing by M/s L&T. Institute  shall 
also ensure proper planning and periodic monitoring with coordination of implementing 
agencies leading to optimum and judicious utilization of funds. All efforts are being made to 
complete the remaining work, at the earliest. 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
1.13.6 The Committee is not convinced with the reasons given for underutilization of funds 
as these routine activities are often faced in the functioning of any institution. The delay in the 

18 
 
completion of projects has an adverse impact on the health care services to be provided by the 
Institute. The Committee expects the Department to uphold the principles of fiscal discipline 
and sound financial management by judiciously utilizing the remaining funds. Needless to 
say, that only proper planning, co -ordination with implementing agencies and suitable 
monitoring mechanism could have ensured optimum utilization of funds. 
 (Para 4.8 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
 
1.13.7 The observations / recommendation of the Hon‘ble Committee has been noted  for 
future guidance. With proper planning, coordination with implementing agencies and close 
monitoring, it has been possible to substantially improve the fund utilization position in 2018 -
19 as brought out in Para 4.3 above. Attempts have been made by Ministry to furt her fine-
tune the releases using PFMS so as to maintain a fund balance of about 03 months 
requirement. The Institute and Ministry shall take necessary action for optimum utilization of 
funds and shall also ensure effective financial monitoring mechanism in future. 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
1.13.8 The Committee opines that diversion of funds is a result of lack of effective financial 
control and monitoring of actual utilization. Such diversion amounts to misappropriation of 
allocated fund for the intended purpose. The Committee, thus, recommends framing of proper 
guidelines to control such diversion. The Committee, in this connection, strongly recommends

proper accounting procedure for an effective internal financial control. 
 (Para 4.10 of the Report)

1.13.9 The observations / recommendation of the Hon‘ble Committee have been noted 
carefully and Institute would ensure due care for utilization of GIA f or the intended purpose

1.14 STATUS OF CONSTRUCTION WORK 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
1.14.1 The Committee expresses its anguish to observe faulty drawings in the construction 
project and subsequent shifting of OT from 2nd floor to 6th floor in AIIMS, Jodhpur as the 
same constituted the reasons for delay in the completion of construction projects. Th e 
Committee wonders that the faulty design in the original drawing was not taken seriously at 
the initial stage. The Committee, therefore, recommends that accountability for such faulty 

19 
 
design should be fixed and a detailed report on the reasons for the de lay in the 
operationalization of the OTS be submitted to the Committee for its consideration. The 
Committee also recommends that the remaining work of package II be completed within the 
specified deadline. The Ministry in tandem with institute management m ust oversee and 
ensure timely execution of all projects. 
 (Para 4.13 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
 
1.14.2 The observations / recommendation of the Hon‘ble Committee has been noted  for 
future guidance. The Institute is working to ensure that remaining work to be completed at the 
earliest possible without further delay.  It is submitted that the Operation Theatres (MOT) 
were not shifted from 2nd to 6th floor. The Operation Theatres at AIIMS Jodhpur are from 
2nd to 6th floor and further only internal changes in drawing were made keeping the 
functionality in mind. As the drawings of the construction project were completed well before 
the tender of modular operation theatres were envisaged/planned at All India Institute of 
Medical Sciences (AIIMS), Jodhpur. The bas ic modular operation theatre designs and the 
tender requirement for Modular operation theatres necessitated the following changes: - 
 
1. Provision for Dedicated Air Handling Units (AHU‘S) for individual operation theatres 
is a mandatory part of Modular ope ration theatre with each modular theatre requiring a fine 
control of both the temperature and humidity as per the revised guidelines for air conditioning 
in operation theatres issued by NABH (Extract of relevant page of Guidelines is enclosed for 
reference). This was not provided for in the original drawings and needed to be added as per 
the requirements for modular operation theatres. 
 
2. Setting up of Modular operation theatre also required the creation of Uninterrupted 
Power Supply (UPS) for each operati on theatre complex to ensure continuous trouble free 
service. This was not provided in the original drawings and needed to be added as per the 
requirement for modular operation theatres. 
 
3. There is also a requirement for an internal passage/connectivity between the Intensive 
Care Units and the operation theatres to allow for movement of sick patients between these 
two interdependent and critical areas of the hospital. The connectivity was not provided for in 
the original drawings necessitating modifications. 
 
4. Due to the above mentioned mandatory provisions for AHU, UPS and ICU 
connectivity, a partial rework of the floor plan and drawings was extremely vital and 
indispensable. Only the vital and necessary changes were incorporated. 
 
1.14.3 At present, al l 30 Nos Modular OTs have been completed in all respect and are fully 
functional. The works awarded to all the 04 packages of AIIMS Jodhpur have already been 
completed. 
 
 
 
 

20 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
1.14.4 The Committee would like to draw the attentio n of the Institute to the recent 
observation by the CAG in context of AIIMS Jodhpur, where it has mentioned about price 
escalation in violation of contract, repeated grant of time extension, release of payment 
despite poor workmanship, excess release of mo bilization advance and avoidable/extra 
contractual payments. The Committee is also of the view that replies of the Ministry are not at 
all acceptable and the difference between the original and the final cost cannot be considered 
beyond the purview of cost  escalation. From the information provided by the Ministry, it is 
evident that there has been cost overrun of Rs. 9.00 crore under package I and Rs. 18.00 crore 
under package II. Even if the cost of construction of these projects did not increase during th e 
staggered period of six years, it implies that cost evaluation/calculation was inflated to such a 
great extent in the initial stage itself. The Committee wonders as to how the original cost -
estimation of the projects was done. The Committee, therefore, s eeks reasons/explanation 
over the cost-estimation of the projects in all the four packages. 
 (Para 4.15 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
 
1.14.5 It is submitted that the work under package I and Package II AIIMS Jodhpur had been 
executed as per Good for Constru ction (GFC) drawings issued by the Design DPR. The 
increase in completion cost of Package-I is due to variations. These variations occurred due to 
erroneous BOQ and difference in BOQ & GFC drawings. There was no escalation clause 
existed in package I contr act agreement and hence accordingly no payment toward escalation 
had been allowed.  The sanction for package II was based on tendered BOQ cost only, the 
escalation to be paid as per in built clauses of contract was left out from the sanctioned cost, 
may be due to an oversight. The escalation had been allowed in package II as per contract 
agreement only after Financial Advisor AIIMS Jodhpur scrutiny & concurrence.  There has 
been saving in package III & package IV completion cost. The total project cost of all the four 
packages together is within permissible limits of 10%. 
 
1.14.6 The works were in progress so provisional extensions were granted to keep the 
contract alive without prejudice to the right of the government to levy compensation in 
accordance with the provisions under clause 2 of contract agreement and also as per provision 
of CPWD Works Manual.  The works had been executed as per approved drawings, 
specifications and contract agreement. The original cost estimation of all the four packages 
had been p repared by Design DPR consultant through in house consultant M/s HLL.  As has 
been apprised to the CAG, the additional mobilization advance was paid to the respective 
contractors due to financial crunch being faced by them. Several firms in the civil 
construction business were facing liquidity crunch during that period. 
 
1.14.7 It would be relevant to bring out here that the Government charged market rate interest 
from the contractors and hence the advance may not be viewed as a financial assistance. 
Further, the mobilisation advance including first mobilisation advance was sanctioned to 
contractors against a bank guarantee. The advances were recovered in full along with interest. 
It would also be a relevant consideration that this intervention did actually h elp in completion 

21 
 
of the Medical college package in the respective Institutes. The Ministry might have landed 
up with contractual complications and incomplete works as has actually happened with 
respect to many other packages, if the Ministry had not suppo rted the contractors facing the 
financial crunch. 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
1.14.8 The Committee, further, observes that under package III and package IV, there has 
been time overrun of approximately three years. The Committee feels that the delayed 
execution of the projects in turn, has severely hampered the healthcare services to the patients 
during this period. Such delays have impaired the capacity of the Institute to provide the 
envisaged levels of treatment, health care and medical education. Th e Committee desires the 
Ministry to assess the genuine reasons for delay in the execution of the projects under 
construction and apprise the Committee in this regard. The Ministry must conduct detailed 
site investigation, hold regular meetings and formulat e effective monitoring mechanism to 
ensure that the project is managed efficiently after meticulous scheduling of work. 
 (Para 4.17 of the Report) 
Action Taken

1.15 Procurement of Medical Equipment 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
1.15.1 The Committee appreciates the role played by the Assessment Committee in 
procurement of medical equipment. However, the Committee is constrained to note that no 
separate analysis has been done for the procurement of equipment, thus indicating  that the 
equipment have been purchased without analysing the cost of the equipment vis -à-vis its 
actual utility. The Committee is of the view that procurement of equipment without proper 
cost-benefit analysis may result in underutilization/non -utilization/ duplication of equipment 
and procurement of equipment at higher prices. The Committee, therefore, recommends to the 
Institute/Ministry that proper cost -benefit analysis must be done by the Assessment 
Committee before the procurement of the equipment so t hat the utility of the equipment is 
explicit commensuration to its cost leading of effective delivery to health services. This 
analysis should form the part of the procurement process. The Committee also reiterates its 
observation made in context of AIIMS,  Rishikesh (para 3.26) for the procurement of da -vinci 
robotic arm. The Committee also recommends that the Assessment Committee must go into 
the details of reasons for proprietary/ single bid purchases and submit a status Report to the 
Committee along with a quarterly update on the usage of da-vinci robotic arm. 
 (Para 4.22 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
 
1.15.2 The observations / recommendation of the Hon‘ble Committee has been noted for  
future guidance. As the institute is being established, the procurement of medical equipment 
is being done for the first time and is in line with usual equipment available in similar 
departments across other similar INIs. No formal cost -benefit analysis has been done for 
procurement of medical equipment. However, whenever depa rtment requests for an 
equipment, it does an internal exercise regarding its requirement / essentiality patient care. 
The assessment committee, then thoroughly evaluates the cost justification, the proposed 

23 
 
benefit for healthcare and a proper justification  for expenditure over other competing 
requirements of other departments. It is only after a thorough deliberation & discussion that 
the assessment committee approves the purchase of each and every equipment.  However, the 
institute wishes to put on record t hat the other AIIMS were established with a mandate to 
establish a centre of excellence in healthcare and to reduce the workload on AIIMS Delhi. 
The recommendation that high -end equipment should only be limited to AIIMS Delhi goes 
against the mandate of th e new AIIMS and is likely to be counterproductive by stymieing the 
future growth of the institution. Till date 104 robotic surgeries have been done in the Institute. 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
1.15.3 The Committee is anguished to observe the delay in installation of equipment on the 
account of procrastination in the construction of new OTs. This is a peculiar situation when 
equipment has been purchased without ascertaining a place for its installation. The Committee 
believes that delay in installation of equipment may lead to expiry of guarantee/warranty of 
the equipment, service period. The Committee, thus, recommends that equipment should be 
procured only when space for their installation is ready so as to avoid undue delay in the 
installation and allay the fear of expiry of guarantee/warrantee of the equipment. Not just this, 
equipment should not be allowed to remain idle / unutilized. The Committee, further, 
recommends that the Ministry should expedite the process of construction of new OTs 
immediately so that the installation of procured equipment is ensured at the earliest. 
 (Para 4.24 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
 
1.15.4 The observations / recommendation of the Hon‘ble Committee have been noted for  
future guidance. Anaesthesia work stations pending installation (HLL/PCD/PMSSY/AIIMS-
II/03/14-15/7344) were received at AIIMS Jodhpur in January 2018 and OT table for CTVS 
department (HLL/PCD/PMSSY/AIIMS -II/21/15-16/6428) in March 2016. The procurement 
process for the above medical equipment was done by M/ s HLL Life Care Ltd. based on the 
directions of the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare for all the new AIIMS including 
AIIMS, Jodhpur way back in 2014 -2015 and 2015 -2016 respectively. AIIMS, Jodhpur 
ensures that the procured instruments are installed pr omptly and in time as soon as the 
site/user department is ready for installation. 
 
1.15.5 It is also stated that the delays in construction also adversely impacted the equipment 
delivery schedule leading to delays in supply and installations of equipment's . The concerns 
highlighted in the CAG report have been noted. In fact, realizing the problems of delays in 
installation of equipment's, since 2016 the procurement orders have been synchronized with 
progress of construction and progress of manpower recruitm ent. The human resource has also 
been appointed in almost all cases. Presently, there are hardly any cases where the installation 
of medical equipment's is being delayed or the same is lying unused.  Guarantee/ warranty and 
service period usually starts fro m the date of installation of machines/ medical equipment. 
Hence, it will not affect the guarantee/ warranty period. AIIMS, Jodhpur is committed to early 
installation of procured equipment and the same will be done as soon as the new OTs is ready

Recommendations/Observations  
 
1.15.6 The Committee understands that AIIMS, Jodhpur is meant for t he needy and poor 
patients requiring tertiary health care facilities  where quality of equipment can be lifesaving 
for the patients. The Committee, however, observes that since basic equipment like OT Light 
System, Laparoscopic Set, Suction Machine, Multipa ra Monitor and many others are easily 
available with European and also with Indian manufacturers. The procurement of these 
medical equipment with USFDA certification should have been resorted to only in the rarest 
of circumstances, after ensuring, in writi ng, that no alternative with CE/BIS certification is 
available. The Committee desires to be apprised of the reasons for procurement of the above 
mentioned devices with USFDA certification when equivalent quality and lower price 
CE/BIS certified equipment were available. 
(Para 4.29 of the Report) 
 
1.15.7 The Committee is of the considered view that procurement of equipment with BIS 
certification will encourage companies to manufacture their products in India and also 
increase their investment. This will also  contribute to ―Make in India‖, programme of the 
Government of India to promote domestic manufacturers. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends to the Ministry to issue strict directions to all AIIMS like institutions to procure 
equipment with wider certification standards so as to promote competitive pricing and also to 
encourage ―Make in India‖ scheme. 
 (Para 4.30 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
 
1.15.8 It has been submitted by AIIMS Jodhpur that the OT Lights, Laparoscopic sets, 
suction machines for operation t heatres, multipara monitors etc are high end equipment and 
are critical components towards providing quality care especially in Intensive Care Units, 
Operation Theatres and for emergency services. Especially, All India Institute of Medical 

25 
 
Sciences, Jodhpur, being an apex tertiary care Institution in the country, has the mandate to 
provide the best healthcare to the needy population being served by it and never attempts to 
dilute the patient care being provided to them by procuring substandard equipment. Regarding 
the use of USFDA, the technical committee evaluated the requirement for quality 
certifications and used USFDA only in following circumstances –  
 
1.  Required circumstances on advice of technical committee. 
 
2. The committee is of the opinion that optimal quality of medical equipment will be diluted 
in case of utilizing any other quality certification. 
 
 3. Or in cases where adequate indigenous medical device certifications have not been laid 
down for a particular medical equipment in India. 
 
1.15.9 It may also be mentioned here that the Ministry vide OM dated 20.02.2018 has issued 
guidelines for adopting the BIS standards also as an option to bidders, wherever available, and 
since then procurement is being made accordingly. The Ministry has already initiated action 
in this regard. Secretary, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare vide letter dated 7 th May, 
2018 to Director General, Bureau of Indian Standards requested formulation of specifications 
for all the commonly procured medical equipment to pro mote ‗Make in India‘ policy of the 
Government of India. Bureau of Indian Standards has already started creation of BIS 
standards for Medical Equipment and Devices. As per information available with the Ministry 
around standardization list for around 1000 medical devices have almost been completed.

for MRI scans. The Committee also notes that AIIMS Patna on an average conducted only 5

machine at its disposal, the Institute could have easily carried out more than twenty scans in

study visit observed that RIMS Imphal conducted 30 MRI scans per day on a very old 
machine and also carried out over 50 CT scans. The Committee desires a quarterly update 
from AIIMS Patna on the per day usage of MRI machine along with the daily pending cases .

only be done when the present MRI machine is optimally utilized.

Recommendations/Observations

procurement of the equipment. The Committee observes that sometimes even after multiple 
floating of tender, only single bid is received and there are few cases when multipl e bids are

there is a need to advertise the tender to be floated on a large scale so that more and more

advertise their tenders in the national dailies and also integrate into the system of the Central

proprietary / single bid basis should be avoided under all circumstances. The Committee 
would like to highlight that the problem areas as identified by AIIMS, Bhubaneswar are 
welcome since it would help the procedural hurdles and help in overall streamlining of the 
whole process of procurement of medical equipment. The idea of finalizing uniform  technical

1.46.1 The Committee fe els that the Ministry has not devised scientific criteria/parameters 
for the selection of GMCs under PMSSY. The Committee feels that the criteria of socio -
economic indicators, mainly the presence of already existing tertiary healthcare facilities, 
should also be taken into account. The Committee also take into cognizance that many GMCs 
have been selected without consulting the respective States and even without considering their 
financial condition and even without entering into any MoU with the State Gover nments.

the agencies has been taken into consideration. To consider HLL/HSCC as a panacea for all

Committee recommends for involvement of better professional agencies or other reputed 
construction majors to ensure cost effective and timely execution especially in projects where 
HSCC has failed t o ensure timely completion of the construction projects. The Committee

1.52 CONCLUSION 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
1.52.1 The Committee observes that upgradation project of GMCs under PMSSY has failed 
to provide the desired results which were expected from the project. The Committee opines 
that there is a big gap between planning and the execution of the project due to lack of 
synchronization and coordination of activities and serious gaps between planning and 
implementation of the scheme. The Committee feels that the inadequate project management 
and related delays impacted the delivery of envisaged benefits in terms of improve ment in 
health infrastructure. The reasons for delay in upgradation project are mainly due to non -
availability of encumbrance free land, delays in getting clearances for excavation and tree 
cutting and other site related conditions, changes made in the sco pe and quantum of work, 
delay in finalization/tendering of medical equipment. Apart from all these, poor planning and 
coordination contributed to delays in upgradation of GMCs. The Committee appreciates the 
potential in the scheme to transform the Governme nt Medical Colleges in providing quality 
health services to the people. The Committee is therefore of the firm view that projects 

65 
 
require meticulous planning and consistent efforts for timely execution/completion. The 
Committee believes that preparatory ac tivities should be completed beforehand which should 
include realistic assessment of requirement of equipment, availability of site, analysis of 
manpower and utilization of funds for the purpose it is earmarked. The Committee 
recommends to the Ministry to work in tandem with the State Governments to work in a  
coordinated manner to accomplish the objective and mission of up - gradation of GMCs as 
envisaged in PMSSY. 
  (Para 8.67 of the Report) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.52.2 As per Memorandum of Understanding signed be tween the Ministry of Health and 
Family Welfare and the concerned State Government for upgradation of GMCIs under the 
PMSSY, the responsibility of providing encumbrances -free land rests with the concerned 
State Government. Given the fact that the State Gov ernment is advised to provide the land for 
development of campus, invariably some hindrances, both natural and manmade like nalah, 
road, pipelines, etc are encountered. As the delay in land availability and securing all statutory 
clearances for the project s are critical conditions precedent for the start of any project, the 
Ministry actively coordinates with the concerned State Government authorities for  timely 
resolution of such land related issues and statutory clearances.

1.54 SITE SELECTION OF AIIMS LIKE INSTITUTIONS 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
1.54.1 The Committee is of the view that site selection for any AIIMS like Institution 
requires a detailed assessment of the geographical location and the demographic distribution. 
Easy accessibility and transportation availability is one major concern. The Committee is also 
concerned at the duplication and concentration of tertiary care services at a particular place. 
The Committee notes that at several places like Guwahati, Patna and now in Madurai (where 
a new AIIM S has just been announced) the Government had already selected GMCs for 
upgradation programme under PMSSY. In the places that have been selected for setting up of 
AIIMS like Institutions, the critical gap in the tertiary health care is already being filled  by 
private sector. The Committee strongly believes that AIIMS should be located in an area with 
low Human Development Index that lags behind in tertiary health care. 
  (Para 9.4 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
 
1.54.2 Observations / Recommendations of the Committee have been noted for future 
guidance. The Ministry while finalizing the upgradation projects has given higher priority to 
the States generally considered ―backward‖ with respect to the broad socio -economic 
indicators. The State has also agreed to ope rate and maintain the facilities created, so 

67 
 
willingness of the State to contribute its share and participate in the scheme is also important 
factor apart from backwardness. As per the EFC notes available with the Ministry, all projects 
have been selected on the basis of demands raised by States and therefore the States were 
fully involved in the selection process. 
 
1.54.3 The Ministry has its own database under National Health Mission on penetration and 
reach of healthcare facilities throughout the country . Each State in the country also vies for 
central assistance in setting up of more medical facilities in their respective States.  The 
Ministry has also adopted the ―Challenge method criteria‖ as conveyed by Cabinet Secretary 
(vide D.O. 272/1/3/2016 – CA.V dated 20.9.2017) for selection of sites so that most suitable 
sites get selected for setting up of AIIMS.  ―Gaps in the availability of tertiary healthcare 
facilities is also a consideration under the ―Challenge method‖ in selection of Sites. However, 
the M inistry is also dependent on the States in this matter as, in the first place, the States 
offers alternative sites and a site can only be selected out of the sites offered.  The ―Challenge 
method Criteria‖ referred above is being strictly followed in the ma tter of selection of sites 
out of the sites offered by the State Governments. 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
1.54.4 Attention of the Committee has also been drawn to a strange criterion for selection of 
site for AIIMS like Institute. Air connectivity to t he place has been one of the major basis for 
site selection for AIIMS. It has been reasoned out that airport services will facilitate 
employment of better trained human resources as most doctors are reluctant to serve in remote 
areas. 
 
(Para 9.5 of the Report) 
 
1.54.5 The Committee observes that all the six AIIMS under Phase I are well connected and 
are major cities in their respective States but still these new AIIMS are plagued by acute 
shortage of manpower. There is no faculty from AIIMS Delhi or other p remier Institutes 
working full time as Head of Department or as Professors in the new AIIMS. Therefore, the 
Committee is of the opinion that the perception that availability of an airport facility results in 
faculty retention is based on a false premise. T he Ministry and the Institute could have 
addressed this issue with better manpower planning rather than focusing on feasibility of 
airport. 
 
  (Para 9.6 of the Report) 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.54.6 AIIMS is a tertiary care Institute hence quality of doctors and me dical personnel is of 
paramount importance. It is also a fact, that availability of quality faculty, medical personnel, 
engineering and others is the most crucial impediment in functionalization of the AIIMS. 
Considering that most of the faculties and othe rs are recruited from existing Institutes of 
National Importance (INIs) / prestigious Institutes; they are not based in site locations of 

68 
 
respective AIIMS. Hence to facilitate their movement one of the criterions for setting up of 
AIIMS considers air connectivity of that particular location.  
 
1.54.7 In new AIIMS, most of faculty who have joined are trained in INIs like AIIMS, New 
Delhi/PGIMER/JIPMER/NIMHANS and other reputed Institutes like SGPGI & CMC, 
Vellore at their PG level or as SR / Faculty or in ot her capacity. Many of the Head of the 
Department in AIIMS are from different INIs or from other reputed Institutes.  Air 
connectivity is one of the many issues plaguing the availability of faculty in these Institutes. 
From the faculty perspective, there are  other constraints like availability of quality 
infrastructure like Schools, Colleges and Higher Education etc. at par with metros. Hence, 
faculties from AIIMS, Delhi or other premier Institutes do not generally prefer to join these 
Institutes as facilit ies are not at par with Delhi. Hence, there are multiple reasons for which 
availability of faculty suffers. Attracting the best Talent for the Medical faculty positions is of 
paramount necessity and apart from the aspects like Air connectivity being one of t hem, best 
Schooling facilities and Higher Education facilities, Infrastructural facilities/support systems, 
recreational and Entertainment facilities are important for life beyond office hours. 
 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
1.54.8 The Committee strongly recommends that the Ministry while deciding the location of 
the new AIIMS must take note of the already existing healthcare infrastructure in the vicinity 
of the earmarked area so that duplication of healthcare facilities are avoided. The healthcare 
system should be such that delivery of medical facility and care is regionally distributed and 
even the remotest region is well within its outreach so as to address regional imbalances in 
provision of health care facilities. 
  (Para 9.7 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
 
1.54.9 Observations / Recommendations of the Committee have been noted for future  
guidance. Under the challenge method, the availability of already existing Health 
infrastructure is also taken into consideration. 
 
1.55 SELECTION OF PROJECT CONSULTANTS/CONTRACTORS 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
1.55.1 The Committee during the examination of the Demands for Grants has repeatedly seen 
unprofessionalism and delay in almost all the projects being executed by HSCC. During the 
course of its study visit to Gu wahati the Committee had a firsthand view of the manner in 
which improper planning by HSCC had resulted in major design flaws. The Committee, 
therefore, strongly feels that the Ministry should follow a fair and transparent method for the

competent to complete such big infrastructure projects, given the mixed track record of 
HLL/HSCC in other projects. 
  (Para 9.10 of the Report) 

69 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.55.2 Observations / Recommendations of the Committee have been noted. The new AIIMS 
works are now being assigned to empanelled PSUs having experience of building large 
hospitals and other building infrastructure. The PSUs are appointed as Executing Agencies 
(EAs) with full empowerment to take decisions on all contractual matters including power to 
award construction tenders. With this arrangement, the contractual matters need not have to 
come to Ministry for decision thus simplifying the process and also avoiding delays. The 
system of appointing Project Consultants (PC) has been discontinued in view of the 
unsatisfactory experience with Project Consultants in the first six AIIMS Projects. The system

and engineering and thus the problems of coordination between the Design Consultant and the

Recommendations/Observations  
 
1.55.3 The Committee observes that in all the new AIIMS like institutions, undue delay in 
construction activities resulted in cost and time overrun. It is surprising to note that the 
timeline for completion of the construction project was not met in any of the new AIIMS and 
was further extended by 5 to 7 years. CAG in its Report No 10 had also observed that the 
scheduled dates of completion of six new AIIMS of Phase -I were between August 2011 and

AIIMS and there were delays of about four to five years. 
(Para 9.11 of the Report)

buildings which in turn led to more delays and escalated the cost. A lot of time had to be
