(Para 9.12 of the Report) 
 
1.55.5 The Committee is aggriev ed at the failure of the Ministry to monitor the timely 
completion of the project, mainly the construction activities in all the new AIIMS like 
institutions. The Ministry should also ensure proper planning and timely execution for 
completion of project. Th e Institute should always conduct detailed site investigations with 
careful monitoring, collective working and effective coordination among all the stakeholders.

most common reason behind the inordinate delay. The Committee is of the view that the 

70 
 
Ministry could have explored the idea of appointing a single agency for architectural

of the consultants/contractors and employ a trusted company with a prove n track record of

  (Para 9.13 of the Report)

1.55.6 Observations / Recommendations of the Committee have been noted for  future 
guidance. In the light of the experience g ained with the first six AIIMS projects, the new

1.56 PROCUREMENT OF MEDICAL DEVICES AND EQUIPMENT 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
1.56.1 The Committee notes that the Procurement Support Agency (PSA) failed miserably in 
its task to ensure timely delivery and installation of the medical equipment. Reasons cited for 
non-installation of the medical equipment clearly highlight the fact that the PSA faile d to 
coordinate with the Institute that led to unnecessary delays. The Committee is of the opinion 
that the PSA in collaboration with the Institute should have resolved the user requirement, site 
details and other specific requirements with respect to the Medical Equipment well in 
advance. The Committee is highly disappointed by the performance of PSA and recommends 
for a strong monitoring of the function of PSA along with quarterly submission of a status 
Report on the procurement of medical devices/equipment to the Committee under the PMSSY 
scheme. 
  (Para 9.21 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
 
1.56.2 Observations / Recommendations of the Committee have been noted for future 
guidance. The deficiency as highlighted by the Hon‘ble Committee had been noted during 
implementation of the project. Hence in subsequent phase i.e. Phase  III of PMSSY, the Roles 
and Responsibilities of the Procurement Support Agency has been clearly demarcated in the 

72 
 
Procurement Policy of the PMSSY Division. Not only the role of the Procurem ent Agency 
but also the Roles and Responsibilities of the Executing Agency and respective Govt. Medical 
College under upgradation have also been spelt out. The quarterly status report on the 
procurement of medical devices/equipment to the Committee under t he PMSSY scheme will 
be submitted by PSA regularly. First Report from PSA (HITES) submitted. 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
1.56.3 The Committee notes that several medical devices and other equipment have been 
procured on single bid basis in all the AIIMS . In cases where multiple bids were allowed, 
many companies were rejected on technical grounds. The Institutes have insisted on US FDA 
certification even for basic equipment for which BIS/CE certified equipment of equivalent 
quality were available in the m arket. Superfluous expenditure was done to purchase beds, 
cushions, LED TV etc with US FDA certification. 
(Para 9.22 of the Report) 
 
1.56.4 The Committee strongly underlines the need to follow a competitive tendering 
mechanism for procurement of any equipm ent rather than a single bid tender procurement. 
Downright rejection on technical grounds should be avoided and any such rejection, if made, 
should always be substantiated by a detailed evaluation. The requirement of US FDA 
certification for even some of t he basic equipment is not only a burden on the exchequer but 
is also an outright contempt of the Make in India campaign. The Committee, therefore, 
strongly recommends that procurement of equipment/medical devices by the Institutes and the 
procurement agencies should be determined by quality, price and fair trade practice. 
(Para 9.23 of the Report) 
 
1.56.5 The Committee again emphasizes that non -transparent methods in tendering and 
award of contracts raises high chances of corruption, irregularities, non -value addition and 
encourage restrictive trade practices. Fair and equal opportunity to all the tenders promotes 
healthy competition and also offers the best price to the procurement agency. 
  (Para 9.24 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
 
1.56.6 Observations / Recommendations of the Committee have been noted for future 
compliance. Drugs Regulation Se ction of the Ministry issued guidelines regarding 
requirement / non -requirement of USFDA / CE certification, etc. in procurement of medical

intimated that they are allowing the standard of BIS or European CE or US FDA for PMSSY 
Procurement. In addition to above, in the MoA with the Procurement Support Agency (PSA),

73 
 
Recommendations/Observations

technical grounds and unnecessa ry delays caused during finalizing the technical specification 
of the equipment by individual AIIMS. In this regard, the Committee appreciates the 
suggestion of AIIMS Bhubaneswar and strongly recommends finalizing uniform technical 
specifications for equip ment especially high end/sophisticated equipment for all the AIIMS.

experts only after a detailed and scientific assessment. The Committee strongly recommends 
that the Ministry/Institute should give serious consideration to the suggestions of AIIMS 
Bhubaneswar for streamlining the procurement process. 
(Para 9.25 of the Report) 
 
1.56.8 The Committee further recommends that the other AIIMS like Institutions should 
emulate AIIMS Bhubaneswar that has procured 130 medical equipments with ISO/BIS

manufacturers thus boosting Government's flagship Make in India campaign. 
(Para 9.26 of the Report)

guidance. The procurement process is being further streamlined in view of various 
suggestions and recommendations of the Committee. A Team of technical expe rts is involved

1.56.10 The Committee also appreciates the guidelines regarding requirement/non -
requirement of US FDA /CE certification etc. in the procurement of medical devices. The 
Para 2(i) of the guideline clearly states that wherever the Indian Standards are available th e 
Hospitals/Health Institutes/Organizations shall not insist on USFDA or CE certification. The

opportunity to the indenting organization to purchase medical equipme nt with USFDA 
certification in the name of quality. 
(Para 9.27 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
 
1.56.11 Observations / Recommendations of the Committee have been noted for future  
compliance. Every possible step is being taken to minimize procurement of US FDA / 

74 
 
European CE marked equipments by the Ministry / AIIMS and promote Make in India 
medical equipments. For procurement of medical equipments under PMSSY, the

Recommendations/Observations  
 
1.56.12 The Committee notes that even simple devices are being procured with 
USFDA mandatory certification in the backdrop of the discretionary  element in the 
guidelines. The Committee terms such provision as just another attempt to camouflage the

of indigenously produced medical equipment will promote a nd encourage companies to 
manufacture their products under the "Make in India" scheme creating thereby additional

Committee, therefore, recommends that spirit of the guideline under reference must be

1.57 QUALITY OF MEDICAL EDUCATION 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
1.57.1 The Committee observes that providing quality education and producing better trained 
doctors is a major challenge for the new AIIMS like Institutions. The Committee also notes 
that some of the new AIIMS have started Post Graduate courses in diffe rent disciplines. 
Attention of the Committee has been drawn to the fact that the Post Graduates from these 
Institutes lack the required clinical exposure and practical training which should have been 
integral for all Graduates/Post Graduates in the AIIMS. 
(Para 9.37 of the Report) 
 
1.57.2 The Committee is of the considered view that starting PG courses is irrelevant until 
and unless the Institute is able to provide quality training under the supervision of full time 
expert faculties. The Committee strongly emphasizes the importance of proper clinical 
training of the postgraduate students. The Committee further recommends that the AIIMS like 
Institutions should emphasize on the applied aspects of various disciplines through practical 
training. AIIMS like Inst itutions should be the frontrunner in filling the critical gaps in the 
health sector by producing well trained specialists in different disciplines. 
(Para 9.38 of the Report) 
 
1.57.3 The Committee is also concerned to note that most of the AIIMS do not hav e any 
faculty at the HOD/Professor level from AIIMS Delhi or PGI or JIPMER or any premier 
National Institute. The experience and expertise of faculty/HOD has an impact on the quality 
of Medical Graduates. In most of the AIIMS, the faculty lacks any teachin g experience from 
any of the premier Institutes. This raises serious concern about the dilution of the AIIMS 
Delhi benchmark. The Committee would also like to be apprised of the number of clinical 
cases, discipline wise that have been dealt by the PG students from various Departments. 
(Para 9.39 of the Report) 
 
Action Taken  
 
1.57.4 The concerns of the esteemed Committee are noted for future guidance. The Institutes 
have also been sensitized in this matter.  The matter  of starting new PG courses are first 
deliberated in the Academic Committee meeting and courses are added after ensuring that HR 
and facilities are available to provide sufficient clinical exposure and practical training to the 
PG students.  Most of the faculty in all AIIMS has been trained in I NIs and other reputed 
Institutes at the level of PG/SR/Faculty. Many of the existing HODs have worked in AIIMS, 
New Delhi/PGIMER/JIPMER/SGPGI prior to joining at new AIIMS. All faculties have the 
prescribed teaching/research experience and most of them hav e trained from INIs.  The 
faculty members are being selected by the Standing Selection Committee purely on the basis 
of merit maintaining the standards and all faculties have had experience of teaching, research 
and patient care. They train the PGs in accordance with established curricula. 
 

79 
 
1.57.5 AIIMS undertakes their responsibility of training of Post Graduate Students very 
seriously and provide therewith a structural training program in all Departments. Students 
have adequate clinical exposure in all cl inical departments with a wide variety of cases and 
diseases being treated. PG training program is carried out by each department through various 
modalities like Seminars, Journal Clubs, Interactive sessions, Case/Practicals/Community 
discussions. Post graduate students are assessed regularly through formative assessments. Post 
graduate students are involved in all activities of their departments including both teaching, 
research and patient care. The post graduate students are associated with all the clini cal cases 
both in OPD, IPDs, Operation Theatres, both in Surgical and Medical departments. As the 
patient footfall is high, a large number and variety of cases come to these AIIMS ensuring 
adequate clinical exposure of all PGs.  Efforts are made to creating  AIIMS like ―Culture of 
Excellence‖ in new AIIMS and a Visiting Committee under chair of Dr VK Paul constituted 
to identify gaps and help institutionalize systems for training, handholding and Faculty 
exchange programmes.

loans obtained from HEFA may result in a situation where the incumbent Directors of the 
regional AIIMS may retire but the new incumbent would be faced with a fresh challenge of 
servicing the loans obtained from HEFA. 
(Para 9.57 of the Report)

'The Audit Report of the CAG (Report No.19 of 2013 - Union Government -Civil) 
contained observations relating to irregularities in selection of project consultants, irregular 
expenditure on escalation charges amounting to Rs. 1.56 crore, in correct release of 
mobilization advance amounting to Rs. 8.32 crore to contractors, excess payment of Rs.25.20 
lakh to in -house consultant and release of payment to PSU consultants based on estimated 

89 
 
fund requirements instead of on actual progress of work.  In reply to the audit comments, the 
Ministry had stated that the audit findings were noted for avoidance of such occurrence in 
future. However, irregularities of similar nature have been noticed during the current audit 
as mentioned in Paras 2.5, 3.11, 4.4.2 (b) and 4.4.3 (iii) of this Report.' 
(Para 9.69 of the Report)

in setting up of new AIIMS and upgradation programme of Government Medical Colleges. 
The CAG Report No . 10 contains observations relating to cost and time overrun, excess 
payment of mobilization advance, delay in delivery and installation of medical equipment, 
shortage of faculty and non -faculty posts, non -functional speciality and super speciality 
Departments etc. The Committee would like to be apprised of the measures that have been 
taken by the Ministry and the Institutes to overcome all the inadequacies and address the 
CAG observations in its audit Report. 
(Para 9.70 of the Report) 
Action Taken  
 
1.65.6 The position on these observations has been adequately explained in Ministry‘s 
detailed reply. It is further stated that it is not a correct appreciation on the part of the CAG 
that irregularities of similar nature have occurred. The position on these obs ervations of CAG 
has been explained fully in Ministry‘s response to CAG . Institutes are taking necessary action 
to ensure that new construction projects are completed within the stipulated period of the 
contract. Similarly, procurement of medical equipment  are also processed where site for 
installation and faculty to operate the equipment are available.  It is stated that the several 
steps/policy interventions have been taken by the Government to improve the faculty position 
so as to ensure full functionality of all Departments under the six new AIIMS. In addition, the 
Ministry has also taken following policy initiatives for bringing about improved availability 
of trained HR at National Level at large. 
 
1.65.7 A Central Institute Body has been created and emp owered to take common policy 
decisions concerning all AIIMS to bring uniformity in policies across all AIIMS and to 
facilitate effective Governance of the AIIMS.  All AIIMS have been advised to conduct 
recruitments for Non -faculty (Technical) cadres on cent ralized basis. It has also mentioned 
here that presently the construction is being taken up in the EPC mode wherein extensive 
problem of large deviation / escalation would get systematically obviated. Further, the system 
of assigning the construction work to executing agencies on turnkey basis with empowerment 
to handle all contractual matters at their end has been introduced.  The executing agencies 
have been mandated to deploy and use Project Management Software to bring about 
improved project management at their end. The Ministry has also developed an online 
dashboard to facilitate a closer and more effective monitoring. The functional AIIMS have 
been empowered with greater delegation of powers in construction, procurement upto  Rs. 5 
crore in cases and al so in administrative matters. The procedure for procurement of medical 
equipment has been simplified and made more efficient with greater delegation and 
empowerment of the Procurement Support Agency (PSA) which is entrusted with the work of 

90 
 
procurement of medical equipments. All new AIIMS are now being designed keeping in view 
the ―GRIHA‖ norms for green buildings. 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
1.65.8 The Committee besides recommending for decentralization of healthcare facilities in 
the most remote areas  of the country is inclined to emphasize that central Government and 
State Government must make policy and chalk out strategy and formulate/appropriate course 
of action for delivering Health Care Services at the Doorstep with the purpose of making 
Ayushman Bharat a successful scheme. 
(Para 9.71 of the Report) 
 
Action Taken  
 
1.65.9 Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri - Jan ArogyaYojana (AB PM -JAY) is a flagship 
scheme of the Government which provides Rs 5 lakh health cover per beneficiary family 
annually for sec ondary and tertiary care to approx. 55 crore beneficiaries (12.37 crore 
economically vulnerable families). Recently, it expanded to cover approx. 6 crore senior 
citizens (70+) from 4.5 crore families, regardless of socio -economic status. Under Ayushman 
Bharat Pradhan Mantri Jan ArogyaYojana (AB PM -JAY) initially, 10.74 Crore beneficiary 
families under AB PM -JAY were targeted on the basis of the Socio -economic Caste Census 
(SECC) of 2011 using select deprivation and occupational criteria across rural and urb an 
areas respectively to identify the families. Further, in January 2022, on the basis of decadal 
growth rate of 11.7%, the Government of India, revised the beneficiary base to 12 Crore 
families. 
 
1.65.10 Further, in April 2022, as per the approval of Govt  of India, NHA had 
provided the flexibility to States/UTs to use non -SECC Aadhaar verified databases of similar 
socio-economic profile for verification of beneficiaries against such SECC beneficiaries who 
couldn't be identified and verified. Accordingly, m any States have used databases of poor and 
vulnerable families against unidentified SECC families. (including National Food Security 
Act, State specific datasets, etc).  In March 2024, 37 lakh families of ASHA, Anganwadi 
Worker and Anganwadi Helpers were al so included in the scheme.  Further, on 29th October 
2024, the Government expanded AB PM -JAY to provide free treatment benefits of up to ₹5 
lakh per year to all senior citizens aged 70 years and above, irrespective of their socio -
economic status. This aim to benefit approx. 6 crore s enior citizens from 4.5 crore families 
across the country.  In addition, many States/UTs implementing AB PM -JAY have expanded 
the beneficiary base under the scheme, at their own cost.

 Scheme has been implemented in all the States/UTs except West Bengal 
 Ayushman Cards Created: As on 01st April 2025, more than 40 Crore Ayushman 
cards have been created. 
 Hospitals Empanelled: A total of 31,005 hospitals are empanelled under the scheme 
out of which 13,879 empanelled hospitals are private and the rest are public.

 Fund Released to States:  In FY 2024 -25, approx. 6637 Cr have been released to 
States/UTs.

2.2 PROCUREMENT OF MEDICAL EQUIPMENT 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
2.2.1 The Committee understands that United States Food and Drug Administration 
(USFDA) is a regulatory mechanism/certification for protecting and promoting public health 
by way of control and supervision of food and drugs including medical devices with specif ic 
reference to the United States but there is hardly any country in the world besides the United 
States which makes a provision for allowing USFDA as a mandatory condition. The 
Committee fails to comprehend the reasons for procuring 50 equipment s with USF DA 
certification, some of which are easily available with CE marking and Bureau of Indian 
Standards (BIS) (CE/BIS) certification. The Committee, therefore, recommends to the 
Institute to procure equipment with CE/BIS certification so as to encourage Medica l Device 
Industry in India and participate in the Government's "Make in India" initiative. 
(Para 2.17 of the Report) 
 
Action Taken 
 
2.2.2 Drugs Regulation Section of the Ministry vide letter dated 20.02.2018 issued 
guidelines regarding requirement/ non -requirement of USFDA/ CE certification, etc. in 
procurement of medical devices/ equipment which was also circulated by the PMSSY 
Division to HLL/ HITES (Procurement Support Agency) / HSCC and all functioning AIIMS. 
PSA has intimated that besides USFDA they ar e also allowing option of BIS or European CE 
standard to the vendors as available, for PMSSY procurement . Procurement of Equipment in 
AIIMS, Bhopal is being done through their Procurement Support Agency (PSA) i.e. M/s 
HLL-HITES (PSA)/e-Tender/GeM in which following options are generally mentioned in the 
tenders for the purpose of wide range for economic selection of the equipment proposed to be 

95 
 
procured i.e. DCGI/CE (Europe)/USFDA/WHO/GMP/BIS/IS/CDSCO (whichever is 
applicable for medical devices /Equipment/ consumables). Besides above, adopting clause 
regarding purchase preference policy is also mentioned wherever possible to give thereby 
importance to ―Make in India‖ products. At present, the procurement of medical equipment at 
AIIMS Bhopal is carried out in  accordance with government guidelines through mandatory 
online platforms such as the GEM portal, CPP portal and procurement support agencies like 
HLL/HITES as per MOU.  The tender documents are designed to facilitate a broad  and cost-
effective selection of the equipment to be procured. 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
2.2.3 The Committee believes that the lackadaisical approach of the Institute has resulted in 
non-installation of the equipment which has delayed operationalization of the critical 
healthcare f acilities, thus, depriving the patients of key diagnostic and in -patient facilities. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends to the Institute to have a system in place for ensuring 
timely procurement as well as installation of the equipment so that the equipment are properly 
and optimally utilized for the purpose for which they were procured. The Committee also 
recommends for immediate installation of 21 types of equipment costing Rs. 27.9 crore that 
have been procured but not installed yet. The Committee furt her calls upon the Ministry to 
look into matter of procurement of 25 equipment costing Rs. 84.7 crore which are yet to be 
received and installed in AIIMS, Bhopal. In view of the delays in procurement and 
installation of equipment in the Institute, the Comm ittee impresses upon the Ministry to 
ensure effective monitoring through ABC analysis (Always a better control) by the Technical 
Specification Committees at the Ministry and institutional level to ensure much needed 
synchronization and coordination of acti vities with regard to procurement and installation of 
equipment. 
(Para 2.23 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
 
2.2.4 Presently, the construction of all infrastructure works has been completed. In the 
present system, there exist a check and balance to ensure time ly supply of equipment by 
forecasting the site readiness from the user end and other resources linked with installation of 
the equipment. Further, a suitable provision has been incorporated in tender document for 
work on turkey basis for smooth installatio n and commissioning of the equipment wherever 
applicable.  At present, AIIMS Bhopal does not have any equipment which is procurement 
and uninstalled.

2.4 ISSUE OF CONTRACTUAL APPOINTMENTS 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
2.4.1 The Committee was informed that the doctors of AYUSH Hospital have been working 
on contractual basis for the past several years. The Committee during its study visit found that 
the OPD footfall in the AYUSH centre was muc h higher despite limited infrastructure. The 
Committee appreciates the work ethics of the three AYUSH doctors in treating a large 
number of patients having faith in the Indian system of Medicine. The Committee feels that 
given the positive response towards  AYUSH services, the Ministry should contemplate of 
having a permanent staff instead of engaging contractual workforce. This would ensure job 
stability and security to the employees and in turn the organization would be benefitted from 
huge experience of t hese doctors gained during their service at AYUSH Hospital. The 
Committee, therefore, strongly recommends the Department to revisit the rules regarding 
contractual appointments so as to regularize the existing AYUSH doctors to permanent 
appointments in view of their dedicated service and outstanding performance.

D. AIIMS PATNA 
 
2.7 STATUS OF CONSTRUCTION WORK 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
2.7.1 It is a proven fact that delay in any construction activity leads to unnecessary 
additional costs and time extensions. Inflation, abrupt ending of contracts, arbitration cases, 
disputes etc further increases the cost of any delayed project. Systemic analysis at the 
inception of any project and regular monitoring can easily control all these factors  and 
minimize the chances of delay. Sadly, the Ministry and the Institute remained ignorant of both 
time and cost deadlines for the completion of the project as envisaged for AIIMS Patna. 
 (Para 5.10 of the Report) 
 
Action Taken 
 
2.7.2 In continuation of t he position explained in para 5.9, it is clarified that there has been 
no cost escalation as the project is within the original Cost estimates of approved DPR. The 
total Tender cost under four packages in this project was Rs.554.28 Cr., against which 
Rs.554.47 cr. has been incurred  and the project is almost completed which is well within the 
deviation limit. 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
2.7.3 The Committee observes with anguish that AIIMS Patna has failed to realize the 
implications of this sluggish rate of construction activities and is of the view that the reasons 
cited by AIIMS Patna for the construction delays are inexcusable and could have been easily 
avoided had the Institute been alert and committed for the Project. Moreover, the argument of 
AIIMS P atna that professional expertise in constructing hospital building is missing in the 
country is not tenable and bereft of fact and logic. 
(Para 5.12 of the Report) 

103 
 
 
2.7.4 The Committee is dismayed to note that no project management tool/strategy has been 
employed for construction of an AIIMS like institution that is intended to be the beacon of 
light for the tertiary healthcare sector in the State. A PERT or Program Evaluation Review 
Technique Chart is one such project management tool that helps in better a nalysis of the 
resources and the timeline of any project. In the absence of any evaluation technique, the 
Committee is really sceptical about the completion of the construction work under the 
remaining packages. The Committee recommends that a special project monitoring system for 
AIIMS Patna must be devised to track the progress of construction activities undertaken by 
the Institute so as to ensure better project management. The Committee strongly recommends 
that the work under Package II, III and IV must be completed on time with no further delays. 
 (Para 5.13 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
 
2.7.5 The observations/ recommendations of the Committee have been noted for future 
compliance.  All Project Packages are completed. 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
2.7.6 The Committee is at pains to take into account the improper estimation of quantities of 
items pointed out by CAG in its report. Surprisingly, the deviation is upto 173% in case of 
AIIMS Patna which clearly indicates that the requirement of different items  had been under-
assessed and unrealistic assessment of the site conditions were made. The green building 
norms and the Energy Conservation Building Code (ECBC) should have been implemented 
before the beginning of the construction activities. The Committee is highly distressed at the 
inadequate technical estimation made before the construction of AIIMS Patna. 
(Para 5.16 of the Report) 
 
2.7.7 The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should make a detailed 
technical and realistic assessment befor e setting up of other new AIIMS under PMSSY by 
carrying out proper field and site surveys and the errors while constructing AIIMS Patna 
should not be repeated. 
 (Para 5.17 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
 
2.7.8 It is submitted that there is no overall deviatio n in the project. The up to date payment 
made in PKG -1 is Rs.159.46 crore in final bill against tender cost of Rs. 160.69 crore. The 
final bill has not been paid so far. In PKG-II, the up to date payment made is Rs.306.03 crore , 
including escalation cost o f Rs.25 crore (approximately) against the tender cost of Rs.284.70 
crore. There is no overall deviation in package -1 & a minor deviation in package -due to 
escalation of Rs.25.00 crore. PKG-III-total cost incurred Rs.42.23 crore as against tender cost 
of Rs.42.60 cr. which well within the permissible limit and there is no deviation.  PKG-IV-
Total cost incurred Rs.46.74 crore as against tender cost of Rs.66.29 crore. The work is 
almost completed and there is no deviation. 

104 
 
 
2.7.9 The deviation of 158 -173% repor ted by CAG in its report is regarding certain 
individual items of work and not overall deviation. The deviation in individual items is due to 
less quantity taken in the estimate against the G.F.C. drawing issued by DOPR for 
construction of the buildings.  However, there are also savings in work quantity in number of 
items which is either not required or less quantity is required as per GFC drawing. It is also 
mentioned here that the contract agreement itself has provision of deviation limit of 30% or

being designed keeping in view the "GRIHA" norms for green buildings.  The status of 
different packages is provided as under:-

E. AIIMS RAIPUR 
 
2.8 PROCUREMENT OF EQUIPMENT 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
2.8.1 The Committee is of the further view that quality of medical equipment needs to be 
looked into because defective equipment result in frequent break down of health care services. 
Given the importance of medical equipment in diagnosis as well as treatment and the high 
price involved in purchase of several hi -tech equipment, it is imperative that the equipment 
are put to their best use for optimum utilization of re sources. Non-installation of equipment is 
indicative of lackadaisical approach of the Institute in letting them remain idle which is mere 
wastage of resources at the cost of taxpayers‘ money. The Committee, accordingly, 
recommends the Institute to take str ict action against the manufacturers for delayed delivery 
or delivery of defective equipment. The Committee, further, recommends that Institute should 
either exchange the defective equipment with new equipment or scrap the contract with the 
manufacturers by seeking adequate legal redressal. The Committee recommends for an action 

105 
 
taken status report on the specific observations of the CAG in context of procurement of  
medical equipment and recommends the Ministry to take strict action against the errant 
officials. 
 (Para 6.29 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
 
2.8.2 Due care is taken to ensure that there is no defective equipment delivered/ supplied by 
vendor.  In case of breakdown of any equipment, the warranty or the CMC clause takes care 
of the interest of patien t care. The Institute ensures strict action if any defective equipment is 
supplied or scrap the contract with the manufacturer by seeking adequate legal redressal.  
Some of the equipment as mentioned in the CAG report could not be installed as necessary 
civil infrastructure was not available at that time. The progress regarding installation of these 
equipment is monitored very closely at Institute level as well as in MoHFW. The delay due to 
non-availability of site and the reasons thereof have already been brought out against the reply 
of Point No 6.12.  Some defective equipment supplied through PSA, has been notified to M/s 
HLL so as to take necessary action against respective vendors as per the tender terms and 
conditions. However, the equipment as mentioned  in the CAG have since been installed and 
put in use. 
2.8.3 It is informed that AIIMS Raipur is an institute established under the PMSSY scheme 
of the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW), where patients receive treatment. 
The institute purchases medical equipment, ensuring adequate precautions are taken during 
the procurement process. Additionally, repair and maintenance of the equipment are 
performed in accordance with the tender conditions and contract. If any vendor fails to meet 
these conditions, the institute takes strict action. 
2.9 MEDICAL EDUCATION 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
2.9.1 The Committee feels that clinical training is a vital part in a medical education for 
becoming a successful doctor. The Committee is, however, apprehensive ab out the quality of 
the clinical training imparted at the Institute to the undergraduate and postgraduate students 
due to shortage of faculty at the Institute as many key Departments are being handled by a 
single faculty. The Committee wonders how an Instit ute is accomplishing the objective of 
imparting clinical training to the medical students with limited number of faculty. The 
Committee also notes that seats under many PG courses are lying vacant which raises a 
question mark about the quality of clinical training facilities available at the Institute. Poor 
clinical training hampers the professional pursuit of doctors which amounts to risking the 
lives of the patients. The Committee, therefore, recommends to the Institute to ensure 
adequate faculty at the I nstitute for imparting quality medical education and clinical training 
to the students aspiring to be well-trained doctors. 
 (Para 6.36 of the Report) 
 
 

106 
 
Action Taken 
 
2.9.2 So far as teaching of MBBS and BSc Nursing is concerned, it is to inform that AIIMS  
Raipur is having sufficient Faculty members and other required infrastructure from the 
beginning of these courses as Faculty members of Pre -clinical and Para -clinical and Broad 
Specialty departments were already available. The teaching and training of the se students are 
carried out without any compromise on quality and adequacy. Eight batches of MBBS and 
B.Sc. (Hons.) Nursing have successfully completed their course. A good performance of

2.10 STATUS OF OPERATION THEATRE (OTS) AND INTENSIVE CARE UNIT 
(ICUS) 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
2.10.1 The Committee notes with concern that only 26 beds out of total sanctioned strength 
of 100 beds are functional at the Institute. ICUs are used to provide sp ecialized rehabilitative 
care to patients as they start to recover from their critical illness or injury. The Committee 
believes that bed scarcity in ICU may result in refusal of admission to initial patients, thereby, 
depriving them the benefit of ICU services. The Committee observes that there are as many as 
35 ventilators for 26 ICU beds, indicating that 9 ventilators are lying unused in the ICUs. The 
Committee feels that the value of the equipment starts depreciating immediately after they are 
procured and non-functioning of the equipment results in loss of their value. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends to the Institute to increase the number of beds so that critically ill 
patients are not refused the service of ICUs due to scarcity of beds and focus on optimum 
utilization of resources available. 
 (Para 6.41 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
 
2.10.2 50 ICU beds are functional. AIIMS Raipur efficiently uses its available resources and 
equipment to provide care to the patients. However, patients are referred o nly for step down 
hospital care after diagnosis and essential treatment and stabilisation is done, so that more 
critical cases requiring immediate care may be accommodated.

2.13 STATUS OF OPERATION THEATRES AND WARDS/BEDS 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
2.13.1 The Committee is surprised to note the wide difference in the cost per bed in these two 
Institutes that have the same functional capac ity and the same number of beds. The 
Committee takes a serious note of this high cost incurred by AIIMS, Bhubaneswar especially 
when the other AIIMS like Institutions, providing the same tertiary health care facilities, have 
submitted relatively less cost. The Committee, therefore, recommends the Institute to limit its 

108 
 
redundant expenses. The Committee demands that the Institute should submit a status note on 
how the cost per bed was calculated and the reasons behind this high cost so that cost per bed 
may be calculated for other AIIMS also on the same parameters. 
 (Para 7.49 of the Report) 
 
Action Taken 
 
2.13.2 The Institute calculated the cost per bed at the time of furnishing information taking 
into consideration all recurring/non -recurring expenditure di vided by number of functional 
beds which was 560 at that point of time. The variation has occurred due to dividing 560 
functional beds with the total expenditure whereas AIIMS, Raipur might have calculated by 
dividing the total number of sanctioned beds i. e. 960. The numbers of functional beds have 
been taken as a lot of more expenditure will be incurred to make functional the remaining 
beds. Further, the recurring expenditure of AIIMS, Bhubaneswar may be higher in 
comparison to AIIMS, Raipur as the Hospita l services has started here earlier and the patient 
load is higher in comparison with AIIMS, Raipur.  The basis on which the Committee has 
determined that the cost per bed is significantly high remains unclear. It is important to note 
that AIIMS Bhubaneswar  is currently operating with 1,019 functional beds and 351 
temporary beds, bringing the total functional capacity to 1,370 beds.  If the cost per bed is 
recalculated based on this total capacity, the overall cost per bed may come significantly 
lower.

2.15 SELECTION OF PROJECT CONSULTANTS/CONTRACTORS 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
2.15.1 The Committee is of the view that the careless selection of the Project Consultants did 
more harm than good and caused unwarranted delays in the construction activity. The 
Ministry failed to make a comprehensive assessment of selection of proj ect-
consultants/contractors before the execution of the scheme. The CAG has also raised concerns 
regarding the award of consultancy work to PSUs on nomination basis in its Report. The 
Committee also notes that M/s HSCC and M/s HLL were appointed as consult ants on 
nomination basis under the garb of Rule 176 of General Financial Rules (GFR) 2005. This 
rule is always read with the section 1.5.3 that states the selection by direct negotiations/ 
nomination is permissible in terms of Rule 176 of General Financial  Rules, 2005 only under 
exceptional circumstances and such selection may normally be restricted to a financial ceiling 
of Rs ten lakhs. The Committee notes that the cases did not fall under any of the special 
circumstances stipulated in the section 1.5.3. 
(Para 9.9 of the report) 
Action Taken 
 
2.15.2 In addition to the above para the following pertinent points are mentioned below:  
 
The Project Consultants selected for six AIIMS are as under: 
 
Sl. AIIMS Project Consultant 
1. Bhopal M/s Enarch 
2. Bhubaneswar M/s Hospitech 
3. Jodhpur M/s Hospitech 
4. Patna M/s Enarch 
5. Raipur M/s Mukesh Associates 
6. Rishikesh  M/s SMEC 
 
2.15.3 HLL and HSCC were selected as Project Consultants after following due procedure as 
per extant rules, regulations and guideline s. It may be observed that all these companies are 
reputed ones in their respective fields. However, their abandonment of project at crucial time 
did create problems in continuation of works. From perusal of the para, it is noted that the 
Hon‘ble Committee is referring to reading of Rule 176 of GFR 2005 in consonance with Rule 
1.5.3. of Manual of Policies and Procedure of Employment of Consultants prepared by 
Ministry of Finance, Department of Expenditure in August, 2006. The attention of Hon‘ble 
Committee is being sought with the last para of the preface issued by the then Secretary, 
Department of Expenditure along with the Manual wherein it has been clearly stated that the 
manual is to be taken as generic guideline and to be interpreted broadly.  Moreover,  Section 
1.5.3 (b) explicitly permits appointment on nomination basis is done in situations where 
timely completion is of utmost importance. In view of the above the appointment of PSU, on 
nomination basis does not violate the Rule 176 along with Section 1 .5.3 of the Manual of 
Policies and Procedure of Employment of Consultants is followed.

Recommendations/Observations  
 
3.7.1 The Committee welcomes the positive response of the Minis try w.r.t. the merger of 
BMHRC with AIIMS Bhopal. The Committee also appreciates the concurrence of Director, 
BMHRC and the Department of Health Research to this merger proposed in public interest. 
The Committee is of the considered view that at present th ere is duplication of resources and 
services being offered in various medical fields leading to non -optimal utilization of high cost 
equipment and medical services. The BMHRC caters to a substantial population of gas 
tragedy victims and their dependents, i t may continue to do the same subsequent to the 
merger. BMHRC is well equipped to train paramedical workforce which can be produced by 
the hospital easily if the requisite faculty is made available. The Committee feels that merger 
of both hospitals would h elp in attracting and retaining medical faculty. The Committee feels 
that merger of BMHRC with AIIMS, Bhopal would increase scope of teaching and training 
avenues for doctors and students. The Committee, therefore, lends its full support to the 
merger of b oth Institutes for the benefit of the society. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that Department of Health & Family Welfare should work towards chalking out 

123 
 
necessary course of action for bringing BMHRC under its purview by merging it with AIIMS 
Bhopal. While doing so, the Department of Health & Family Welfare can look into utilizing 
the huge set up of BMHRC, Bhopal for putting in place a dedicated resource centre for both 
medical faculty and paramedical staff in order to have paramedical/clinical techni cians 
workforce in various fields. The synergy arising out of the merger of BMHRC with AIIMS, 
Bhopal would result in optimal utilization of the existing infrastructure and resources. The 
Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that administrative hurdles towards the merger of 
both the institutes should be removed as early as possible. 
(Para 2.60 of the report)

BMHRC, the recruitment rules which are different from  AIIMS (which happens to be an

complete merger is done so that the promotional avenues of the BMHRC doctors are 
protected. No fresh recruitment should be done under  BMHRC rules and the cadre of serving 
doctors be treated as a dying cadre for smooth transition of the merger process. The

the progress made within three months of presentation of this Report. 
(Para 2.61 of the report)

3.7.4 The Committee recapitulates the positive response of the Ministry w.r.t. the 
merger of BMHRC with AIIMS Bhopal before the Committee during it s discussion on

BMHRC with AIIMS Bhopal is in larger public interest and would ensure optimum 
utilization of resources, better faculty retention, and expanded traini ng and teaching 
opportunities, particularly while continuing to cater to the needs of gas tragedy victims. 
While noting that the Department of Health Research has decided against the merger, 
the Committee urges the Department of Health and Family Welfare  to revisit this 
decision in consultation with all stakeholders, keeping in view the long -term benefits for 
patients, medical faculty, and students. The Committee, therefore, recommends the 

124 
 
Department of Health and Family Welfare  to devise  a concrete roadmap  and time -
bound plan for resolving administrative hurdles and ensuring that the merger, along 
with protection of service conditions of existing BMHRC doctors during the transition, 
in the interest of public health and medical education.

Ministry to enhance faculty recruitment, including the steps initiated through the 
Central Institute Body (CIB) and the ongoing policy interventions. However, the 
Committee expresses the  concern that despite repeated advertisements, approxi mately 
one-third of the sanctioned faculty posts remain vacant, and recent recruitments were 
delayed due to the revision of the reservation roster. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that AIIMS Rishikesh must urgently finalize and operationalize the revised 
reservation roster and ensure that the pending faculty recruitment advertisement is 
issued without further delay. To avoid recurring procedural setbacks, the Committee 
further advises instituting a streamlined and time -bound recruitment protocol. Regul ar 
biannual recruitment cycles, as envisaged by CIB, must be strictly adhered to, and the

like to have a status report on efforts taken by  AIIMS Rishikesh and the Ministry

Professor are lying vacant. Further, four Departments i.e. Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation, 
Transfusion Medicine, Gastroenterology and Biochemis try are being handled by a single

The Committee is of the considered view that adequate incentives should be offered at Super 
Specialty l evel to attract faculty at senior level from premier institutes like AIIMS,

3.9 MEDICAL EDUCATION 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
3.9.1 The Committee observes that there are new courses being offered at the Institute viz. 
PhD, MSc Nursing, DM/M.Ch and there has been a increase in the number of seats in existing 
courses as also the number of courses being offered at the Institute. The Committe e 
recommends that enhancement of the PG seats at the Institute should be done only after 
ensuring that AIIMS, Rishikesh meets at least the minimum benchmarks as per MCI norms 
applicable to other medical college throughout the country. The Committee does no t accept 
the argument of the Institute that it is governed by the AIIMS Act and hence the minimum 
bench mark as per MCI norms are not applicable to it. This argument puts a question mark 
over the quality of learning and clinical experience given to graduat es passing out of regional 

127 
 
AIIMS. The Committee is of considered opinion that graduates and post graduate passing out 
of AIIMS, Rishikesh should be equal to other medical graduates passing out of premier 
Institutes of the country. The Committee is of the c onsidered opinion that autonomy as per 
AIIMS Act was given only with respect to AIIMS, Delhi which has always exceeded the MCI 
benchmarks in every single aspect. However, the Committee is extremely concerned that the 
reference to the AIIMS Act and conseque nt autonomy available to regional AIIMS by virtue 
of this Act is being audaciously misused to dilute the medical education standards in a very 
blatant manner with the justification that the Institute meets US/UK standards. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends the Ministry to ensure that autonomy must not be used to 
dilute educational standards under any circumstances. The Committee is distressed at the 
medical education standards of the new AIIMS and is of the opinion that vacant PG seats in 
these Institutes are a reflection of lower standards of medical education. 
(Para 3.46 of the report) 
Action Taken 
 
3.9.2 The observation / recommendation of the Hon‘ble Committee has been noted for 
future guidance. The Institute have been sensitized in this regard.  The o bservation 
/recommendation of the Hon‘ble Committee have been noted for future guidance & we are 
trying to implement all suggestions. 
 
Further Recommendation 
 
3.9.3 The Ministry's response, stating that the Committee's observations have been 
"noted for fut ure guidance" and that the Institute has been "sensitized" and is "trying 
to implement all suggestions," lacks specific details or a concrete action plan to address 
the Committee's serious concerns regarding the potential dilution of medical education 
standards at AIIMS Rishikesh. The Committee's core apprehension centres on the 
perceived misinterpretation and misuse of AIIMS  Act autonomy to justify not adhering 
to MCI /NMC benchmarks, thereby raising questions about the quality of learning and 
clinical exp erience. Therefore, the Committee strongly recommends that the Ministry 
provide a detailed, time -bound action plan outlining how AIIMS Rishikesh will be 
brought into full compliance with MCI /NMC norms for faculty -student ratios, 
infrastructure, and clinica l exposure, particularly for postgraduate seats, without 
compromising the autonomy under the AIIMS Act , but rather enhancing, t he quality of 
medical education.

and in general surgery, there is 45 days waiting t ime for the procedures to be done besides six 
months for ENT. The Committee feels that such instances of long waiting time due to non -
availability of operation theatres defies the very purpose of setting up of AIIMS like 
institution as patients have to fac e hardships. The Committee finds the reasons for long 
waiting time at AIIMS, Rishikesh are inadequate infrastructure and constraints even after six 
years of its operationalization. The Committee recommends for optimum utilization of the 
existing OT infrastructure. The Committee also recommends for a comparative analysis with 
AIIMS Delhi regarding the number of major/minor surgeries per OT per day. Despite these 
lacunae the Institute is aiming for setting up of advanced centres at exorbitant costs without 
getting the basics right. The Committee recommends that optimum functional status of the 
originally conceived infrastructure be achieved and resources be utilized for achieving this 
objective instead of just focusing on rapid expansion. 
(Para 3.56 of the report)

However, as on date 54 OTs including 25 Major OTs, 29 Mino r OT/procedure rooms are 
fully functional. A comparative study with AIIMS Delhi to evaluate utilization of OTs will be 
carried out. OTs were non -functional temporarily during COVID -19 pandemic, but now all 
OTs are fully functional, which will help in reducing waiting time for patient‘s surgery. 
 
Further Recommendation 
 
3.10.3 The Committee appreciates the progress made by AIIMS Rishikesh in 
operationalizing a total of 54 Operation Theatres, including 25 Major and 29 Minor

reiterates that AIIMS Rishikesh conduc t and submit, without delay, a detailed

further recommends that a performance audit be undertake n to assess scheduling 
practices, manpower deployment, and procedural turnaround times to ensure optimum 
utilization of available OT infrastructure. The Committee reiterates that a ny future

showing improved usage of existing facilities and reduced surgical backlogs.

3.11 Procurement of Medical Equipment 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
3.11.1 The Committee expresses its concern tha t 32 types of equipment were procured on a 
single bid basis at AIIMS Jodhpur. Such situation leads to minimizing the options for 
procurement of equipment for the Institute. In case of single bid, the cost of equipment is 
likely to be higher than multiple b ids. The Committee is of the view that multiple bids is the 
only way for procurement of economical and best equipment for the Institute. The Committee 
cautions that the Institute has not followed the General Financial rules for the procurement of 
equipment. As per General Financial Rules, procurement from a single source may be 
resorted to only when there is a single manufacturer, in case of emergency and for 
standardization of machinery or spare parts to be compatible to the existing sets of equipment. 

130 
 
In the event where more than one bid is received, it means that there is more than one supplier 
of the required equipment. The Committee, thus, recommends to the Ministry to comply with 
the GFRs issued by the Government of India and go for procurement of equi pment on 
multiple bid bases so as to achieve competitive advantage. The Committee recommends for a 
probe and analysis for all cases of single bid/ proprietary certificate procurements and a status 
report be submitted to the Committee within three months of the presentation of the Report. 
(Para 4.26 of the report) 
 
Action Taken 
 
3.11.2 The observations / recommendation of the Hon‘ble Committee has been noted for 
future guidance. It is stated by AIIMS, Jodhpur that the process of E -tendering and publishing 
all tenders on CPPP portal & website is being followed w.e.f. November, 2016. Prior to this 
also multiple tendering process has been followed for purchase of medical equipment. This 
approach has been adopted to encourage wider participation for all vendors a nd getting more 
competitive bids and to ensure public trust and transparency in procurement system. 
However, procurement on single bid basis has been made in few cases where multiple bids 
were not received in spite of tendering for multiple times. It is to  mention here that single bid 
has been resorted to only when there is a single manufacturer, in case of emergency and for 
standardization of machinery or spare parts to be compatible to the existing sets of equipment 
under Rule 166 of GFR. Moreover, techni cal committee has also certified in accordance with 
Rule GFR 173(xx) that the specifications prepared are not specific to any brand/ make and 
encourage larger/ multivendor participation in order to get competitive prices and rate 
reasonability has been asc ertain by the committee based on the copies of Purchase Order of 
other Government institution in most of the cases. 
 
Further Recommendation 
 
3.11.3 The Committee takes note of the steps undertaken by AIIMS Jodhpur to ensure 
transparency in procurement, inc luding the use of e -tendering and publication of 
tenders on the CPPP portal, as well as adherence to relevant provisions of the General 
Financial Rules (GFRs) in cases where single bid procurement was undertaken. 
However, the Committee is of the view that instances of procurement through single 
bids should have been avoided and the institute must adhere to mu ltiple tendering 
attempts. The C ommittee feels the need for more proactive vendor outreach and 
competitive specification design to reduce cost of procu rement of components. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that AIIMS Jodhpur should also develop a 
structured vendor engagement strategy, including pre -bid meetings, to increase 
participation. Moreover, the Committee desires that all single bid and propri etary 
procurements should be independently reviewed on a half -yearly basis by an internal 
audit committee, and the summary of such reviews, including justification and cost 
comparisons with peer institutions, should be submitted to the Ministry. A 
comprehensive status report on the findings of the earlier probe into single bid 

131 
 
procurements, as previously recommended, should also be submitted for consideration 
of Committee.

infrastructure at the Institute besides diluting the standa rd of medical education. Such a huge

functioning of the Institute. Vacancy of one category of health personnel is restricted not only 
to a particular Department but als o affects the overall functioning of a healthcare Institute.

process of filling up of the posts in a time bound manner in order to impart the medical 
education at the desired level and to ensure that tertiary level health care services are provided 
to the patients. The Committee also recommends to the Ministry to offer better pay structure 
and incentives to attract Specialist/Super Specialist doctors from premier Institu tes like 
AIIMS/JIPMER/PGI, etc. to join the Institute. The Committee is constrained to observe 
almost negligible presence of faculty from these similar premier Government Institutes and

3.15 BURNS AND PLASTIC SURGERY DEPARTMENT 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
3.15.1 The Committee is of the view that given the high incidences of burn injuries in the 
State of Rajasthan and adjoining areas, a separate Burn Unit at  the Institute is the need of the 
hour. This will ensure that timely and adequate treatment to burn patients in terms of reducing 
their mortality, complications and rehabilitation. The Committee, thus, strongly recommends 
that the Institute must start a se parate Burns Unit in IPD with sufficient manpower and 
necessary equipment to improve the care and facilities for such patients at the earliest. The 
Committee, in this connection, recommends that ambulance services equipped with advanced 
features for transportation of patient from accident site to the burns unit of the Institute should 
be made available. 
(Para 4.63 of the report) 
Action Taken 
3.15.2 The observation/ recommendation of the committee have been noted for future 
guidance. Regarding the observatio n about starting of Burn unit, AIIMS Jodhpur is in the 
process of setting up a Burn and Plastic Service in the Institute. State of the art advanced 
ambulances is available in the Institute round the clock and are being utilized for patient care. 
The institute is in the process of augmenting the services.  One floor in the under construction 
trauma building is designated for state of art burn unit.  Currently construction work is under 
full swing. 
 
Further Recommendation 
 
3.15.3 The Committee notes the availa bility of state -of-the-art ambulance service and 
that a floor, in the new trauma building under construction , has been designated 
towards establishing a dedicat ed Burns Unit at AIIMS Jodhpur. The response of the 
Ministry, however, lacks specific timelines for the completion and operationalization of 
the Burns Unit, including the recruitment of specialized manpower and procurement of 
all necessary equip ment. Therefore, the Committee recommends that the Ministry 
should provide a detailed project completion timeline for the "state of the art burn unit" 
within the trauma building, clearly outlining key milestones such as construction 
completion, equipment procurement, and the specific plan for recruiting and training 
sufficient specialized manpower (plastic surg eons, burn nurses, physiotherapists, etc.) 
dedicated to the unit.

3.17 PROCUREMENT OF MEDICAL EQUIPMENT 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
3.17.1 The Committee is dismayed to note that 16 items of equipment (8.33%) costing Rs. 56 
crore remain undelivered while 34 items of equipment (19.54 %) costing Rs. 34 crore have 
been delivered but not installed. Consignee Receipt Certificate (CRC) has not been issued for 
20 items of equipment (11.49%) costing Rs. 3 crore. The Committee is shocked over the state 
of affairs in this institute of National importance where such grave underutilization of 
resources has become a common phenomenon. The Committee cannot fathom that how can 
the Institute turn a blind eye to the number of medical equipment that are lying uninstalled in 
the hospitals for such long periods. 
(Para 5.27 of the report) 
 
3.17.2 The Committee is not at all convinced by the reasons given by AIIMS Patna for the 
delayed supplies and non -installation of the medical equipment. Delays due to the non -
availability of space or complete power etc. could have been easily addressed by the Institute. 
The Committee believes that the institute had plenty of time at its disposal to obtain site 
approvals and the site should have been prepared well in advance. This undue delay in 
installation also highlights the failure of the Procurement Support Agency in ensuring timely 
supply and installation of the medical equipment in the Institute. The Committee is al so 
highly concerned regarding the role of the Procurement Support Agency that should have 
analysed the area and power requirement for the medical equipment and communicated the 
same to the Institute. The Committee holds the Institute and the Procurement Su pport Agency 
responsible for the delay in operationalization of these equipment and also warns that this lax 
attitude of the institute has proved to be the biggest roadblock in its path to establish itself as a 
centre of excellence in medical education. 
(Para 5.28 of the report) 

147 
 
Action Taken 
 
3.17.3 The observation/recommendation of the Hon'ble Committee has been noted for future 
guidance. In pursuance of the observations of the Committee, the delivery status of the 16 
Items of equipment has been checked up and the position is as under: 
 
(i) Out of 16 items, only four items were not delivered due to some issues between HITES 
(PSA) and the Vendor. PSA is being directed to sort out the issues and get the equipment 
delivered and installed. 
 
(ii) All the deliver ed equipment was installed except two equipment s delivered but not 
installed by the vendor l.e. High Speed Steam Glass Sterilizer & Lyophilizer. 
 
Further Recommendation 
 
3.17.4 The Committee takes note of the updated status indicating progress in the 
delivery and installation of most of the previously undelivered and uninstalled medical 
equipment at AIIMS Patna. The Committee, however, expresses serious concerns over 
the fact that some critical equipment remains undelivered or uninstalled due to 
unresolved issues between the Procurement Support Agency (HITES) and vendors 
reflects persistent systemic inefficiencies. The Committee, therefore, recommends that 
the Ministry should monitor and co -ordinate in a time -bound manner for resolution of 
issues pertaining to procurement and installation delays, indicating defined 
accountability for both the Institute and the PSA. A periodic review system should be 
institutionalized, involving all stakeholders, to ensure proactive site readiness, 
infrastructure support, and timely vendor coordination. The Ministry should consider 
developing a centralized dashboard for real -time tracking of equipment procurement 
and installation across all AIIMS. 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
3.17.5 The Committee, therefore strongly recommen ds that the institute should be proactive 
in taking suomoto cognizance of the delay in delivery of the equipment and ensure that 
medical equipment are delivered on time. The Institute should also make sure that 
unnecessary delay in installation of equipmen t does not take place due to shortage of skilled 
manpower or lack in infrastructure. The Committee also recommends that all the medical 
equipment should be accepted only after a technical inspection by a technical Inspector and 
should receive routine maint enance and calibration. The Institute should also have a 
contingency plan in case of breakdown of equipment so that the diagnostic services are not 
adversely effected. 
(Para 5.29 of the report) 
 
 

148 
 
Action Taken 
 
3.17.6 The observation/recommendation of the H on'ble Committee has been noted for future 
guidance. Efforts are made by the Institute and the Ministry to impress upon the Procurement 
Support Agency i.e. HITES for early delivery and installation of equipment. However, 
whenever there is delay in supply o f equipment, penalty is imposed as per tender clause by 
the PSA. Moreover, skilled manpower is provided for installation of equipment. Also for 
equipment purchased and installed, there is a warranty clause for 5 years warranty and in 
addition all equipment  are covered with Comprehensive Maintenance Agreement for further 
period of five years. 
 
Further Recommendation 
 
3.17.7 The Committee note s the efforts being made to impress upon HITES for early 
delivery and installation, along with the imp osition of penal ties for delays at AIIMS 
Patna. Furthermore, the provision of skilled manpower for installation and the coverage 
of equipment under 5 -year warranty and subsequent 5 -year Comprehensive 
Maintenance Agreements are positive steps towards ensuring operation fun ctionality 
and proficiency. However, the reply does not explicitly address the Committee‟s 
recommendation for a technical inspection by a technical inspector before acceptance of 
equipment, nor does it details a comprehensive contingency plan in case of eq uipment 
breakdown to prevent adverse effects on diagnostic services. Therefore, the Committee 
reiterates that the Ministry, in addition to existing measures, establish a mandatory 
protocol for independent technical inspection and certification of all medic al equipment 
prior to acceptance to ensure quality and functionality at the time of delivery. The 
Committee reiterates that a detailed contingency plan for critical equipment 
breakdowns should be developed at AIIMS Patna outlining alternative arrangements to 
minimize disruption to patient diagnostic and treatment services. 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
3.17.8 AIIMS Patna also submitted that US FDA and CE certification was put in the 
specification due to unavailability of a similar Indian Model. The Commit tee is shocked by 
the false claims of AIIMS Patna that Indian model for basic instruments such as hand drill, 
mouth gags, rib, hooks, chisels etc. are not available in the market. The Committee is of the 
opinion that items such as Navigation system, Surgic al Helmet and Accessories, Surgical 
consumable items and other instruments are easily available with the Indian manufacturers 
but AIIMS Patna, by insisting on US FDA and CE certification even for such basic 
instruments has clearly shown contempt for the Indian manufacturing sector. 
(Para 5.35 of the report) 
Action Taken 
 
3.17.9 With reference to the Committee's observation, it is mentioned here that the Ministry 
has issued guidelines for adopting the BIS standards also as an option to bidders, wherever 

149 
 
available, vide Ministry OM dated 20.02.2018 and since then procurement is being made 
accordingly. All the AIIMS have been advised to comply with the instructions. AIIMS, Patna 
is also following "Make in India" policy and insists on Bureau of Indian Standard ( BIS) 
certification. 
 
Further Recommendation 
 
3.17.10 In the light of the Ministry‟s response and the adoption of BIS standards 
in procurement practices following the OM dated 20.02.2018, the Committee 
acknowledges the corrective steps taken to promote indi genous manufacturing. The 
Committee, nevertheless,  recommends that the Ministry ensure strict compliance with 
the BIS-inclusive procurement policy across all AIIM S and mandate that procurement 
committees give due preference to quality -certified Indian manufacturers, especially for 
basic instruments. A formal mechanism should be instituted for periodic audit of tender 
specifications and vendor selection processes to prevent unwarranted bias toward 
foreign certifications.  
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
3.17.11 On one side where the Government is taking measures to reduce the country‘s 
dependency on imported medical devices, it is unfortunate to find an institute of national 
importance openly following a mandatory US FDA certification policy for purchasing 
medical equipment. The Committee is distressed to note that medical devices like 
defibrillator, ultrasound machine, neonatal ventilator, surgical instruments etc  are being 
purchased with US FDA certification even though there are many other manufacturers wit h 
CE certification. The Committee strongly recommends to AIIMS Patna to follow a buy 
"Make in India" policy and insist on Bureau of Indian Standard (BIS) certification. 
(Para 5.36 of the report) 
Action Taken 
 
3.17.12 With reference to the observation/recom mendation of the Hon'ble Committee, 
it is submitted that the Ministry has already initiated action in this regard. The Secretary, 
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare vide letter dated 7 th May, 2018 to Director General, 
Bureau of Indian Standards requesti ng for formulation of specifications for medical 
equipment being procured to promote 'Make in India' policy of the Government of India.  
Bureau of Indian Standards has already started creation of BIS standards for Medical 
Equipment and Devices. As per infor mation available with the Ministry, a standardization list 
for around 1000 medical devices has almost been completed. 
 
Further Recommendation 
 
3.17.13 In view of the action taken by the Ministry and the ongoing efforts by the 
Bureau of Indian Standards (BI S) to formulate specifications for approximately 1000 
medical devices, the Committee appreciates the alignment with the "Make in India" 
initiative. However, to ensure that these efforts translate into real -time procurement 

150 
 
reform, the Committee recommends that AIIMS Patna and all other similar institutions 
strictly discontinue the practice of mandating US FDA certification where BIS or CE 
standards are available. Additionally, the Committee recommends monitoring of 
procurement patterns across AIIMS institutions to ensure preference for indigenous and 
BIS-certified products. 
3.18 STATUS OF FACULTY/NON-FACULTY STRENGTH 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
3.18.1 The Committee notes that 122 posts have been filled up against the sanctioned 
strength of 305 for Profess ors/Additional Professor/Associate Professor/ Assistant Professor 
whereas 183 Posts are lying vacant in different Departments of AIIMS Patna. None of the 
posts have been filled up in Trauma and Emergency, Nuclear Medicine, Nephrology, Hospital 
Administration and Endocrinology and Metabolism Departments. The Committee observes 
with concern that important Departments such as Cardiology, Medical Oncology and 
Haematology, Neonatology, Neurology, Radiotherapy, Surgical Oncology, Urology are 
functioning with only  one doctor in AIIMS Patna. The Committee also notes with serious 
concern that AIIMS Patna has the lowest faculty strength among all the new AIIMS 
established under Phase 1 of PMSSY. This casts aspersion on the functioning of AIIMS, 
Patna with regard to Human Resource Management as well. 
(Para 5.39 of the report) 
Action Taken 
 
3.18.2 Matter of Record. At present, 224 seats of various faculty posts against total 305 seats 
are filled up. Only one department, Endocrinology & Metabolism is not functional at AII MS 
Patna due to non-availability of suitable candidates for the post. 
 
Further Recommendation 
 
3.18.3 The Committee acknowledges the progress made in improving faculty 
recruitment at AIIMS Patna with 224 out of 305 faculty posts now filled up. However, 
the Committee expresses deep concern that critical departments such as Endocrinology 
& Metabolism continue to remain non -functional due to the lack of suitable candidates, 
and many other departments don‟t have adequate number of faculty. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the Ministry take urgent and targeted measures to address 
faculty shortages through proactive recruitment drives, relaxation of procedural delays, 
and provision of additional incentives, especially for super -specialty and 
underrepresented departments. 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
3.18.4 The Committee is disturbed by the acute shortage of Professors/Additional 
Professor/Associate Professor/ Assistant Professor in AIIMS Patna and other AIIMS like 
Institutes. The Committee during its study visit to AIIMS Patna also discussed the shortage of 

151 
 
facility with the Director and representatives of the Ministry. The Committee recommends 
that AIIMS Patna should make immediate efforts to implement all the initiatives for 
recruitment of faculty. The  Committee notes that provision has been made to engage faculty 
from other institutes and Government medical colleges on deputation but the Committee 
would also like to emphasize that engaging faculty from the GMCs should not result in 
vacancies in the nearby GMCs. 
(Para 5.41 of the report) 
 
Action Taken 
 
3.18.5 The process of strengthening the faculty in the new AIIMS is being deliberated upon 
by the Institutes & the Ministry on regular basis and the overall situation will improve in near 
future. In additi on, the Ministry has also taken some policy Initiatives for bringing about 
improved availability of trained HR at National Level at large. Measures to improve faculty 
strength in the new AllMS  were also discussed in the meeting of the Central Institute Bod y 
(CIB) held on 13.08.2018 and 10.12.2018 and 24.01.2019. CIB advised that the regular 
recruitment will be done at Institute level while combined contractual recruitment will be 
done by AIIMS, New Delhi through walk in -interview twice in a year for selecti ng students 
passing from premium medical institutes/INIs, in addition to the recruitment done by 
Individual AIIMS. It was also decided in the CIB to allow temporarily, the new AIIMS to fill 
up the senior level posts by selection of candidates at one level below in case the post could 
not be filled up due to non-availability of suitable candidates. 
 
Further Recommendation 
 
3.18.6 The Committee notes the efforts to streamline and decentralize faculty 
recruitment processes and the policy decision to allow comb ined contractual 
recruitment through AIIMS, New Delhi. However, given the continuing faculty 
shortage, especially in critical specialties, the Committee recommends that the Ministry 
and AIIMS Patna urgently operationalize bi -annual walk-in interviews as pl anned and 
closely monitor the success rate of such recruitments. The Committee understands that 
while temporary appointments at one level below may provide only interim relief, 
therefore, the Committee emphasizes the need to maintain academic and clinical 
standards on permanent basis.  
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
3.18.7 The Committee understands that special packages/incentives or higher salary may not 
always be a driving factor to serve in this part of the country, therefore, the Institute has to 
explore alternative means such as paid research collaboration, high end technology, better 
working hours, security, enough leisure time etc. to attract qualified doctors to the Institute. 
 (Para 5.42 of the Report)

3.26 PROCUREMENT OF EQUIPMENT 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
3.26.1 The Committee deprecates the Institute for poor management of crucial equipment 
worth crores. Procurement process involves commissioning , installation, training, warranty, 
after sales services like post -warranty maintenance and assured availability of spares. The 
Committee is of the view that delay in the installation of procured equipment may jeopardize 
after sales services for warranty p eriod may lapse as per the contract. The Committee would 
like the Institute to install the equipment as soon as these equipment are delivered. Further, 
the equipment must be purchased only when the suitable infrastructure and manpower for 
their installation and operation is available. 
(Para 6.27 of the report) 
Action Taken 
 
3.26.2 So far as purchases done by the Institute are concerned, there are no such cases as 
mentioned in this point, where in equipment were purchased and infrastructure and manpower 
was not available. The Institute purchases equipment only when suitable infrastructure and 
manpower for their operation and installation are available and take immediate action to 
install the equipment as soon as it is received.  As per the tender clauses of AI IMS Raipur, the 
warranty will commence only after the installation and commissioning of the particular 
equipment. In addition to this, there is always a clause of Liquidated Damages as prescribed 
under GFR to supplier in case the equipment is supplied afte r expiry of prescribed delivery 
period as mentioned in purchase order to protect the interest of AIIMS Raipur.  So far as cases 

169 
 
relating to equipment purchased through M/s. HLL are concerned, few of the equipment 
could not be installed where the designated area of the concerned departments was not handed 
over timely by the project contractors. The reasons of construction delay have already been 
brought out in the point no. 6.12. 
 
Further Recommendation 
 
3.26.3 The Committee has been informed that AIIMS Raipu r generally adheres to best 
practices by purchasing equipment only when infrastructure and manpower are 
available, and by ensuring warranty periods commence post -installation, with 
provisions for liquidated damages. This is a positive step towards prudent equipment 
management.  However, the submission that "few of the equipment could not be 
installed where the designated area of the departments concerned was not handed over 
timely by the project contractors" underscores a critical gap in coordination betwee n 
procurement and infrastructure development. The Committee , therefore,  further 
recommends that the Ministry implement a more robust, inter -departmental 
coordination mechanism between the procurement wing and the project/construction 
department at AIIMS Ra ipur. Such mechanism should include mandatory, pre -
procurement verification of infrastructure readiness and a staggered procurement 
schedule explicitly linked to the confirmed handover dates of designated departmental 
areas, thereby preventing future insta nces where costly equipment remains uninstalled 
due to construction delays. 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
3.26.4 The Committee feels that delay in the delivery or installation of the equipment at the 
Institute is certainly not a healthy trend. It deprive s patients of diagnostic/therapeutic benefits 
through the usage of such equipment. The delay in the supply of the equipment is the fault on 
the part of the PSA/supplier/manufacturer and the Institute must take suitable action against 
the errant supplier. The Committee is of the view that procurement of equipment is a key area 
and therefore the Institute must resolve these issues by making the PSA accountable for any 
delay and lapse. 
(Para 6.28 of the report) 
 
Action Taken 
 
3.26.5 So far as the procurement c ases pertaining to PSA, i.e. M/s HLL, adequate Liquidated 
damage have been imposed on delayed supply of the equipment whenever there is 
delay/defect on the part of PSA/ Supplier/ Manufacturer. The Final Acceptance Certificates 
against such equipment issued  by the Institute clearly mentions the date of installation and 
commissioning. The PSA, in turn, imposes suitable penalty against errant suppliers as the 
conditions of the tender.  However, the concern raised by Hon‘ble Committee is well taken 
and the Institute will take up suitable action/measures against the PSA. 
 
 

170 
 
Further Recommendation 
 
3.26.6 The Committee has been apprised that the Committee‟s concern over delays in 
equipment delivery and installation has been addressed by imposing liquidated damages 
on errant suppliers and that AIIMS Raipur generally ensures infrastructure and 
manpower are available before procurement. The Committee , however, recommends 
that the Ministry, be side imposing penalties must  establish a more integrated and 
proactive system t o ensure seamless coordination between procurement, infrastructure 
development, and departmental readiness at AIIMS Raipur. This system should 
mandate a pre -procurement checklist and real -time monitoring of project completion 
milestones, enabling a "just-in-time" equipment delivery and installation strategy.

Recommendations/Observations

also to do clinical practice in society. While for non -clinical and para clinical courses, the job 
opportunities are mainly in Academic Institutions.  The choice of seats by students is beyond
