  III  CENTRALLY SPONSORED SCHEMES
3.1  Development and Upgradation of AYUSH Institutions/Colleges
The Scheme has the following components –
-                     Development of AYUSH UG colleges.
-                     Assistance to PG medical education.
-                     Reorientation training programme for AYUSH personnel.
-                     Renovation and strengthening of hospital wards of teaching hospitals of AYUSH.
-                     Establishment of Computer Labs in selected AYUSH colleges.
-                     Upgradation of Academic Institutes to the status of State Model Institutes.
3.2       The Committee notes that   against an allocation of Rs. 37.56 crores in 2005-06, expenditure reported upto 7th
March, 2006 is Rs.27.82 crores.  Receipt of less proposals due to pending UCs of previous years has been cited as the
main factor responsible for underutilization of allocated funds.  The Committee notes that level of overall expenditure
under the scheme has been more or less satisfactory during 2003-04 and 2004-05.   However, the Committee would like
to point that status of some components indicate a different position.   Funds meant for development/assistance of
UG/PG AYUSH colleges remained under utilised during 2003-04 and 2004-05 due to revision of the component and
receipt of less number of feasible proposals.  The Committee observes that during 2005-06, the physical targets set
under these components could not be achieved fully.   Under ROTP/CME for AYUSH personnel, the Committee notes
that against a target of 105-110 colleges to be benefited, achievement level is restricted to 64 colleges only.   The
Committee understands that the component in its revised form is being closely monitored.    The Committee would like
to know about the number of beneficiaries (institution and statewise) during 2005-06.  
3.3       The physical targets set for establishment of computer labs for selected colleges could not be met during 2005-
06 as central assistance of Rs.20 lakhs could be provided to only two colleges against a target of 7-8 colleges.  The
Committee finds that the scheme, very much required under the present scenario has not been getting due impetus.  
While there was nil achievement during 2003-04, performance level during 2004-05 showed noticeable improvement.    
Status of this component during 2005-06 is again discouraging.   The Committee strongly feels that this component
needs to be focussed more.

 IV     
HOSPITALS AND DISPENSARIES
4.1       Budget allocation of Rs.90 crores for the two schemes of AYUSH hospitals and dispensaries in 2005-06
was enhanced to Rs. 100.82 crores at the RE stage and the actual expenditure reported is Rs. 119.71 crores.      
The Committee notes that separate allocation  for the two schemes indicates that whereas for AYUSH hospitals,
allocation of Rs. 45 crores was enhanced to Rs.67.65 crores and the final  expenditure was even higher, being
Rs.85.02 crores.  In contrast provision for AYUSH dispensaries was reduced from Rs. 45 crores to Rs.33.17
crores and the actual expenditure was only Rs.32.32 crores.   
4.2       The Committee observes that there are about 21000 AYUSH dispensaries in the country and the scheme
calls for financial assistance @Rs.25000 per dispensary per annum.  The Committee notes that during 2003-04
and 2004-05,  utilisation was optimum and the funds were not found sufficient for the projected requirements of
the existing dispensaries.    The Committee is not aware about the reason for the reduction in the allocated funds
for AYUSH dispensaries during 2005-06.   The Committee would however like to point out that the core
strategy of mainstreaming of AYUSH under NRHM is to make available AYUSH services at the PHC/CHC
level, either by reallocation of AYUSH doctors from existing dispensaries or by hiring of additional doctors on
contract basis for which funds will be provided under NRHM.  The Committee apprehends that  on the plea of
providing  AYUSH doctors at PHC/CHC with  the funds being provided therefor under NRHM, AYUSH
dispensaries  spread across the country may perhaps  not continue to provide the services as being done uptil
now.  Out of the 10000 AYUSH dispensaries and units located in rural and backward areas, only 7936
dispensaries could be covered for improving the supply position of essential AYUSH drugs during the year
2005-06.  The Committee would, therefore, like to emphasize that every effort should be made for effective
functioning of the existing AYUSH dispensaries.

      5.1       The scheme has the following components –
-        strengthening and establishing of state govt. drug testing labs for AYUSH drugs.
-                     strengthening and establishing of state govt AYUSH pharmacies.
-                     Strengthening of state Drug Controllers of AYUSH Enforcement Mechanism.
-                     Assistance to AYUSH drug manufacturing units for meeting GMP practices.
 
5.2       The Committee notes that  provision of Rs.10 crores  for the scheme of Drug Quality Control   made in

5.3       The Committee has been given to understand that fund constraint if any in the provision of Rs.11 crores

5.4       The Committee has been informed that during 2005-06, 26 State Drug Testing Labs and 45 State
Pharmacies were provided assistance.  Besides that, a review meeting has also been convened with the
representatives of State Drug Testing Labs/Pharmacies to take stock of the position and review their
functioning.  
5.5       Assistance amounting to Rs.2.52 crores was provided to units obtaining GMP certificates.       The
Committee has been given to understand that a subsidy amount of 25% subject to a maximum of RS. 5 lakh
being provided to AYUSH units for becoming GMP compliant was not proving to be sufficient enough.   
Keeping in view increasing number of cases of spurious and fake drugs available in the market, the Committee
feels that there is a need for   increasing the quantum of financial assistance under this component.   This would
enable individual units or a group of units to set up a joint quality control lab and acquire requisite equipment for
testing of heavy metals and raw materials etc.  The Committee strongly recommends that a decision for 
enhancing the funding for units obtaining GMP certificates should be taken well before the beginning of XIth
Plan.
            5.6       The Committee has been given to understand that the implementation of the provisions of the
Drugs and Cosmetics Act and Rules made thereunder is the responsibility of the State Govt. licensing authority.  
The Committee would, however, like to emphasize that there is an urgent need for the Department for taking a
pro-active role by making persistent efforts for strengthening of drug testing labs and the other allied controlling
authorities.

due to the fact that there were unspent balances available with the Council. 
 6.1.3   Maintenance of Central Register of Homoeopathy is the responsibility of CCH.  However, the
Committee notes that there has been undue delay in the publication of such registers.  As per the information
made available to the Committee during 2005-06 central registers of homoeopathy for 1993, 1996 and 2003

6.2  Central Council of Indian Medicine
6.2.1   The Council is a statutory body set up in 1971 with the main objective to maintain the Central Register of
Indian Medicine and also for maintenance of minimum standard in education of Indian Medicine and issues
related to recognition of new colleges of increase in seats and starting of new courses. 
6.2.2   The Committee notes that   allocation of Rs. 15 lakhs in 2005-06 was brought down to Rs. 10 lakhs and
the actual expenditure reported is only Rs. 1.08 lakhs.   The reason given is delay in the formulation of a new
proposal and availability of Rs. 3.32 lakhs as unspent balances. The Committee finds the position was the same
during 2004-05.  The Committee apprehends that availability of unspent balances might have been the factor
responsible for initialization of allocated funds.
6.2.3    The Committee observes that the status of Central Register of Indian Medicine as on 28.02.2006 clearly
reveals that almost all the concerned states are lagging behind in sending the requisite information of updation of
Central Register.  States like J&K have sent the details which date back to March 1993.  The Committee
understands that at present information relating to the period April 1983-October 2005 is under process by the
Council.  In respect of other States also the Committee observes that although information have been received
from the State Councils for 10-15 years on an average in each case, the same is yet to be incorporated in the
Central Register.  It is not known that since when this information is under compilation by the Central Council. 
Even if has been received the recent past, the Committee would like to emphasize that the process needs to be
expedited.  The plea of the Central Council due to non receipt of inputs from some states, there is delay in
updating the Central Register can not be considered to be very convincing.  The Committee is of the view that in
the event of non-submission of required information by any state council, a mechanism needs to be evolved so as
to ensure that the updation of Central Register does not get unduly delayed.  In the event of the AYUSH
practitioners of a particular state being deprived of the opportunity of getting registered in the state council, the
fault should lie with that council. 
6.2.4    The Committee has observed that the funds duly allocated for conduct of Election for the Council during
the last three years remained underutilized, making the Council not fully constituted. On a specific query in this
regard the Committee has been informed that the Council is fully constituted inspite of delay in election of
Members from some States due to the very fact that the members elected previously are still holding office. 
From the Statewise information furnished by the Department, the Committee finds that elections have been
delayed in Bihar, MP, Rajasthan, Maharashtra, Punjab, Tamil Nadu and W. Bengal either due to delay in

VII    HOSPITALS AND DISPENSARIES
Plan allocation of Rs. 37 crore was made in 2005-06 which was meant for Hospitals and Dispensaries. However, this
allocation had to be drastically reduced to      Rs. 64 Lakh at the RE stage and expenditure reported is also of about the
same level.  Background of the funds remaining unutilized   is indicated as follows: -
7.1   All India Institute of Ayurveda, New Delhi
            The Committee has been observing the progress being made in the construction of the building for the past few
years.  The Committee is surprised to note that till 2004-05 the issue of allotment of land for the institute was the reason
for the undue delay.  Although the additional land is yet to be acquired, another development has taken place during
2005-06.   As informed to the Committee, the EFC in its meeting held on 3.10.2005 has directed that the proposal be
reformulated with focus on R&D, safety evaluation and quality standard in AYUSH. Accordingly a Committee has been
constituted to look into the suggestion made by the EFC and prepare a concept paper accordingly.  The Committee
apprehends that not much progress would be made during 2006 also as the planning for the project of building continues
to be under consideration.  The Committee is not aware of the original estimate approved for the construction of the
building for the hospital.  However, as things stand, it would be definitely on a enhanced level when completed.
7.2     Ayurveda Hospital, New Delhi
            The hospital set up in 1978 is meant for extending Ayurvedic treatment facilities to CGHS beneficiaries and
general public. The Committee observes that in spite of funds being made available for expansion of the hospital, so far
no progress worth mentioning is visible. The Committee finds that the expenditure of the hospital is being managed
from the non-plan side. Not only this there is delay in the matter of creation of posts for the hospital. Year 2005-06 was
also no exception. Provision of Rs. 1.00 crore was brought down to Rs. 32.00 lakhs and expenditure reported upto 7
th
March 2006 was only Rs. 7.43 lakhs. The Committee notes that the proposal of upgradation of 25-bedded hospital to
50-bedded hospital has been finally approved. However, against the proposed 82 posts, the Ministry of Finance has
agreed to only 13 regular posts and 39 posts on outsourcing basis. The Committee strongly feels that in order to expand
the services of the hospital, required number of permanent posts need to be created. The Department should once again
approach the Ministry of Finance in this regard.
7.3  Expansion of AYUSH Dispensaries in CGHS
            The Committee has been observing the non-performance of this scheme during the Tenth Plan. It has not been
possible so far to either strengthen the existing AYUSH dispensaries or to set up additional dispensaries. Every year,
targets are set and funds allocated therefor. But the Department has not succeeded in fulfilling them. The Committee has
been given to understand that out of seven AYUSH dispensaries sanctioned in 2003-2004,five have become functional. 
The Committee would, however, like to point out that ground realities are entirely different. These seven dispensaries
have been made functional by deployment of medical officers from the existing strength of CGHS dispensaries. The
Committee has been informed that a norm study of ISMH Dispensaries conducted by SIU is at present under
examination. Additional posts of medical/para-medical staff will be created only after implementation of SIU Report.
The Committee finds that in the meantime nine more AYUSH dispensaries have been sanctioned in 2004-05. The

VIII  NATIONAL MEDICAL PLANT BOARD  
8.1       An enhanced allocation of Rs. 38.00 crore has been made for the Board for 2006-07 against an allocation of Rs.
30.00 crore in 2005-06. The Committee observes that there has been optimum utilization of funds allocated for the
Board during the Tenth Plan period.
8.2       The Board was set up in November 2001 with the objective of development of medicinal plants used in AYUSH
medicines for sustained availability. The Committee observes that the Board was set up on the recommendation of a
Task Force constituted by the Planning Commission. Quite a few achievements could be credited in the name of the
Board.  So far, 32 State Medicinal Plant Boards have been set up. 32 medicinal plants have been identified at national
level for cultivation, conservation and development.
8.3
              The Committee has observed that the Board has not been provided with the required manpower. Perhaps this
issue has neither been emphasized enough nor seen in the proper perspective. Only one post of Chief Executive Officer
was created at the time of setting up of the Board. Since then, the Department has made attempts to get the required staff
but without any success so far. The only activity worth mentioning has been circulation of a Cabinet note on 20.01.2005
for creation of 30 posts and grant of status of a registered society to the Board to the concerned Departments.
Subsequently, a memorandum for EFC be has also been circulated to all concerned on 18.07.2005.

dissatisfaction on this turn of events. The Committee, accordingly, reiterates once again to expedite the decision about
the mandate and structure of the Board acceptable to all concerned. The Committee is afraid that continuance of an air
of indecisiveness about this vital Body would lead to our endangered medicinal plants reaching the brink of extinction.

XII.     Use of Animal and Marine Products in Ayurveda, Sidha and Unani Drugs.
 
12.1     The Committee observes that some of these animal products namely Praval (coral), Shankha (conch shell),
Kapardika (cowrie) and Mrigashringa (stag horn and deer horn), tiger nails, musk, discharge of civet cat have been
banned under Wild Life                  ( Protection) Act, 1972. The Committee was informed that the Department has taken
up with the Ministry of Environment and Forest who are exploring the possibility of providing some of these items to
the Ayurveda drug industry without causing and harm to the environment. 
12.2     The Committee strongly feels that the Department has to play a more pro-active rote in this sensitive area by
banning all animal products and wild honey in all preparation. Pig and cow products are likely to take on communal
colour. Other items like Ambrgris and elephant parts are internationally banned. Earthworm, animal teeth, peacock
feathers have no medicinal value and reduce the medicine to a placebo.   
 
XIII. Standardization of Naturopathy Courses
13.1     The Committee observes that naturopathy centers, purporting to be medical centers have sprung up all over the

as a medical science, the Committee attention has been drawn by the following disturbing ground realities: -
(a)                There is no naturopathy council to decide norms.
(b)               No norms have been decided.
(c)                Quack treatments have not been banned.
(d)               No licensing is required.
(e)                No courses have been decided for colleges or syllabuses regulated or standardized.

(g)                There is no degree. People who have studied it by correspondence for less then a week have become
practitioners. In fact, degrees have been gotten by mail.
13.2     The Committee is not inclined to agree with the contention of the department that it is not feasible to constitute a
separate Central Council for regulation of Yoga & Naturopathy. States have therefore been advised to set up their own
mechanism for regulation of  Yoga & Naturopathy in states. The Committee was given to understand that few steps
have been taken by the Department to regulate the naturopathy courses. WHO draft guidelines on Naturopathy are being
examined for adoption in Indian context. 13.3            The Committee was given to understand that a Morarji Dasai
National Institute of Yoga has already started work on preparation of draft curriculum for various courses and norms for
accreditation of yoga institutions. The National Institute of Naturopathy, Pune has also been asked to prepare similar
guidelines. These guidelines will be circulated to states for their guidance and enforcement.
13.4     The Committee strongly feels that there is an urgent need for regulation of education of naturopathy. There are
ten degree colleges of naturopathy in the country. But in the absence of any council having the power to regulate the
education of naturopathy, such colleges are running courses in a haphazard way, without any Central Standardization or
and any accountability whatsoever. The Committee is of the firm view that the Department should initiate immediate
action so that people are not put to any trouble. The Committee is happy to note that Department is reviewing the status
of both education and treatment aspects of naturopathy and would be coming out with a proper regulatory system in this
regard within a period of three months. The Committee would like to be apprised of the same.

 XVI.   Miscellaneous
            Tibetan Medicine has become quite popular amongst the people although it is not a recognized system in India. 
In states like Himachal Pradesh, Amchis are the medical practitioners in the Tibetan system of medicine.  There have
also been reports about violations concerning wildlife and usage of huge amount of bone material in this system of
medicine. The Committee has been given to understand that the Tibetan Medicine does not find any mention in our
existing legislation.  The Drugs and Cosmetic Act 1940 has a chapter on Indian Medicine but it does not mention
anything about the Tibetan medicine.  The Committee is of the opinion that the Tibetan system of medicine should be
brought within the ambit of law.  The Committee urges the Department to consider the inclusion of Tibetan system of
medicine in the legislation so as to regulate and recognize it for the benefit of the people.

The Committee is not fully satisfied with the justification given by the Department.  The Committee hopes that
the Govt. would be bringing forward the amended Bill relating to the CCIM before Parliament which would take care of
these anomalies. (Para 6.2.4) 
VII.         HOSPITALS AND DISPENSARIES
7.1   All India Institute of Ayurveda, New Delhi
The Committee apprehends that not much progress would be made during 2006 also as the planning for the
project of building continues to be under consideration.  The Committee is not aware of the original estimate approved
for the construction of the building for the hospital.  However, as things stand, it would be definitely on a enhanced
level when completed. (Para 7.1)
7.2       Ayurveda Hospital, New Delhi
The Committee strongly feels that in order to expand the services of the hospital, required number of permanent
posts need to be created. The Department should once again approach the Ministry of Finance in this regard. (Para 7.2)
7.3      Expansion of AYUSH Dispensaries in CGHS
            The Committee does not appreciate this kind of approach. Implementation of SIU Report needs to be given
priority so that dispensaries already set up can become fully functional. The Committee would, accordingly, recommend
the creation of additional posts for AYUSH dispensaries without any further delay. (Para 7.3)
VIII.   NATIONAL MEDICAL PLANT BOARD  
            The Committee is surprised to note that the proposal and projected requirements did not find favour with the
Department of Expenditure and the Planning Commission. Instead it was suggested that 5 posts including 2 posts on
outsourcing basis suggested by the Department of Expenditure would serve the purpose and accordingly there was no
justification for creation of 30 additional posts. (Para 8.4)
The Committee, accordingly, reiterates once again to expedite the decision about the mandate and structure of
the Board acceptable to all concerned. The Committee is afraid that continuance of an air of indecisiveness about this
vital Body would lead to our endangered medicinal plants reaching the brink of extinction. (Par 8.5)
            The Committee observes that the existing monitoring mechanism has perhaps not proved to be effective enough.
Basis for this assessment made by the Committee is the alarming increase in the number of pending Utilization
Certificates under both the schemes. (Para 8.8)
The Committee apprehends that the pendency is likely to arise further in view of sanctioning of as many as 1233
projects worth Rs. 32.10 crore and 233 projects worth Rs. 25.65 crore under the Contractual Farming Scheme and
Promotional Scheme respectively during 2005-06 alone. (Para 8.10)
The Committee observes that both pendency rate of UCs involved therein is very high. During the course of
discussion with the representatives of the Department as well as the National Medicinal Plant Board, it was

COMMITTEE ON HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE
file:///D/health_family/17threport.htm[29-06-2016 14:48:05]
categorically stated that amount involved in pending UCs would be negligible. However, the following information
forwarded by the Department proves the contention to be wrong and misleading. The Committee takes strong exception
to this.
            The Committee is not convinced by the justification given by the Department that pending UCs was a common
problem with all Ministries administering Centrally Sponsored Schemes on account of delay in release of CHS grants by
the states to implementing agencies and consequent delay in submission of UCs. The plea of the Department that the
requirement of vetting by Chartered Accountants under the Contractual Farming Scheme was difficult to be complied
with by farmers is also not acceptable to the Committee. The Committee would like to emphasize that the pendency is
bound to increase keeping in view the level of central assistance released under both the schemes during 2004-05 and
2005-06. (Para 8.11)
The Committee hopes that reports of these studies would provide critical input to the Board to modify and recast
the scheme accordingly. The Committee has a suggestion to make in this regard. Involvement of Forest Department will
not be helpful simply because they do not have any expertise in growing trees. The Committee is of the firm opinion
that agriculture universities like Pant Nagar need to be involved in the implementation of schemes like Promotional and
Contractual Farming. The Committee fails to understand the reason for not initiating the provision of recovery of funds
provided in the terms and conditions of both the schemes. The Committee strongly feels that a review of the functioning
of state Boards also needs to be done. They need to be strengthened and made accountable for the drawbacks being
noticed in the two schemes.   (Para 8.12)
IX.          STRENGTHENING OF PHARMACOPOEIAL LABORATORIES
The Committee is constrained to observe that the post of Director, PLIM, still remains to be filled up.   The
Committee has been given to understand that the post had to be readvertised under the directions of UPSC. The
Committee does not have much hope of further progress in the matter during the last year of the Tenth Plan. (Para 9.2) 
The physical targets and the achievement level during 2005-06 with regard to various activities undertaken by
the lab also indicate a good track record.           (Para 9.3)
The Committee finds that the building of PLIM although completed structurally is yet to be handed over by the
CPWD.   At present, the matter is being pursued vigorously with the CPWD engineers.     Statement of the Department
that the building for HPL is reportedly complete indicates that there may be some formalities to be completed in respect
of this project also.   The Committee is not aware whether the buildings for both the labs were handed over on 10 th
April, 2006 after fulfilling all mandatory requirements as assured by the CPWD.   The Committee would like to be
apprised about the final position.  The Committee would also like to know about the original estimate and the actual
expenditure of both the projects.  (Para 9.4)
X.        DEVELOPMENT OF NORTH-EAST UNDER PLAN SCHEMES OF THE DEPARTMENT
The Committee has been observing the progress of this project for quite some time.  In the beginning of every
year, nominal provision for this project is being religiously made.  The proposed allocation for the entire Tenth plan was
Rs. 5 lakhs and the beginning of last year has started without any progress whatsoever being made.  As per the latest
information furnished by the Department, the matter has been reviewed by the Minister on 4 th October 2005 in the light
of observations made by the Ministry of Finance, Department of Expenditure about the viability of   the project.  The
Committee is surprised to note that a decision has now been made to locate the Institute of Health and Medical Sciences
at Shillong and allotment of land  for the Institute has also been made.   At present, approval of CCEA is awaited.  The
Committee is not very happy with the way the project of Institute  to be set up for the benefit of NE region has been

COMMITTEE ON HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE
file:///D/health_family/17threport.htm[29-06-2016 14:48:05]
handled.  It has taken about four- five years to do the planning which has since been reviewed.  The Committee
apprehends that another plan period would perhaps be over in taking a final decision and starting the preparatory
exercise for this much needed institute.  The Committee can only emphasize that the Department should vigorously
pursue this matter with all concerned authorities.   (Para 10.2)
XI.    PERFORMANCE AUDIT OF DEPTT. OF AYUSH FOR THE PERIOD OF 2000-01 TO 2004 – 05 BY
CAG
 
The Committee notes that a number of areas which deserve to be seriously viewed have been raised in the CAG
Report.  The Secretary of the Department admitted before the Committee that most of the observations made by the
CAG were valid and exercise has been started at the Department level to take the corrective measures.  The Committee
would like to be apprised about the full details of follow up action to taken by the Department.   (Para 11.2)
XII.     USE OF ANIMAL AND MARINE PRODUCTS IN AYURVEDA, SIDHA AND UNANI DRUGS.
 
            The Committee strongly feels that the Department has to play a more pro-active rote in this sensitive area by
banning all animal products and wild honey in all preparation. Pig and cow products are likely to take on communal
colour. Other items like Ambrgris and elephant parts are internationally banned. Earthworm, animal teeth, peacock
feathers have no medicinal value and reduce the medicine to a placebo.    (Para 12.2)
XIII.    STANDARDIZATION OF NATUROPATHY COURSES
 
            The Committee strongly feels that there is an urgent need for regulation of education of naturopathy. There are
ten-degree colleges of naturopathy in the country. But in the absence of any council having the power to regulate the
education of naturopathy, such colleges are running courses in a haphazard way, without any Central Standardization or
and any accountability whatsoever. The Committee is of the firm view that the Department should initiate immediate
action so that people are not put to any trouble. The Committee is happy to note that Department is reviewing the status
of both education and treatment aspects of naturopathy and would be coming out with a proper regulatory system in this
regard within a period of three months. The Committee would like to be apprised of the same. (Para 13.4)
XIV.            INTERNATIONAL EXCHANGE PROGRAMME
The Committee would like to have an idea about the contributions of AYUSH made by such Exchange Programme /
Conferences.  (Para 14.3)
 The Committee would like to have full details in this regard, amount of sanction, expenditure (industry-wise) users.
The Committee would also like to understand the criteria fixed for participation of drug industries in international fairs.
(Para 14.4)
 
XV.      ACQUISITION AND PUBLICATION OF TEXT BOOKS AND MANUSCRIPTS 
 
The Committee would like the Department to furnish information regarding the nodal agency involved in this
process. Details like the date of release of grant and the time given to complete the project and the selection of textbooks
and manuscript which are to be acquired should also be given.  (Para 15.2)
           
XVI.    MISCELLANEOUS
              The Committee is of the opinion that the Tibetan system of medicine should be brought within the ambit of
law.  The Committee urges the Department to consider the inclusion of Tibetan system of medicine in the legislation so
as to regulate and recognize it for the benefit of the people. (Para 16)

PREFACE 
 
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Health and 
Family Welfare, having been authorized by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, 
hereby present this 170th Report of the Committee on Action Taken by the G overnment on the 
Recommendations/ Observations contained in the 163rd Report on ―Demands For Grants 2025 -26 
(Demand No. 46) of the Department of Health and Family Welfare (Ministry of Health and Family 
Welfare)‖.  
2. The 163rd Report of the Department -related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Health 
and Family Welfare was presented to the Rajya Sabha and laid on the Table of Lok Sabha on  12th 
March, 2025. The Action Taken Notes of the Government on the recommendations containe d in the 
Report was received from the Department in the Month of July, 2025.   
3.  The Committee made a total of 176 recommendations in the 16 3rd Report, out of which 96 
recommendations have been accepted by the Department and have been categorized under 
Chapter-I. There are 09 recommendations that the Committee does not desire to pursue in view of 
the Department‘s replies that have been categorized under Chapter-II. There are 65 
recommendations/ observations, in respect of which replies of the Department have not been 
accepted by the Committee and the Committee has made further recommendations thereon and has 
been categorized under Chapter-III. While 06 recommendations/observations in respect of which 
final reply of the Department has not been received, have been categorized under Chapter- IV. 
4. The Committee, in its meeting held on  9th December, 2025 considered the Draft Report and 
adopted the same.

1.1 Vision Mission and Objectives 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
1.1.1 The Committee takes note of the vision, mission and objectives of the Department of 
Health and Family Welfare which determines the roadmap for activities of the Department. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should undertake the 
projects/schemes/plans in consonance with the vision and mission of the Department and 
execute the same with the intention to achieve the cherished objectives. The Committee 
believes that the Department would move forward with Management by Objective (MBO) 
rather than Management by Activities (MBA) to achieve the targets set in National Health 
Policy (NHP) 2017 and under specific projects.   
(Para 1.3.2 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
 
1.1.2 In line with the Committee‘s recommendation, the Key Deliverables (KDs) under 
National Health Mission aim to monitor progress against the objective of the programmes. In 
the recently concluded Mid Term review, all the KDs were discussed and areas where states 
need to focus were emphasized.  These interventions are closely monitored thro ugh 
measurable outputs and outcomes, ensuring alignment with the Department‘s strategic 
priorities and desired health impact, such as operationalization of Ayushman Arogya Mandir, 
integration of NCD services, digital health interventions, and capacity buil ding efforts. 
herefore, Department is moving forward with Management of Objective (MBO) approach by 
regular monitoring of the KDs and taking regular state reviews on progress on targets set at 
the beginning of every 2 years PIP period.

Recommendations/Observations  
 
1.2.1 The Committee is of the view that Institutions/Organisations are the organs of the 
Department which play pivotal role in the successful functioning of the Department, 
therefore, efficient and effective working of the organisations/institutions is indispens able for 
result-oriented implementation of the undertaken projects/schemes. The Committee, 
therefore, desires that the officers at the top of the Department should ensure to set up 
dynamic working equilibrium amongst various institutions in order to achiev e the objectives 
of the Department. The Committee feels that a streamlined monitoring mechanism with 
Always Better Control (ABC) would further ensure the desirable Rate of Returns (RoR). The

alignment of activities with desired outcomes etc. within the Outcome Output Framework.

Expenditure (GHE) as a percentage of General Government Expenditure (GGE) has increased 
from 3.78% (2013-14) to 6.12% (2021 -22). Thus there has been a steady increase in keeping 
in mind the initiatives of the Department and the overall resources availability of the 
government. 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
1.7.10 The Committee is of the view that strengthening of public health infrastructure, 
enhancing preventive and primary care services, leveraging Public -Private Partnerships 
(PPP), exploring additional revenue sources,  innovation in health, robust monitoring and 
evaluation mechanism to track the utilization of health funds and assess the impact  are crucial 
for establishing an affordable and accessible healthcare delivery system, especially for a 
developing economy like India. The need of the hour is to recognize health as a key sector for 
economic as well as social development. The Committee, therefore , strongly recommends the 
Government to make health a priority and increase its investment in the health sector.   
 
(Para 2.3.6 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
 
1.7.11 Department of Health and Family Welfare is initiating steps to use ‗Public Private 
Partnership model‘ for augmenting the health infrastructure in the country and for improving 
the delivery of health services. Towards this end, recently a dedicated PPP Cell has been 
created in the Department.  The PPP Cell is working with different Program  Divisions and 
State Governments to identify projects, which can be taken up in the PPP mode. The 
Department has written to the States/UTs to utilize schemes of the Department of Economic 
Affairs to sponsor PPP projects and to consider setting up a dedicated PPP Cell in their Health 
Departments to ensure focus on this matter and to help create an enabling environment for 
PPP mode of Infrastructure in the State/UT.‖ Regular monitoring of utilization of health funds 
is being done through use of different digi tal platform/portals. Regular interactions are held 
with different stakeholders (States) to assess implementation of schemes and do optimum 
utilization of available resources. The main objective of the National Health Policy 2017 is to 
improve health statu s through concerted policy action in all sectors and expand preventive, 
promotive, curative, palliative and rehabilitative services provided through the public health 
sector with focus on quality. 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
1.7.12 The Committee unders tands that increasing the public investment on health depends 
on several factors such as State Government‘s health budget depending on their allocations, 

11 
 
capacities and fund position, transfer to states on the recommendation on Finance 
Commission, allocati on made under Centrally Sponsored Schemes by Union Government 
based on total budgetary resources. The Committee appreciates that the 25 States and the 
Union Territories of Delhi and Puducherry as per the NHA Estimates for FY 2021 -22 have 
achieved the Natio nal Health Policy target of 8% of their budget allocated to health . The 
Committee recommends that other State/UT Governments should follow the same.  
 
(Para 2.3.13 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
 
1.7.13 Some of the initiatives undertaken to encourage the States to allocate a higher share of 
their budget to the health sector: - 
(i) Policy-based intervention: The National Health Policy 2017 has recommended 
increasing State health spending to more than 8% of their budget. 
(ii) Incentivizing states to spend more: The GoI adopted a conditionality framework under 
the National Health Mission. The framework follows Result Based Financing (RBF) 
where the States get more budgetary support if they perform well on the agreed 
indicators. 
(iii) Indian Public Health Standards (IPHS) 2022: These standards enable service provision 
of quality services through assured infrastructure, human resources, diagnostics, 
equipment, medicines etc. 
(iv) National Quality Assurance Standards (NQAS): With the commitment of GoI to 
achieve NQAS certification o f all facilities by Dec 2026, States are encouraged to 
expedite their development and adoption of standards to provide quality care to all. 
Other initiatives: -  
(v) It is agreed that higher budgetary allocations are essential to bolster  healthcare 
infrastructure and service delivery mechanisms across the country. 
(vi) Proposals for additional funding through the 16th Finance Commission are also being 
prepared by the MoHFW. 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
1.7.14 The Committee, in its 134 th Report, had highlighted the existing wide inter -State and 
intra-State disparity in healthcare infrastructure across the country. The Committee observes 
that States with poor financial resources and inefficient fiscal capacity face umpteen 
challenges in es tablishing a robust health infrastructure. The Committee, accordingly, 
reiterates its recommendation that the Union Government must persuade the remaining 

12 
 
State/UT Governments to achieve the prescribed budgetary health expenditure to 8% of State 
General Government Expenditure. 
(Para 2.3.14 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
 
1.7.15 The Government has undertaken the following initiatives to encourage the states to 
allocate a higher share of their budget to the health sector: -  
(i) The Department of Health and Family Welfare (DoHFW) has taken up with States to 
prioritize allocation to health sector and enhance their health budgets at least to 8% of 
total State budget. 
(ii) The GoI adopted a conditionality framework under the National Health Mission. The 
framework follows Result Based Financing ( RBF) where the States get more 
budgetary support if they perform well on the agreed indicators. 
(iii) Further, under National Health Mission, the Government has taken many steps 
towards universal health coverage, by supporting the State Gov ernments in providing 
accessible & affordable healthcare to people. The National Health Mission provides 
financial and technical support for improvement in health infrastructure, availability of 
adequate human resources to man health facilities, to improve  availability and 
accessibility to quality health care especially for the underserved and marginalized 
groups in rural areas. National Free Drugs Service Initiative and National Free

Dialysis Programme, various activities under Reproductive &Universal Immunization

1.8 Central Government Health Scheme (CGHS) 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
1.8.1 The Committee acknowledges the Government's efforts to digitize healthcare 
resources through the Healthcare Management Information System (HMIS), establish new 
Wellness Centres in tier -II cities, and promote Ayush Centres. However, the examination of 
budget allocation and utilization under Revenue Head reflects a significant gap between the 
RE allocation of Rs. 2245.82 crore for CGHS and the actual expenditure of Rs. 1842.51 crore, 
representing only 82% utilization as of February 7, 2025. The Committee, the refore, 
recommends that the Department conducts a thorough and immediate review of the CGHS 
expenditure process, specifically focusing on identifying and addressing the bottlenecks 

13 
 
causing the underutilization of allocated funds. By streamlining administra tive procedures, 
improving procurement processes, and ensuring timely disbursement of funds, the 
Department can ensure that the allocated resources are effectively used to enhance healthcare 
services for beneficiaries, thereby maintaining the intended cont inuity between budget 
allocation and service delivery. 
(Para 3.1.4 of the Report) 
 
Action Taken 
1.8.2 The utilization of budget up to February 2025 was less because various orders that 
were placed under GeM Portal were not delivered till that time and also  bills for various 
projects were not yet settled. By the end of FY 2024 -25 out of the allocated Revised 
Estimates (RE) of Rs. 2245.82 crore under Revenue head, expenditure was Rs. 2079.95 crores 
i.e. 92.61% at the end of financial year 2024-25. 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
1.8.3 In its 155 th Report, the Committee observed that, as of August 2023, 26% of the 340 
allopathic wellness centres (spread across 80 cities) were concentrated in the Delhi NCR 
region. Additionally, only six states (excluding Delhi NCR) have more than ten CGHS 
centres, while Arunachal Pradesh and the Union Territories of Ladakh, Andaman & Nicobar 
Islands, and Lakshadweep have none. The Committee noted that CGHS services are unevenly 
distributed, limiting accessibility in many regions. The Committee, therefore, wishes to 
highlight that numerous cities and towns with a significant population of Central Government 
employees, pensioners, and their dependents lack CGHS wellness centres. As a result, 
beneficiaries—particularly retirees —have to travel long distances for medical tr eatment, 
causing financial strain and other hardships. To address this, the Committee urges the 
Ministry to proactively advocate for new CGHS centres in underserved areas, particularly in 
suburban regions with a substantial number of serving and retired be neficiaries. The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry engage with the Ministry of Finance for speedy 
approval of new CGHS Wellness Centres. Moreover, the Committee suggests that the 
Government should consider revising existing norms or introducing new on es to facilitate the 
establishment of wellness centres in rural, hilly, remote, and Northeastern regions. 
 
(Para 3.1.5 of the Report) 
 
Action Taken 
1.8.4 Approximately 29% of CGHS Wellness Centres are concentrated in Delhi NCR (i.e. 
99 out of 342) because out of total registered 47,43,192 beneficiaries across India, majority 
lies in Delhi NCR (i.e. 20,38,394) which is approximately 43% of the total beneficiaries.  
Moreover, the proposal to open 22 new Wellness Centres is also approved by this Ministry 
and is currently under discussion with Ministry of Finance. 
 
 

14 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
1.8.5 The Committee wishes to express an observation regarding queue -management of 
patients seeking treatment in the CGHS dispensaries. It has been seen that in some of the 
private/public establishments, the queue of patients is managed through electronic token 
system displaying the queue number of the patient with corresponding token slip with the 
patient. The Committee would like the Department to establish electronic t oken system in all 
dispensaries of CGHS displaying the name and queue number of the patient to facilitate better 
queue management of patients in order to avoid high patient load at the doctors‘ cabin and 
give convenience to critical patients waiting for their turn.  
 
(Para 3.1.15 of the Report) 
 
Action Taken 
1.8.6 The Queue management system (electronic token system) is installed in some of the 
CGHS centres. Instructions has been passed on to all the CGHS units to get the queue 
management system (electronic  token system) installed at the earliest. Moreover, in the new 
mobile software application, CGHS has introduced Queue Display in my CGHS app for 
convenience of CGHS beneficiaries.

significant bottlenecks in the timely completion of AIIMS projects. As evident by the 
situations in Darbhanga, Madurai, and Rewari, these delays lead to cost escalations and hinder 
the delivery of essential healthcare services. 
 
(Para 3.6.9 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
 
1.13.7 For setting up of new AIIMS, a MoU with the respective Sate Government is signed 
by the Ministry wherein State Governmen t commits to provide encumbrance free site with 
four lane road connectivity, water and electricity supply adequate to cater to requirement of 
fully functional AIIMS.  Through such MoU, the State Government also commits to make 
adequate provision for disposal of STP, ETP waste and storm water drain beyond the limits of 
AIIMS campus. In this context, it is further to state that to set up an AIIMS, a very large land 
parcel (approx. 200 acres) is required. Given the scale of the land requirement invariably both 
natural hindrances, like tree cover, water body, undulating rock outcrops as well as manmade 
hindrances like nallah, pipelines, high tension lines, religious structures etc. are encountered. 
Availability of encumbrance free land and securing all statutory clearances is critical before 
start of any project of this scale. The Ministry, therefore, actively coordinates with the 
concerned State government authorities for timely resolution of a land related issue and early 
grant of statutory clearances.  Project r eview meetings are held by senior officers of the 
Ministry with the State Governments, Executing Agencies, etc. for addressing the site -related 
hindrances and expediting statutory clearances. 
 
1.13.8 The issues affecting progress of the projects are also t aken up with the State 
Government through letters from Secretary (HFW) to the Chief Secretary of the concerned 
State Government.  Such issues are also taken up the State Government through Project 
Monitoring Group (PMG) being chaired by Secretary (Coordinat ion) in the Cabinet 
Secretariat. Thus, all efforts at every level are taken for early resolution of land related issues 
and statutory clearances for timely implementation of the projects. 
 
 
 

24 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
1.13.9 The Committee takes into account various challenges confronting the Department that 
result into delay in implementation of projects and strategy measures chalked out to combat 
those challenges for effective utilization of funds earmarked for various institutions under 
PMSSY and ti mely completion of projects though the Committee understands that certain 
challenges are really a Himalayan barrier, the resolution of which is of course herculean task. 
Despite that the Committee believes that the Pro -Active Governance and Timely 
Implementation (PRAGATI) Portal, reviewed by the Prime Minister for expeditious 
resolution of various issues like land acquisition, utility shifting, contains the strength of 
mount-melting capacity with quick and effective decision -making for speedy resolution of all 
vexing issues/challenges. The Committee feels that the two components of PMSSY i.e. 
setting up of new AIIMS and up -gradation of Government Medical College/Institutions 
equipped with basic infrastructural facilities and equipment‘s contain capacity meas ures for 
correcting regional imbalance in the availability of affordable/reliable tertiary healthcare 
services and to augment facilities for quality medical education in the country. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends the Government for identifying more GMCs (beyond 
already identified 75 GMCs) and setting up of more AIIMS -like institutions as requests 
received by the Department from Karnataka, Kerala, Goa, Tripura, Sikkim, Mizoram, 
Manipur, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar (in Kosi region) and Maharashtra in the next  phase of PMSSY 
keeping in view the density of population, distance from existing AIIMS and regions from 
where patients inflow to AIIMS, New Delhi for treatment, increasing its workload and 
pushing up the waiting time even for critical patients. 
 
(Para 3.6.16 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
 
1.13.10  The present phase of PMSSY scheme is up to 2025 -26. The recommendations of the 
Committee would be duly considered during the process of extension of the scheme beyond 
2025-26. 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
1.13.11  The Committee recommends that the Ministry further strengthen its monitoring and 
coordination mechanisms for PMSSY projects, including both AIIMS and GMC upgrades. 
This should involve enhancing the effectiveness of Project Review Committees and ut ilizing 
the PRAGATI portal for timely issue resolution; conducting regular site visits by senior 
ministry officials to monitor progress and address challenges; improving coordination with 
state governments and executing agencies to ensure seamless implementation. The Committee 
considers that effective monitoring and coordination are essential for ensuring the timely 
completion of PMSSY projects and the efficient utilization of funds. Strengthening these 
mechanisms will help mitigate delays and improve overall project outcomes. 
(Para 3.6.18 of the Report) 
 

25 
 
Action Taken 
 
1.13.12  In order to ensure regular review of the projects and their timely completion and 
operationalization the following mechanisms have been put in place by the Ministry: - 
(i) In accordance with Rule 141 of General Financial rules, 2017, Project Review 
Committees under the chairpersonship of Joint Secretary (PMSSY) has been set for 
each ongoing project of setting up of AIIMS. 
(ii) Further, progress of projects is reviewed regularly in the Ministry  by Secretary HFW 
with the Executing Agencies and Procurement Support Agency to ensure timely 
completion of projects. 
(iii) The Project Monitoring Group (PMG), in the Cabinet Secretariat is another institutional 
mechanism for milestone -based monitoring of projec ts and expending issue resolution 
and regulatory bottlenecks in projects with investments upward of Rs. 500 crore. It 
ensures proactive monitoring of projects and in time resolution of issues with the State 
Government and other stakeholders to prevent dela ys and cost overruns. PMG has been 
helpful in fast -tracking of approvals, sectoral policy issues and removal of bottlenecks 
for expediting project commissioning.  
(iv) Pro-Active Governance and Timely Implementation (PRAGATI) is a multi -purpose 
and multi -modal platform for simultaneously monitoring and reviewing important 
programmes and projects of the Central Government as well as projects flagged by 
State Governments. Through PRAGATI the progress of AIIMS has been reviewed 
resulting in quick and effective deci sion making and swift resolution of issues with the 
State Governments. 
(v) Further for each project Third Party Quality Assurance (TPQA) Agencies including 
RITES/IIT Roorkee etc. have been appointed for independent periodical check on 
quality of construction, technical audit of the records, bills raised, testing of 
construction materials from approved independent Laboratories etc. If any deviations 
are found they are highlighted for rectification and the payment of consultancy to the 
Executing Agencies is made after duly considering the observations and compliance of 
the TQPA. 
1.13.13  In addition to the aforesaid institutional arrangements, the issues affecting progress 
of the projects are also taken up with the State Governments by the Secretary (HFW) with the  
chief Secretary of the concerned State Government. Need based directions are also given to 
Institutes/Executive Agencies/PSA for expeditious resolution of the issues between them.  
Further, site visits by senior officers of the Ministry are also undertaken  to comprehensively 
monitor all aspects of project execution, including civil construction, procurement & 
installation of equipment, accreditation, recruitment etc.

1.14 National AIDS and STD Control Programme (NACP) 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
1.14.1 The NACP program highlights the importance of integrated health campaigns among 
high-risk and bridge populations for early HIV identification. The Committee recommends 
the Department to increase the frequency and scope of integrated health campaigns  in select 
high-risk districts, focusing on early HIV detection and STI/RTI management; the 
strengthening of link worker schemes by providing enhanced training and resources, ensuring 
they can effectively reach and engage with high -risk populations; increase in the usage of the 
SOCH MIS system to better track the beneficiaries and services offered to them; and to 
complete and utilize the data from the round 2 of programmatic mapping and population size 
estimation to refine targeted interventions. 
(Para 3.7.7 of the Report) 
 
Action Taken

Health Campaigns have been made a significant part of Annual Action Plan 2025 -26 for all 
SACS to go for targeted campaign. Training of staff of SACS is being imparted periodically 
for improving usage of SOCH portal and beneficiary tracking. A dedicated IT Helpdesk is 
operational to resolve queries in SOCH usage. The national training of trainers for 
implementation of round 2 of programmatic mapping and population size estimation has been

partners and biological children of HIV -positive persons and Lost -to-follow-up tr acking

recommends the Department for institutionalizing and expanding index testing campaigns,

technology and community health workers to reconnect individuals with treatment services 
should be implemented to achieve the objective of the Programme.   
 
(Para 3.7.8 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
 
1.14.4 The recommendation of the Committee has been noted. NACP Programme continues 
to focus on index testing of sexual partners, biological children and spouses of HIV -positive

enabling environment for their long -term retention in care. For seamless real -time tracking of

1.14.5 The Committee takes into consideration the Intensify and Tailor IEC Campaigns and

NACP recognizes the importance of 360 -degree multimedia campaigns and community 
outreach with reducing stigma and discrimination as a key objective. The Committee,

providing targeted training and sensitiza tion programs for key stakeholders, including Self -
Help Groups, Anganwadi workers, ASHAs, etc. to promote understanding and reduce stigma.

1.14.6 The recommendation of the Committee has been noted. The targeted IEC plan has

television, radio, digital platforms, print and outdoor media. These ca mpaigns are designed to 
be inclusive, culturally sensitive and evidence -based, aiming to normalize discussions around 
HIV and encourage testing, treatment adherence and social acceptance of People Living with 
HIV (PLHIV).

Recommendations/Observations  
 
1.15.1 Given that the Rs. 355.07 crore has been allocated in BE 2025 -26 under the Global

Committee recommends expedited and efficient utilization of these funds with a focus on 
sustainable capacity building and infrastructure development. The Committee is of the view 
that immediate procurement of handheld X -rays for TB screening and strengthening of 
oxygen infrastructure should be prioritised. Simultaneously, integrated public health 
laboratory enhancements and staff training should also be accelerated. The Department should 
also create a plan for how these systems will be maintained and funded after the global fund 
grant expires.

strengthening of oxygen infrastructure, HITES has been selected as the procurement agency 
for procurement of booster pumps for oxygen cylinder refilling. The requirements from the

priorities and accoridingly the conceptualization, formation and creative finalization of the 
communication strategy is done. The target audience is also chosen  carefully and media 
strategy formulated accordingly. There is a collaboration mechanism for analyzing the 
feedback received which is used to fine tune and revive the communication channels 
including digital media and community outreach programmes. The inp uts of the 
Parliamentary Standing Committee on a comprehensive communication strategy have been 
duly noted.  
1.16.8 The co-ordination and collaboration among various programs is essential to build up 
synergy between various components of RMNCHA+ and enhanc e awareness, promote 
healthy behaviours, and improve service uptake. The continuum of care approach under 
RMNCHA+ strategy reinforces Government‘s commitment to safeguard the health and well -
being of the girl child—from pre conception to the antenatal period, through infancy and early 
childhood, adolescence and entire reproductive span to ensure a nurturing environment for 
improved health outcomes and gender equity. The PNDT Division, in collaboration with the 
Swastha Nagrik Abhiyan (SNA) Division, is formu lating a focused advocacy and IEC 
campaign to promote a positive behavioural shift in societal attitudes towards the girl child.  
The campaign includes targeted audio -visual content such as radio jingles and short video

bearing on the health and well -being of mother and c hild. The IEC activities under the FP

1.17 Establishment and Strengthening of NCDC Branches and Health Initiatives, 
Inter Sectoral Co -ordination for Preparation and Control of Zoonotic Diseases and 
Other Neglected Tropical Diseases, Surveillance of Viral Hepatitis, Anti Microbial 
Resistance 
Recommendations/Observations 
1.17.1 The Committee recommends a sustained and expanded focus on capacity building 
across all programs, with a particular emphasis on AMR containment and zoonotic disease 

32 
 
management. Leveraging the existing network of laboratories, training sites, and regional 
coordinators, the program should prioritize consistent, high -quality training delivery to 
strengthen expertise and ensure standardized practices. For AMR containment, the Committee 
recommends the expansion of laboratory networks must be accompanied by rigor ous, 
standardized training in bacteriology and HAI surveillance, ensuring quality -assured testing 
and evidence -based treatment. Similarly, for zoonotic disease management, the successful 
approach of multi-stakeholder consultations and hands-on training should be scaled up, with a 
strong focus on developing and implementing standardized training modules for medical 
officers and frontline workers. Additionally, the expansion of Regional Venom Centers and 
the establishment of Poison Information Centers for sna kebite management should be 
supported through comprehensive training programs. The Committee recommends for wider 
dissemination of IEC material for snakebite prevention and control, and protocols on initial 
management of snakebite especially in remote/rura l areas. The Committee also recommends 
for launching snakebite Helpline Project and training for medical officers on snakebite in all 
States/UTs. The Committee is of the opinion that a continuous investment in human resource 
development will be the key to ensure long-term success and sustainability of these critical 
public health initiatives. 
(Para 3.10.5 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
1.17.2 The recommendations of the committee are noted.  National Programme on AMR 
Containment was launched by MoHFW during the 12th five -year plan (2013 -14) and is 
coordinated by NCDC. Under the programme, National AMR Surveillance Network (NARS -
Net) involving State Medical College labs have been established an d are being expanded in 
phased manner. The programme has been expanded from 8 labs in 7 States/UTs in 2014 to 60 
Medical Colleges in 33 States/UTs till March 2025.   
1.17.3 For Standardized, consistent high-quality trainings, the following steps are taken: - 
(i) Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) have been developed for laboratory testing 
including internal quality controls. These SoPs are regularly updated and translated to 
training modules and used for trainings. These are also made available on NCDC 
website for countrywide dissemination. 
(ii) SoPs have also been developed for AMR data management and trainings are provided 
across the country at National and State level. 
(iii) National infection prevention and control guidelines for healthcare facilities including 
surveillance of Healthcare Associated Infections (HAIs) have been developed and 
translated to training modules. These have been used to conduct National training of 
trainers for all States and UTs. Trainings are being cascaded by States using the 
standardized modules.  
 
1.17.4 For AMR data surveillance, the following steps are taken: - 
(i) To ensure robust data surveillance protocols Standard Operating Procedures (SOP) 
have been developed and are used by all sites submitting data under the programme  

33 
 
(ii) To ensure data quality all labs submitting AMR data are participating in EQAS and are 
maintaining good scores and all AMR alert pathogens identified at programme sites are 
confirmed at AMR NRL established at NCDC.  
(iii) Annual AMR surveillance data is collated to develop annual National AMR 
Surveillance reports which are available on NCDC website and the data is also 
submitted to the Global AMR Surveillance System (GLASS) 
1.17.5 For Expansion of laboratory networks and standardized trainings in bacteriology and 
HAI, the following steps are taken: - 
(i) Capacity building on AMR containment is being expanded to additional Medical 
Colleges in States through State level AMR surveillance networks.  
(ii) Standardized HAI surveillance trainings for sites under National Programme  on AMR 
containment are being conducted in collaboration with AIIMS, New Delhi. 
1.17.6 National One Health Programme for Prevention & Control of Zoonoses(NOHP -PCZ) 
is being implemented since 12th FYP. Under the programme, the strengthened Regional 
Coordinators are mandated to conduct Multi -stakeholder sensitization trainings and hands -on 
training on Zoonotic Diseases.  In addition, the Programme Division (PD) routinely conducts 
consultation workshops and capacity-building sessions with relevant stakeholders to enhance 
Inter-sectoral collaboration and field -level preparedness.  Learning resource package (e -
learning module) for Medical Officers and frontline workers on zoonoses have been 
developed. Under snake bite prevention and control activities, trainings of  Medical Officers 
and health workers are being undertaken through National Health Mission. To enhance 
surveillance and reporting of snakebite cases and associated mortalities, the Ministry has 
communicated with all States/UTs to declare snakebite as a Noti fiable Disease under the 
State Public Health Act or other applicable legislation (Ref. D.O. No. 
ISCP/57155/06/DZDP/NCDC dated 27th November 2024) (Annexure -6). In line with the 
Committee‘s recommendations to raise community awareness and support health wor kers in 
rural and remote areas, the Ministry has developed a comprehensive suite of Information, 
Education, and Communication (IEC) materials and protocol on management of snakebite 
focused on prevention, first aid, and timely referral and the same has bee n shared with the 
States/UTs and made available on the NCDC website for wider dissemination. Snakebite 
Helpline number has been launched for five States/UTs (Andhra Pradesh, Puducherry, Delhi, 
Madhya Pradesh, and Assam). 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
1.17.7 The Committee recommends strengthening surveillance systems and data integration 
to enhance proactive disease management. Building on the AMR surveillance network and 
NOHP-PCZ integration into IHIP, programs should implement robust surveillance prot ocols 
and data management systems. For AMR, data collection and reporting to Global 
Antimicrobial Resistance and Use Surveillance System (GLASS) should be complemented by 
facility-based antibiograms to support evidence -based antibiotic treatment. For zoono tic 
diseases, implementing the Augmented Zoonotic Disease Surveillance (AZDS) proposal is 

34 
 
critical for strengthening pathogen surveillance in hotspot areas. Additionally, the Rabies 
Helpline expansion and snakebite case notifications should be integrated i nto a unified 
national surveillance platform for timely data analysis and informed decision -making. The 
Committee is of the view that establishing a Programme Management Unit (PMU) at NCDC 
will ensure coordinated surveillance, data quality, and rapid information dissemination. 
(Para 3.10.6 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
1.17.8 The recommendations of the committee are well noted. Under the national programme 
on AMR containment, the network Medical Colleges are being trained to utilize the AMR 
data locally for development of antibiograms to guide evidence based antibiotic treatment.  
NOHP-PCZ portal is onboarded on IHIP portal. Preliminary process of scanning data 
collection points related to One Health from different Ministries is undertaken by NCDC.  
Augmented Zoonotic Disease Surveillance (AZDS) is critical for identifying early warning 
signals for zoonotic diseases originating from wildlife and coordination with relevant 
institutions for the same has been initiated. 
Recommendations/Observations 
1.17.9 To ensure  the sustained effectiveness and responsiveness of the Integrated Disease 
Surveillance Programme (IDSP), the Committee recommends a targeted initiative to enhance 
data collection and analysis to arrive at a decision in specific time -frame in the Integrated  
Health Information Platform (IHIP). The Committee believes that it can be achieved through: 
(i) intensified training and capacity building for healthcare workers at all levels on IHIP data 
entry & analytics and utilization; (ii) streamlined data entry pro cesses and user interface 
improvements to minimize reporting burdens; (iii) regular monitoring and feedback 
mechanisms to identify and rectify reporting challenges; and (iv) leveraging the recently 
launched community reporting tool to supplement and valida te data from health facilities, 
thereby fostering a more comprehensive and robust surveillance system. 
(Para 3.10.12 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
1.17.10  The recommendation of the committee is well -taken for incorporating in the current 
& future training plans of IDSP and NCDC.  Before the transition of IDSP reporting, an 
intensive training exercise was undertaken at State, district, and sub -district levels to ensure 
that all the healthcare workers viz. ANMs, Medical Officers, Lab Personnel, and Private 
Practitioners are well -versed in reporting IDSP data on IHIP.  The routine trainings under 
IDSP are also geared towards enhancing the understanding of the trainees of all levels 
towards use of IHIP.  The trainings of other divisions of NCDC such as FETP, Sector  
Connect, and PHEDM are also aimed at capacitating the district surveillance units of IDSP in 
better understanding & utilization of surveillance data on IHIP.  Applications have been 
developed for all levels of users (Syndromic [S], Presumptive [P], and Lab oratory [L] form 
users) to report the data through hand -held devices such as mobile phones and tablets.  
Integrating IDSP -IHIP with Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission [ABDM] is in an advanced 
stage and once completed will enable data entry through the use of A BHA ID. IDSP-IHIP is 

35 
 
compliant with e -Governance standards of Government of India facilitating seamless 
exchange of data with other platforms through APIs.  The IDSP-IHIP is designed to generate 
auto-analysed reports to all levels of users serving as an eff ective feedback mechanism. 
Dashboards to indicate reporting performance, disease trends, outbreak investigation scores, 
and non -performing units are in -built in IDSP -IHIP. A daily SMS based feedback on 
reporting is sent to District, State, and Central Surv eillance Unit [CSU] level users. A weekly 
feedback bulletin identifying the better performing & lagging units is shared with the senior 
officials of the State health department.  A monthly feedback report is also shared with State 
Surveillance Units of IDSP  detailing their performance, identifying key challenges, and 
recommendations for improvement.  The community reporting tool was launched in January‘ 
2024 and efforts are on to increase the community awareness towards the use of this tool. 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
1.17.11 The Committee recommends building on existing collaborations with NACP and 
NFHS, it should implement a standardized framework for data collection and scientific 
analysis of data, integrating seroprevalence data across multiple disease areas to ensure 
continuity and clarity between surveillance of data and programmatic action. This expansion 
will optimize laboratory infrastructure, generate a comprehensive dataset essential for 
informed policymaking, targeted interventions, and effective disease control. 
(Para 3.10.14 of the Report) 
Action Taken 
1.17.12 The program is already integrating with the population level surveys/programs for 
carrying out surveillance of chronic viral hepatitis as also recommended by the Committee . 
The program is also implementing the same through standardized framework for data 
collection and scientific analysis of data. This is to ensure optimal utilization for laboratory 
infrastructure and generate comprehensive data set essential for program pl anning and 
prioritizing interventions: -

after the State/UT submits 60% utilization of the fund released under 1st tranche. Funds in FY 
2024-25 have been released only to those states who have submitted UC up to 2022 -23.

25, 6.32 lakhs food handlers have been trained in 11900 trai nings which include 53660 Street 
Food Handlers and 2500 Food Safety Officers have been trained in 27 trainings. 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
1.22.4 The Committee notes that FSSAI is actively deploying Mobile Food Testing 
Laboratories (MFTLs) to enhance on-the-spot food testing and awareness, and while progress 
is made in this connection, achieving the target of one MFTL/FSW per district by 2026 is

directly with state governments to identify and address specific barriers to FSW deployment.

(Para 3.17.13 of the Report)

1.32 Strengthening of State Drug Regulatory System 
Recommendations/Observations 
1.32.1 The Committee recommends the urgent implementation of a proactive, structured 
engagement strategy with all States and Union Territories well in advance of each fiscal year's

(SSDRS) scheme. This strategy  should focus on providing clear guidelines, technical 
assistance, and regular communication to ensure that States understand the SSDRS scheme's 
requirements, and to assist States in developing comprehensive, eligible proposals. This 
process should also in volve regular monitoring of fund utilization by states, providing early 
feedback and support to address any bottlenecks hindering the 75% utilization requirement.

to insufficient or non -compliant state proposals, actively facilitating state participation will 
mitigate the risk of underutilization and ensure the crucial strengthening of drug regulatory 
systems, particularly as the scheme's extension is being considere d. Specifically, the 
department should establish a dedicated team to conduct workshops, provide templates for 
proposals, and track state progress, thereby ensuring that the allocated funds are effectively 
utilized to improve drug quality and accessibility across the nation. 
(Para 4.3.3 of the Report) 
Action Taken

physical progress and resolving outstanding issues, regular state visits are conducted. Periodic 
review meetings are also held with State Drug Controllers/State Health Administration for

funds to upgrade their infrastructure. To further improve capacity of the St ates, CDSCO is

1.32.3 To ensure a consistently high standard of drug regulation across India, mirroring the 
success achieved in vaccine regulation, the Committee recommends the immediate 
implementation of a comprehensive, nationwide, and phased "Medicines Regulatory Maturity 
Enhancement Program." This program should be modelled after the WHO NRA re -
benchmarking process used for vaccines, involving a detailed scientific review of state and 
union territory drug regulatory systems against the WHO Global Benchmarking Tool. It 
should include: i) mandatory, challenging -mode state audits conducted by a central team of

international and national experts, focusing on the quality, safety, and efficac y of medicines, 
APIs, and formulations; ii) targeted regulatory capacity building and infrastructure upgrades 
in states/UTs, informed by the audit findings and stakeholder consultations; iii) the

levels, with progressive implementation based on the turnover of the manufacturers as done 
with GMP revisions; iv) continuous professional development and training for state drug 
regulatory officials, leveraging existing CDS CO training programs and expanding to

Licensing System (ONDLS) with the benchmarking process to track and monitor progress,

completion of the project.

1.36 Ayushman Bharat-Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (AB-PMJAY) 
Recommendations/Observations 
1.36.1 The Committee is of the opinion that the Ayushman Bharat -Pradhan Mantri Jan 
Arogya Yojana (AB -PMJAY) is a pivotal and visionary health initiative aiming to provide 
financial protection and healthcare access to a large number of India's vulnerable po pulation. 

71 
 
While the scheme has seen substantial growth in terms of state participation, card creation, 
and hospital admissions, several key areas require attention like Budget Utilization and State 
Participation. The Committee observes a persistent trend o f underutilization of allocated 
funds, particularly in the previous year as well as in the current financial year. The Committee 
observes that, in the FY 2023 -24, an amount of Rs. 7200.00 crore was allocated as BE 2023 -
24 which was reduced to Rs. 6800.00 c rore at RE stage, however, the actual expenditure was 
Rs. 6670.47 crore.  In the FY 2024 -25, Rs. 7300.00 crores was made in BE 2024 -25 which 
was revised to Rs. 7605.54 crores at RE 2024 -25, however, the actual expenditure was to the 
tune of Rs. 5034.03 Cro res till 09.01.2025. In FY 2025 -26, the enhanced amount of Rs. 9406 
crore has been allocated as BE 2025 -26.  This indicates potential inefficiencies in fund 
disbursement or implementation bottlenecks. The Committee, therefore, recommends a 
thorough review of the fund release mechanisms to states/UTs. This review should focus on 
identifying and eliminating bottlenecks that contribute to underutilization. Specifically, the 
Department should implement a system of proactive monitoring of fund utilization by sta tes, 
coupled with targeted support to address any implementation challenges. This support could 
include technical assistance, capacity building, and simplified reporting procedures. 
Furthermore, the committee suggests that the release of funds be linked to  the performance of 
states in terms of card creation, hospital admissions, and beneficiary feedback, ensuring that 
funds are directed to areas of greatest need and impact. The Department should also create 
and publish a clear and concise guideline for stat es, explaining the process of fund requests, 
and the expected timelines. To ensure that the allocation of fund to the tune of Rs. 9406.00 
crore in BE 2025 -26 is utilized, a quarterly review system may be set up to avoid any delays 
in release of fund to States/UTs. 
(Para 4.8.7 of the Report) 
Action Taken

over the past few years, reflecting the scheme‘s expanding implementation and increasing 
utilization across the country. In alignment with this growth, the total funds released to States 
and Union Territories have also shown a steady increase. In the financial year 2024 -25, Rs. 
6,881.65 crore representing 90% of the allocated budget was utilized, reflecting a slight 
increase from the Rs. 6,554.15 crore spent in financial year 2023 –24. Notably, in addition to 
the regular Implementation and administration funds, separate funds are now also being 
released for ASHA, AWW, and AWH workers, as well as under the Vay Vandana Scheme for 
the treatment of senior citizens aged 70 years and above. These allocations represent 
additional support measures aimed at enhancing outreach and ensuring inclusive healthcare 
access.  Further, a comprehensive review of the fund release mechanisms is be ing initiated to 
identify and address bottlenecks at both central and state levels.
